title: Drones from Iraq attack and set pipeline on fire in Saudi Arabia
author: Ricardo Figueira
content:
The East–West pipeline is crucial for shipping Saudi oil to the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. This latest incident risks driving oil and fuel prices even higher.
An oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia, deemed "essential" for bypassing the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, has been shut down after a fire that, according to the authorities, followed a drone attack launched from Iraq.
The East-West pipeline links Abqaiq, near the Persian Gulf, to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, and is used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for transporting Saudi oil to the Red Sea. A statement from the Saudi foreign ministry referred to a fire near Medina, said to have caused "human and material damage".
A government official in Riyadh had already told the media that people had been injured in the drone attack and the subsequent blaze. The same official said the pipeline had been shut down as a precaution.
The Iraqi government acknowledged that the attack was launched from its territory and announced that it had dismissed the commander of Maysan province in the south of the country as a consequence.
Saudi Arabia frequently accuses Iran-linked armed groups based in neighbouring Iraq of targeting its oil facilities with drones.
The Gulf Cooperation Council, which brings together six countries in the region, issued a statement expressing concern and describing the incident as "a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia".
The government in Riyadh said it would not respond to the attack for the time being, stating that it intended "not to react at this stage and to support the efforts of the Iraqi government to prevent attacks launched from its territory against the Saudi kingdom and neighbouring countries".
This incident comes just a day after the Houthi rebels in Yemen, backed by Iran, took control of an island of strategic importance in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a location of crucial importance for global oil trade. It marks an escalation in the Houthis' attempts to block Saudi Arabia's trade; Riyadh backs Yemen's government. According to the rebels, navigation in the strait was "safe for everyone except the Saudis".
This latest attack adds another layer to the series of incidents in the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February, which has pushed oil and fuel prices to new record highs. The price of a barrel of oil climbed above 100 dollars on Friday, with fuel prices hitting fresh records.
summary: An oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia was shut down following a fire caused by a drone attack launched from Iraq, resulting in injuries and material damage. The incident risks driving global oil and fuel prices even higher as it bypasses the blocked Strait of Hormuz. In response, the Iraqi government dismissed a regional commander, while Saudi Arabia stated it would temporarily refrain from retaliating to support Iraqi prevention efforts.
key_points: A drone attack launched from Iraq caused a fire and injuries at an essential Saudi oil pipeline, leading to its precautionary shutdown.
The Iraqi government dismissed the commander of Maysan province after acknowledging the attack originated from its territory.
Saudi Arabia announced it will not immediately respond to give the Iraqi government time to prevent future attacks.
The incident coincides with rising oil and fuel prices exceeding 100 dollars per barrel amid broader regional conflicts.

title: Donald Trump says he would ‘love’ to see united Ireland
author: Rory Carroll
content:
Donald Trump has said he would “love” to see a united Ireland and that it “may as well happen now”.
The US president appeared to endorse the push for constitutional change on the island at the start of a two-day visit to Ireland on Saturday. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and Northern Ireland’s unionist leaders.
“I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told reporters at joint press conference with the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, in Dublin. “I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.”
The unification of Northern Ireland with the republic of Ireland would be “fantastic”, Trump said. “The UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”
![Micheál Martin reaches to shake Donald Trump’s hand in front of soldiers standing at attention](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6fd6266b7b959d335faf4123846b492b9aeda957/0_0_3936_2632/master/3936.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The intervention jolted his hosts and came two weeks after Andy Burnham said a referendum on unification was “off the table”, which angered Sinn Féin and other Irish nationalists.
Speaking later on Saturday, Trump acknowledged that his comments on unification, made in response to a reporter’s question, would be controversial. “No matter what you say or how you say it, there’s no good answer,” he said. “I gave a nice answer, I think. We’ll worry about it tomorrow.” Unification, he added, would be a “very cool thing”.
A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister still believed there was not the required support for unification to trigger a referendum, as set out in the Good Friday agreement.
Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, said Northern Ireland’s constitutional future would be decided by its people, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.
“Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people. I am confident Northern Ireland will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers. As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish republic.”
Colum Eastwood, an MP and former leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP), and frequent critic of Trump, posted a clip of the president’s remarks on social media and wrote: “Always liked him.”
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: “President Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state. This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension.”
![People hold a banner saying ‘No welcome for Trump: genocide enabler, climate denier, Epstein class, racist, warmonger’](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1df5ba43a6618cdaacc650d70241559a5c7b2f09/0_0_5500_3659/master/5500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Trump’s comments strayed from predecessors who sought to keep the White House neutral on Ireland’s constitutional future, but the off-the-cuff nature of the remarks suggested there was no change in US policy.
Trump’s unofficial visit is centred on golf – he flew on Saturday afternoon to his resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open – but started with a courtesy call in Dublin to Áras an Uachtaráin, the official residence and workplace of the Irish president, Catherine Connolly.
Before her election to the ceremonial post last year, Connolly called Trump a bully and criticised his policies in Gaza and Iran. Their brief encounter, behind closed doors, appeared to go smoothly despite a coded critique of White House policies.
after newsletter promotion
![Donald Trump and Catherine Connolly sit in chairs beside a table laden with tea cups and drinks](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/62a40c0ec171f6fb21cf12de1e93debbe24d00bb/0_0_2862_2122/master/2862.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Connolly said in a statement afterwards that she “conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted” and stressed the importance of the United Nations – an organisation Trump has disparaged. Trump said they had a wide-ranging discussion, including about energy and water, and that Connolly was “terrific”.
Trump held a separate meeting with Martin at the Phoenix Park, where he told the press that Iran would seek peace after the US midterm elections and repeated his claim that his war had prevented Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Asked about protests against his visit – a large crowd was expected in central Dublin, 5 miles away, as well as at Doonbeg – the president said he had not seen any protests.
![Spectators watch as Air Force One flies Trump over the Irish Open in Doonbeg, County Clare.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/538ac604361d00504bad958cad643dc06e8d1858/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Addressing guests as at the US ambassador’s residence, Trump assailed US Democrats as extremists and criticised Europe’s approach to immigration.
He lauded US-Irish relations but reiterated a complaint about the American pharma giants in Ireland. “You took all our medical companies, we’ve got to get a couple of them back. You fleeced us but that’s OK. There’s a lot of room to go around and our relationship with you is fantastic.”
As he left Dublin a crowd at the Garden of Remembrance waved banners and chanted: “Donald Trump, can you hear? We don’t want you here.”
Trump is expected to stay overnight in Doonbeg and present the Irish Open trophy before returning to Washington on Sunday.
summary: During a visit to Ireland, US President Donald Trump stated that he would love to see a united Ireland and suggested it may as well happen now. His remarks drew swift rebuked from the UK government and Northern Ireland's unionist leaders, while diverging from the historical neutrality of previous US administrations. Trump's trip also included meetings with Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Irish President Catherine Connolly, alongside protests against his visit.
key_points: Donald Trump stated at a press conference in Dublin that he would love to see a united Ireland.
The UK government and Northern Ireland's DUP leader criticized the comments as unhelpful and emphasized that Northern Ireland's future will be decided by its own people.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called Trump's remarks loose talk that creates unnecessary tension.
Trump also met with Irish President Catherine Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin during his visit centered around a trip to his Doonbeg golf resort.

title: Trump says he would ‘love’ to see unified Ireland and ‘it may as well happen now’ as he visits Dublin – live
author: Taz Ali
content:
Trump has weighed in on the question of Irish unity, saying he would “love to see it unified” and predicting that a united Ireland is “going to happen eventually”.
He suggested it “may as well happen now” and appeared to cast Micheál Martin as the person to help make it happen.
He said:
Well, I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you I’d love to see it unified.
I have friends on both sides, great people. They’re Irish people. How can they be bad, right?
I’d love to see it unified. I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually.
You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
We’re talking about it and you got the right man over here to get it moving.
But, yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing.
Now the UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”
Donald Trump during a meeting with Micheal Martin at Farmleigh House. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA
Trump has joked about his earlier remarks about Ireland unity (see post at 11:11).
During his speech at Deerfield, he said there was “no good answer” to the unification question, adding: “No matter what you say, no matter how well you say it.”
He then reiterated his view that unification “would be cool”.
Donald Trump delivers remarks at Deerfield. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters
The Irish Times reports that a spokesperson for Micheál Martin was asked if Donald’s Trump’s comments about a unified Ireland would have any impact on government policy.
They said: “No, our Good Friday agreement and programme for government commitments remain.”
Trump has also been asked about the Falkland Islands. In his meandering response, he questioned whether Britain would be willing to travel such a distance to defend the islands and said he could be called upon to help resolve the row between the UK and Argentina.
Donald Trump speaks to reporters during a meeting with Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House, Dublin. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA
Well, the Falkland Islands is very interesting because here we go again.
I remember as a young boy, a pretty young boy anyway, but the Falkland Islands, and I think it was a different country at that time, the UK a little bit, but they went in and they took it over.
I’m not sure they’re doing that. They have a little problem with immigration.
They have a little problem with energy and then have some other problems they have to take care of.
So, I don’t know. You know, I don’t know if they’re going to be willing to travel that far.
That is very far away. You’re talking about weeks by boat. I don’t know.
I’m sure I’ll be called into that potential disaster, but if they do, I’ll probably be able to settle, settle it out.
But right now, you have two countries that are not happy concerning the Falklands.”
Trump said the conflict in Gaza was all but over after he “put out the fires”, and that Iran was two weeks away from obtaining a nuclear weapon when the US and Israel began the war in February.
“If they had it they would have blown up Israel, they would have blown up the Middle East,” he said, adding that Europe would have been a target too.
Trump has weighed in on the question of Irish unity, saying he would “love to see it unified” and predicting that a united Ireland is “going to happen eventually”.
He suggested it “may as well happen now” and appeared to cast Micheál Martin as the person to help make it happen.
He said:
Well, I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you I’d love to see it unified.
I have friends on both sides, great people. They’re Irish people. How can they be bad, right?
I’d love to see it unified. I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually.
You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
We’re talking about it and you got the right man over here to get it moving.
But, yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing.
Now the UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”
Donald Trump during a meeting with Micheal Martin at Farmleigh House. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA
Trump and Martin are now speaking to reporters at the Farmleigh estate.
Commenting on the Saudi pipeline attack, Trump said he believed Iran may have been responsible for the drone strike. “I think they are, probably they are.”
Micheál Martin and Donald Trump speak to reporters at Farmleigh House in Dublin. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
Saudi authorities said drones launched from Iraq had forced the temporary closure of a key oil export route, which has become increasingly important as an alternative to the strait of Hormuz.
The East-West pipeline runs from Abqaiq, near the Gulf, to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Riyadh has stepped up its use of the pipeline since the start of the Middle East war as the route allows Saudi oil to reach global markets without passing through the Hormuz strait, which has been effectively closed by Iran.
Trump: Iran war will end after US midterm elections
Trump said he believed the war with Iran will end after US midterm elections in November and that oil prices will tumble once it does, Reuters reports.
“I think very soon. I think it’ll be probably right after the mid-terms. They’re trying to hold out as long as they can to complicate the election. But I think people are wise to it,” he told reporters in Dublin.
“When that happens, oil prices will come tumbling down.”
summary: During a visit to Dublin, Donald Trump expressed his support for a unified Ireland, suggesting that the unification should happen now and indicating that Micheál Martin could help make it happen. An Irish government spokesperson stated that Trump's remarks would not impact current government policy, reaffirming commitments to the Good Friday agreement. Trump also discussed international topics, including the Falkland Islands, the conflict with Iran, and oil prices.
key_points: Trump stated he would love to see a united Ireland and suggested it may as well happen now.
A spokesperson for Micheál Martin confirmed that Trump's comments would not alter Irish government policy regarding the Good Friday agreement.
Trump questioned whether the UK would travel far to defend the Falkland Islands and offered to help resolve the dispute.
Trump commented on global conflicts and predicted that the war with Iran would end after US midterm elections.

title: Saudi Arabia shuts key oil pipeline after drone attack launched from Iraq
author: Tiffanie Turnbull
content:
![Satellite images show blackened areas where the East-West pipeline was hit](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/960/cpsprodpb/1ea8/live/13141950-ae5a-11f1-96a4-f736214d52e1.jpg)
Satellite images show sites where the East-West pipeline was hit
- Published
Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was attacked by drones launched from Iraq, as conflict in the Middle East widens.
Iraq said it had fired a military commander and launched an investigation after admitting the drone attack on its neighbour's East-West pipeline had originated in one of its provinces bordering Iran.
The 1,200km (745 mile) pipeline has helped Saudi Arabia - the world's largest crude oil exporter - bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
The incident comes amid a major advance by the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, putting more pressure on global oil shipping routes as the US-Iran war stretches into its seventh month.
Riyadh on Friday said it had shut the pipeline as a precaution, as satellite images of scorched ground and smoke near the site emerged.
The foreign ministry said the attack resulted in some injuries and damage, which was still being assessed.
The pipeline has been moving 4% to 5% of global oil supply, news agency Reuters has reported, citing ship tracking companies and analysts.
Saudi Arabia has chosen not to retaliate at this stage, its foreign ministry says, following a call from Iraq's prime minister.
It said the kingdom would "support the efforts of the Iraqi government" to "prevent attacks" launched from the country against neighbouring states.
"The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia affirms that it reserves its right to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and security, protect its facilities, and ensure the safety of its citizens and residents," the statement added.
The Iraqi prime minister's office in its own statement said the operations commander in the Maysan governorate - a province which borders Iran - had been removed from his post following confirmation the drone attack had been launched from that region.
How Houthi gains in Yemen could drive up oil prices
The Gulf Co-operation Council â made up of representatives from the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Oman, Qatar and Kuwait â also issued a missive condemning the attack.
"This attack represents a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its territorial integrity, and its vital installations, as well as a flagrant violation of the principles of international law," secretary general Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi.
This week, a lightning advance in Yemen has also seen Houthi militants seize control of much of the country's coastline, sources say.
The group claims it has control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, though it says maritime navigation is "safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels".
The developments have squeezed both sides of the Arabian Peninsula, pushing crude oil prices to over $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
  - Published10 hours ago
 ![Houthi fighters in uniforms march with raised fists during mobilisation drive in Sana'a, Yemen, 10 September 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/82b5/live/066e1ff0-ae16-11f1-aa28-67f8824e7b72.jpg)
summary: Saudi Arabia has shut down its critical East-West oil pipeline following a drone attack launched from Iraqi territory. Iraq admitted the attack originated from a province bordering Iran and subsequently launched an investigation while firing a local military commander. The incident, alongside Houthi advances in Yemen, has put pressure on global shipping routes and pushed crude oil prices above $100 a barrel.
key_points: Saudi Arabia closed its 1,200km East-West oil pipeline as a precaution after a drone attack.
Iraq confirmed the drones were launched from its Maysan governorate and removed a military commander from the post.
The pipeline transports 4% to 5% of the global oil supply and helps Saudi Arabia bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
The attack, combined with Houthi advances in Yemen, pushed crude oil prices past $100 a barrel.
Saudi Arabia has chosen not to retaliate at this stage following a call from Iraq's prime minister.

title: How US leaders remembered the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![US President Donald Trump and US First Lady Melania Trump bow their heads during the 25th anniversary commemoration of the September 11, 2001 attacks at the Pentagon in Washington, DC, on September 11, 2026. (Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/afp_6aa437952271-1789147029.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
A quarter-century after the attacks on September 11, 2001, officials across the United States have taken part in tributes and memorials to honour the 2,977 victims and those who risked their lives as part of the rescue efforts.
The incident is considered the deadliest “terrorist” attack in US history.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trial for 9/11 accused, including Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, set for June 2028
- list 2 of 3Mamdani releases records on toxic air in New York after 9/11 attacks
- list 3 of 3Trump pays tribute to the victims of 9/11 at Pentagon ceremony
Four planes were hijacked. Two crashed into the World Trade Center, causing its Twin Towers to collapse. A third struck the Pentagon outside Washington, DC. And the fourth plummeted into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers and crew rose against their attackers.
Through social media messages, public speeches and appearances at ceremonies, US leaders on Friday took different approaches to remembering the lives of the thousands who perished on the fateful day.
Here’s what they said:
US President Donald Trump
![US President Donald Trump speaks at the 25th anniversary commemoration of the September 11, 2001 attacks at the Pentagon in Washington, DC, on September 11, 2026. (Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/afp_6aa435852a37-1789146501.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
US President Donald Trump chose to stay in Washington, DC, to observe the 25th anniversary.
During the attacks, 184 people died near the capital when American Airlines Flight 77 struck the Pentagon, the headquarters of the US military.
Trump opted not to attend a Friday ceremony at the World Trade Center site in New York, where all his living presidential predecessors were in attendance.
His vice president, JD Vance, travelled to New York instead. The ceremony at the World Trade Center has a policy of not allowing political speeches.
In his remarks at the Pentagon, Trump described what happened as “true evil”. He also paid tribute to those who died in the attacks.
“We will honour their lives, we will cherish their beautiful memories, and we will protect this country and its freedoms for every future generation,” Trump said.
The president also praised US troops as he appeared to link the 9/11 attacks with his administration’s war against Iran.
“We will never, ever forget. That’s why we fight today. We don’t have a choice. There can only be victory,” Trump said.
“We salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror – the Islamic Republic of Iran – will never, ever have a nuclear weapon,” he later added.
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth
![US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks during the 25th anniversary commemoration of the September 11, 2001 attacks at the Pentagon in Washington, DC, on September 11, 2026. (Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/afp_6aa434a13c51-1789146273.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C514&quality=80)
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also spoke at the Pentagon, delivering his remarks shortly before Trump’s.
He warned the audience to practice “eternal vigilance” against what he called continued threats.
“There are still enemies who hate us. Every day, enemies plot to curb our power and kill our citizens, including from Islamic terrorists abroad and at home,” he said.
He proceeded to seemingly use the 9/11 attacks as justification for the US-Israeli war against Iran, which started on February 28.
“Over the past six months, we have laid waste to the world’s most prolific state sponsor of terrorism,” Hegseth said, referring to Iran. “Our warriors have fought an Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century, that cheered on 9/11.”
He went on to claim that the US military has destroyed Iran’s defences and that the US controls the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for international trade.
Iran has stopped commercial traffic through the strait since the start of the war.
“We’re still sending terrorists where they belong, to hell, and tankers to the bottom of the ocean where they belong,” Hegseth said. “And we’re ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. The economic pressure tightens every day. We control the strait. We will finish this fight.”
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani
![(L/R) Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani attend the 25th anniversary commemoration of the September 11, 2001 attacks at the National September 11 Memorial in New York on September 11, 2026. (Photo by Barry Williams / POOL / AFP)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/afp_6aa4350e414d-1789146382.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani attended the New York memorial service, alongside the city’s former mayor, Rudy Giuliani, who led the city through the attacks.
Before the event started, Giuliani shook hands with the mayor, despite previously calling on Mamdani not to attend the event.
Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, had recently come under fire from some conservative politicians and victims’ family members who said his presence at the memorial would offend them.
A Change.org petition garnered more than 100,000 signatures from those who wished to express concern about Mamdani’s participation.
Like all politicians attending the service at the National September 11 Memorial, Mamdani was not permitted to speak.
Instead, the mayor released a video on social media remembering those who were killed and challenging the public to honour their memory by doing good works.
“Twenty-five years later, we have a sacred obligation to those who were stolen from us. To care for one another as they cared for strangers. To live lives worthy of the sacrifices they made. And to build a city worthy of their courage. A city where we run toward one another,” Mamdani said.
“That is how we’ll remember.”
On Tuesday, Mamdani also released a trove of previously undisclosed documents suggesting city officials tried to downplay – or even mislead – first residents about the dangerous air quality following the attacks.
US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed
![WATERFORD, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 3: Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed answers questions from attendees during a town hall event, part of a series of events across Michigan focused on hearing from voters, on September 3, 2026 at the Oakland Expo Center in Waterford, Michigan. El-Sayed is scheduled to hold additional town halls throughout September and early October in Lansing, Grand Rapids, Detroit, Flint and Macomb. Emily Elconin/Getty Images/AFP (Photo by Emily Elconin / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/afp_6aa43447e2ea-1789146183.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C514&quality=80)
Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed took to the social media platform X to honour the lives lost during what he described as a “cruel act of terror”.
El-Sayed is locked in a tight midterm race in Michigan against his Republican opponent, former US Representative Mike Rogers.
Michigan’s open Senate seat is considered a must-win seat for Democrats, if they hope to take back control of the US Senate.
Rogers has sought to create controversy over El-Sayed’s past comments about the September 11 attacks. He has pointed to audio of El-Sayed reportedly saying, “9/11 scarred our country in profound ways, but what we did after 9/11 scarred millions of other people.”
During the Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, on Thursday, Rogers blasted El-Sayed, who is Muslim, for being sympathetic to terrorists. He also sought to highlight El-Sayed’s links to left-wing internet commentator Hasan Piker.
“I never imagined that, 25 years after 9/11, I would be running against somebody who campaigns with Hasan Piker, who thinks America deserved it,” Rogers said. “Yep, but here we are.”
On Friday, however, El-Sayed used his social media post to push back against Rogers’s attacks.
“Nothing can justify the murder of innocent civilians. Nothing,” El-Sayed wrote.
He also called on Americans to help build a country that was “more inclusive, more empowering, more just” in tribute to the lives lost.
“They didn’t just attack America that day. They attacked the idea of America,” El-Sayed said of the 19 al-Qaeda hijackers who participated in the attacks.
“The notion of a nation brought together by ideals where it doesn’t matter how you pray or if you pray at all. A place where freedom and commitment to justice bind us, even if at times we struggle to fully realise it.”
summary: US leaders marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks through memorials, speeches, and social media messages honoring the victims. President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke at a Pentagon ceremony where they also linked the anniversary to the ongoing conflict with Iran. Meanwhile, officials including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed participated in tributes and addressed the legacy of the tragedy amidst political controversies.
key_points: President Donald Trump spoke at the Pentagon during the 25th-anniversary commemorations, describing the 9/11 attacks as true evil and praising US troops.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth warned of continued threats and linked the 9/11 anniversary to the US-Israeli war against Iran.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani attended the World Trade Center memorial and released a video honoring victims, following prior criticism over his attendance.
Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed used social media to honor the victims of 9/11 and pushed back against attacks from his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.

title: US mourns on 25th anniversary of 9/11 – in pictures
author: Julius Constantine Motal
content:
US mourns on 25th anniversary of 9/11 – in pictures
Thousands gather in New York City and across the country to honor the memory of the victims of the 11 September 2001 attacks
Mourners listen to the US national anthem at the 9/11 memorial in New York City, on the 25th anniversary of the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks. Photograph: Adam Gray/AP
The September 11 Memorial in Lower Manhattan before a ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacksPhotograph: Dave Sanders/The New York Times via AP
People place flowers and notes on 2,753 empty chairs in Bryant Park, representing the lives lost at the World Trade CenterPhotograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images
A US flag is unfurled at the Pentagon at a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the attack on the site in Virginia, close to Washington DCPhotograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters
A National Park Service ranger places a wreath at the wall of names at the Flight 93 National Memorial near Shanksville, PennsylvaniaPhotograph: Gene J Puskar/AP
Members of the military look on as two columns appear on the floor inside the Oculus transportation hub at the World Trade CenterPhotograph: Heather Khalifa/AP

summary: Thousands of people gathered across the United States to honor the victims on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks. Commemorative events and ceremonies took place at major memorial sites, including New York City, the Pentagon, and Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Mourners placed flowers, notes, and wreaths to remember those who lost their lives.
key_points: The US marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks.
Thousands gathered in New York City and nationwide to honor the victims.
Commemorative ceremonies were held at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and the Flight 93 National Memorial.
Mourners placed flowers, notes, and wreaths at various memorial locations.

title: 'Never, ever forget' - America marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
author: Grace Eliza Goodwin; Bernd Debusman Jr; Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu; Nadine Yousif
content:
Watch: "We'll never ever forget" - Americans remember 9/11 at 25th anniversary
- Published
Twenty-five years after 9/11, US presidents past and present have commemorated the lives lost when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.
President Donald Trump led a Pentagon ceremony, while US Vice-President JD Vance attended a memorial at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, along with all four living former US presidents and first ladies.
Moments of silence were held to mark the timings of the attacks and the names of nearly 3,000 people who died were read out.
Commemorations were also held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where Flight 93 crashed after passengers fought back against the hijackers.
![Fire Department of New York (FDNY) firefighters pay their respects at the memorial before a ceremony to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the September 11th terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/996/cpsprodpb/d641/live/64614ef0-ae0e-11f1-b502-e5cdfe1c097c.jpg)
![Former US presidents and first ladies stand under a tent with their hands on their chest. Also in frame is current vice president JD Vance and former New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/eb6a/live/dc7ebed0-adf6-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
All living former US presidents attended a memorial in New York City
![U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick pauses at the memorial ahead of a ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks on the World Trade Center at the National 9/11 Memorial & Museum in New York.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/9681/live/9b0258c0-adee-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick lost his brother Gary and several colleagues in the attack
![US President Donald Trump speaks at the 25th anniversary commemoration of the September 11, 2001 attacks at the Pentagon.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/1dbb/live/02f61330-adf5-11f1-ad53-0d91a06f3150.jpg)
President Trump spoke at the Pentagon
George W Bush, who was president at the time of the attacks, was joined by former Presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama and Bill Clinton at Friday's ceremony.
At the Pentagon, President Trump attended a commemoration alongside cabinet secretaries and Condoleezza Rice, who was US secretary of state on 9/11.
"Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago," Trump said. "We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today."
He sought to link the "war on terror" that followed 9/11, which sparked years of US involvement in Middle East wars, with his current conflict in Iran.
Trump told the crowd that the Islamic Republic "will never, ever have a nuclear weapon".
![Paula Jacobs, sister of Flight 93 victim Louis J. Nacke II and cousin Mary White Henderson, lean on the Wall of Names, at the Flight 93 National Memorial.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/8613/live/2ab7d600-ae00-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
The Wall of Names at Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania
Janice Brooks had only moved to New York a couple of weeks before 9/11 to begin what she calls "the biggest adventure", working for a company on the 84th floor of the South Tower of the World Trade Center.
She told the BBC she was in the office when the first plane hit the North Tower. While she was evacuating, the second plane hit with an "almighty thud".
Brooks said she heard "one of those horror film screams" as a woman was hit by debris. She looked up and saw a "big gaping hole" where her office should have been.
Every year on 11 September, bells ring to commemorate the exact time that each of the four planes crashed, and the exact time the Twin Towers fell.
Each of the six bells is followed by a moment of silence.
This year, a seventh bell was rung to commemorate the thousands who died from diseases including cancer after the attacks.
Illnesses related to dust and smoke from the towers' collapse have since claimed more than threefold the nearly 3,000 lives lost in the attacks, US health officials say.
![A ceremonial bell sits at the 9/11 Memorial during a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/a14b/live/ae30c1e0-ae00-11f1-9b77-ddcb406ce9c0.jpg)
As the names of the dead were read out for nearly four hours at the ceremony in Manhattan, a 9/11 widow criticised Saudi Arabia and what she characterised as failures by US officials to hold the kingdom accountable.
"You are missed more with each year that passes," Terry Strada said of her husband Tom Strada in remarks broadcast live worldwide.
"But how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?"
The comments by Mrs Strada, national chairperson of 9/11 Families United, drew applause from the audience.
The majority of those who carried out the 9/11 attacks were from Saudi Arabia and planning was led by al-Qaeda founder Osama Bin-Laden, scion of a prominent Saudi family.
But Saudi officials have repeatedly denied any involvement in the attacks, and in 2004 the 9/11 Commission Report cleared the country of any involvement.
![The family of Terrance Andre Aiken stands near the memorial before a ceremony to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks on the World Trade Center at the National 9/11 Memorial & Museum on September 11, 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/5db2/live/2c5c4b20-ade8-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
Families attended ceremonies to honour the lives lost
![People gather at the National September 11 Memorial during the 25th anniversary commemoration of the September 11, 2001 attacks.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/af24/live/b6374db0-adf0-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
Events were also held elsewhere to honour the victims. In London, there was a ceremonial event at Buckingham Palace attended by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the US ambassador Warren Stephens.
The Toronto Stock Exchange also held an event to remember colleagues who died in the attacks.
![Members from the Massed Bands of the Guards Division play on the forecourt of Buckingham Palace in London, during a commemorative Changing the Guard, in honour of the 25th anniversary of 9/11 terror attacks](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/acf0/live/b2358aa0-ade7-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
Buckingham Palace
![Warren Stephens, the United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom, speaks during a memorial service to observe the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terror attacks, at Lloyds of London on September 11, 2026 in London, England.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/2bc7/live/b0c3dcc0-ade8-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
Commemorations were held at Lloyd's of London
In Gander, Newfoundland, the US ambassador to Canada praised the small town that took in thousands of passengers from 38 diverted planes in the hours after the attack.
"When people in America hear the word Gander, our hearts soften," Pete Hoekstra said.
"As a representative of the United States government, thank you for your friendship... to the nation of Canada, thank you for being a partner and for the shared sacrifices that you made with us."
His remarks come amid fraught relations between the US and Canada, with the two countries engaged in a trade war. Ahead of the 9/11 commemorations, some Gander residents had called for Hoekstra's invite to be rescinded.
Still, Hoekstra's speech was met with applause. But in separate remarks afterwards, former Canadian Prime Minister Jean ChrÃ©tien said: "I have message for American friends... never mistake our generosity for weakness." He received a standing ovation.
In Milan, a group of Italian and US firefighters participated in a ceremonial stair climb to honour the emergency responders who died in the line of duty.
Dressed in their uniforms and carrying equipment, they climbed 110 floors up and down the Galfa Tower, in remembrance of the number of storeys on each of the Twin Towers.
![American firefighters walk down as they take part in a memorial stair climb on September 11, 2026 in Milan, Italy. The group of 70 Italian firefighters and seven American firefighters from the Aviano Air Base are climbing Milan's 33-story Torre Galfa in honor of the 343 members of the New York City Fire Department (FDNY) killed during the collapse of the World Trade Center towers on September 11, 2001. The firefighters are undertaking an up-and-down circuit of the stairwells four times, wearing 20-kilogram turnout gear, in memory of the FDNY firefighters who lost their lives responding to the 9/11 terror attacks.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/c157/live/22a59c20-ade9-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
- ![Juliette Scauso and her dad, firefighter Dennis Scauso](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/ebb2/live/5bf48820-ad2a-11f1-980e-4fc6f1211def.jpg)
- ![John Resta is on the left, he has dark hair and is wearing a white linen shirt and his wife Sylvia is on the right, with dark long hair and a blue short-sleeved shirt. She is pressed against him, her left hand on his chest. It has a wedding ring on it. They are both smiling. Behind them is grass with flowers.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/e4b4/live/02617840-ac1c-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
- ![A man wearing a blue shirt and white ID badge stands in the destruction of the twin towers attack. There are metal girders sticking up and a digger behind them too.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/0126/live/bca22f20-ad15-11f1-a540-61c3f7fc4e6c.jpg)
  - Published15 hours ago
 ![A treated image of smoke pouring from the twin towers of the World Trade Center after they were hit by two hijacked airliner](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a0d3/live/fc065030-ada4-11f1-948d-2793442b7bf9.jpg)
summary: The United States and international communities marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks with solemn memorial ceremonies, moments of silence, and the reading of victims' names. Past and present US leaders, including President Donald Trump and living former presidents, gathered at key memorial sites in New York, the Pentagon, and Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Commemorations also took place globally, honoring both those who died in the attacks and the many individuals who have since succumbed to related illnesses.
key_points: President Donald Trump led a Pentagon ceremony, while Vice-President JD Vance and all four living former US presidents attended the New York City memorial.
This year's commemorations included a seventh bell rung to honor the thousands who have died from diseases linked to dust and smoke exposure following the attacks.

A 9/11 widow publicly criticized Saudi Arabia during the Manhattan ceremony for its perceived role in the attacks, though Saudi officials have repeatedly denied involvement and a 2004 commission report cleared the country.
International tributes were held in locations such as London, Toronto, Milan, and Gander, Newfoundland, to honor victims, first responders, and emergency workers.

title: US marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 with tribute to victims of attacks
author: Live Reporting Edited by Johanna Chisholm; With Oliver O'Connell; With Reporting
content:
![](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/128/cpsprodpb//vivo/live/images/2025/9/29/04a8a5a3-2111-43ff-bfdb-98e9c8fd1d2e.jpg.webp) Grace Eliza Goodwin
Reporting from New York
![Firefighters salute and are seen against the World Trade Center in the background during a 9/11 memorial ceremony](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/9/11/6241273a-4de9-4f40-a601-e740cbbadba7.jpg.webp) Image source, Getty Images
Walking around the streets near the World Trade Center and the 9/11 Memorial this cloudy morning, I was struck by just how many people had gathered - 25 years later - to commemorate the attacks.
As someone who grew up in southern California and was in second grade in 2001, I had never experienced the kind of mass reverence that accompanies 9/11 until I moved to New York City. And even seven years into living here, seeing so many people come together to honour this tragedy still moves me.
Downtown Manhattan was eerily quiet this morning, despite the hundreds of people grouped in parks, on sidewalks, in courtyards, and around police barricades.
Some had come from around the country and the world to participate in the 25th anniversary. Others came from nearby to honour their loved ones lost in the attacks.
One man I spoke to, who lived in New York at the time of the attacks, burst into tears while trying to answer one of my questions, motioning to me that he couldn't go on talking.
Elsewhere, in a very fitting tribute to the resilience of this city, commuters still rushed by, passengers still popped in and out of cars, and pigeons still picked at scraps of food.
We are now ending our live coverage, but you can look back to see how the world marked 25 years since the attacks or read how the next generation is keeping the memory of 11 September alive.
summary: The United States marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks with memorial tributes in New York City. Hundreds of people gathered near the World Trade Center and the 9/11 Memorial to honor the victims. Downtown Manhattan remained quiet as locals, visitors, and those who lost loved ones participated in the commemorations.
key_points: The US marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.
Hundreds of people gathered near the World Trade Center and 9/11 Memorial in New York City.
Attendees included visitors from around the world and locals honoring lost loved ones.
Downtown Manhattan was eerily quiet during the morning memorial gatherings.

title: Houthis control key shipping route after gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![A satellite image shows Bab al-Mandeb strait.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2026-07-15T145635Z_188060635_RC2EEMAOW6BY_RTRMADP_3_IRAN-CRISIS-YEMEN-RED-SEA-SATELLITE-1789117807.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
The Houthis have taken control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast, according to reports.
The rebel group seized the last towns on the coast in a rapid advance against the forces of the internationally recognised Yemeni government early on Friday, and has pushed onto islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, government sources and witnesses reported.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3What’s happening in Yemen and how did we get here?
- list 2 of 3Yemen’s Houthis seize strategic Red Sea city of Mocha
- list 3 of 3Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia could activate defence pact, Pakistan says
The advance strengthens the control of the Iran-backed Houthis over the key shipping route of Bab al-Mandeb, which links the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea.
The route has been an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, through which about one-fifth of global energy shipments were carried before the war between the United States and Iran began earlier this year.
Houthi fighters reached the coastal town of Mocha at dawn on Thursday, then moved offshore to seize nearby islands, Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali reported from Taiz city.
Yemeni government sources told the Reuters news agency on Friday that Houthi fighters had reached the town of Dhubab, on the coast of Bab al-Mandeb.
Boats carrying fighters reached Mayyun Island – also known as Perim – that sits at the heart of the strait after government forces withdrew, government officials were reported to confirm.
“The Houthis have completed their takeover of the Bab al-Mandeb area,” one source told the AFP news agency.
The Sanaa-based Yemen Press Agency, citing field sources, said Houthi forces seized the Al-Omari camp overlooking the strait.
Al Jazeera’s Nabil al-Yousefi, reporting from Sanaa, noted there has been no official announcement by the Houthi government confirming control over Bab al-Mandeb.
Leverage
Bab al-Mandeb is the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the approach to Saudi oil terminals, offering a route to ship crude to Europe while avoiding Hormuz. Traffic in the Red Sea decreased significantly during the earlier Houthi campaign that targeted shipping there.
“The Houthis have the strong hand now,” reported Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry from the capital, Sanaa. “They have the leverage and they have control of Bab al-Mandeb and the shipping traffic going through the Red Sea.”
As the Houthi advance was reported, the average price of diesel in the US surpassed $6 a gallon and oil prices on Friday were set to close above $100 a barrel for the first time since mid-May.
The International Energy Agency forecast on Friday that global oil supply and demand are likely to fall further this year than previously assumed, with the US-Iran war delaying normal Middle East flows into 2027.
Iran has successfully applied pressure on the US by choking Gulf exports through Hormuz, suppressing energy supplies and increasing prices worldwide.
A member of the Houthi politburo sought on Friday afternoon to allay fears, insisting that international shipping faces “no danger” from the group.
“Freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and orderly,” Hazem al-Assad told the Al-Araby al-Jadeed news outlet. “There is no cause for international concern, as they face no danger from the Yemeni side.”
Escalation
Al Jazeera’s Mawry noted that there are few signs that Yemeni government forces are preparing a counteroffensive to push the Houthis back.
However, later reports from Houthi, Saudi and international outlets said Saudi air strikes had hit Mocha airport. There was no immediate report of casualties or damage. Al Jazeera was unable to immediately verify the reports.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement calling for an end to Saudi Arabia’s blockade of Yemen, and urging a resumption of negotiations. It was the first statement on Yemen issued by Tehran since the Houthi seizure of Mocha.
The Houthis, which control most of western Yemen, renewed attacks on Red Sea shipping and the Saudi-backed Yemen government earlier this year in response to the US war on their ally Iran. The flare-up of hostilities in Yemen illustrates the potential for that conflict to escalate across the region.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Thursday spoke by phone with Pakistan’s army chief, Asim Munir – a key mediator but also close ally of Saudi Arabia – and separately with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud. Both calls reportedly focused on mutual coordination and regional stability.
The Financial Times reported on Friday that Oman, which has been negotiating with Iran on a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, is organising a meeting with Gulf states to discuss the plan.
summary: The Houthis have taken control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast and pushed onto islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait following a rapid advance against internationally recognised government forces. This strategic gain strengthens the Iran-backed group's grip on a vital global shipping route linking the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea. In response to the escalating conflict, Saudi air strikes reportedly hit Mocha airport, while international energy markets saw oil prices rise above $100 a barrel.
key_points: The Houthis seized the last towns on Yemen's Red Sea coast and islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The advance enhances Houthi control over a key global shipping corridor connecting the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea.
Oil prices surpassed $100 a barrel following the developments and ongoing disruptions linked to the US-Iran war.
A Houthi politburo member stated that international shipping faces no danger from the group.
Saudi air strikes reportedly hit Mocha airport amid the escalating regional conflict.

title: 9/11 families to gather at World Trade Center and Pentagon to remember victims on 25th anniversary – US politics live
author: Tom Ambrose; David Smith; Jason Burke; Sara Braun; Robert Tait; Ramon Antonio Vargas; Moustafa Bayoumi
content:
It is the 25th anniversary of 9/11, as Americans come together to remember and commemorate the devastating effects of the attacks, which claimed the lives of 2,977 victims.
Today’s milestone anniversary will bring memorial rituals – wreath-laying, flag-flying, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names - and volunteer projects in tribute to the day.
“In the course of history, there are a few moments that divide time into, really, what came before” and after, president Donald Trump said at a 9/11 remembrance in Washington this week.
The Republican, who was in New York on 11 September 2001, has often recounted his memories and said he plans to attend the Pentagon’s anniversary ceremony later today.
Vice-president JD Vance is expected to attend the observance at the National September 11 Memorial in New York, while other administration officials are headed to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania.
Planned remembrances extend far beyond the attack sites, from beams of light projecting from New Hampshire’s Mount Washington to a stair climb at Mississippi State University’s football stadium to a ceremony at Honolulu’s 9/11 memorial.
In other developments elsewhere today:
Donald Trump doubled down on his pledge to pay all US adults $5,000 if Republicans hold on to control of Congress in the midterm elections. He’s one of the few people to actually mention the pledge tonight, as many lawmakers and officials – including his vice-president, JD Vance – avoided mentioning the so-called “dividend” altogether. Trump defended his plan: “We can do that because our country has never done better. We’re taking in trillions, trillions of dollars.”
In a shorter address to voters than his nearly two-hour speech on Wednesday, Trump again pleaded with voters to “pretend I’m on the ticket” in November. In an improvised pledge of allegiance to himself, Trump directed the audience to commit to voting in the midterm elections at all costs. The president asked Republicans in the arena to repeat: “I don’t care if I’m registered or not. I’m going to try. And cheat like hell like they do.” Trump also told those gathered in Dallas that they would “go to hell” if they didn’t vote.
Earlier, JD Vanceurged Republicans who may oppose parts of the Trump administration’s agenda not to abandon the party in November’s congressional races. The vice-president pointed to Charlie Kirk – the conservative activist killed a year ago today – to argue that voters shouldn’t “throw the baby out with the bathwater” over “a policy issue here or there”, an apparent nod to dissent over the Iran war that he avoided naming.
Vance’s speech, in many ways, was an audition for a possible 2028 presidential run. He spent much of his time on stage setting out the threats of the so-called “far left”, listing the administration’s greatest hits and slamming Joe Biden’s tenure in office.
Meanwhile, dozens of demonstrators gathered outside the arena to protest Trump’s policy agenda. Dallas police said that two people were taken into custody after an alleged assault involving a counter-protester and for blocking a roadway.
He saw the first one on September 11 itself. “Missing”, said a hastily designed poster on the window of a bar in Tribeca providing food and water to first responders. It was a plea for information about a person who had vanished in the deadliest terrorist attack in US history.
“I was like, ‘Wow, this is going to be …’” recalls Phil Buehler, an artist and photographer who had watched the twin towers collapse from his office window. “But you knew that there would be very few survivors. You knew it then.”
The missing posters kept coming in the days after 9/11, and Buehler kept photographing them. But having amassed more than 500 images, he put them away in a box on a top shelf because he could not bear to look at them.
As the 25th anniversary of the atrocity neared, he decided to revisit them and will put a selection on public display for the first time this week. Countenance: The 9/11 Missing Posters, an installation at Most Holy Trinity – St Mary’s church in Brooklyn, places 144 pictures across 24 translucent vellum panels, in vertical pairs reminiscent of the twin towers.
The World Trade Center was always a favourite subject for Buehler. He had been photographing it since 1973, when he was 16. On September 11 2001, as an advisory board member for a tech startup, he had been invited to a conference at the Windows on the World restaurant at the top of the north tower, but turned the offer down (a friend intended to go but was delayed).
“The guy that invited us died that day and I think my friend feels guilty about it,” he says quietly by phone, recalling the day on which nearly 3,000 people were killed by hijacked airliners in New York, northern Virginia and Pennsylvania. “You realise how close – everybody had a story.”
He has told the story hundreds of times, but it never seems to fade. If anything, it only becomes more vivid. “Oh, gosh,” exclaims Stanley Praimnath, his voice cracking with an “ooooooh!” as if bearing a weight. “It’s like reliving that day.”
Nearly 3,000 people died in the terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC on September 11 2001. But Praimnath and another office worker, Brian Clark, were two of only four individuals known to have survived from above the impact zone in either tower of the World Trade Center. The two strangers met in the smoke and fire of the 81st floor of the south tower, and walked down 1,620 steps into the rest of their lives.
Their split-second decisions that day made all the difference. Over the next 25 years, both men moved from middle age into old age and retirement. Both enjoyed family weddings and watched children and grandchildren grow. Both saw US presidents come and go as old wars ended and new wars began. They remained friends through it all.
They also told their story – countless times – in churches, schools, TV studios and elsewhere. “It could be 800, 1,200, a number like that,” Clark estimates.
Praimnath, in a separate interview, muses: “People refer to me as ‘the 9/11 guy’. It doesn’t feel repetitive. It is like unloading baggage from my shoulder, like washing my soul with tears. It is comforting to know that people out there still want to hear.”
On 11 September, 25 years ago, Osama bin Laden drove with a small number of al-Qaida retainers and aides to a remote location in eastern Afghanistan. His convoy of SUVs was accompanied by a minivan converted into a makeshift communications centre.
The van’s rudimentary equipment did not allow Bin Laden to watch the 19 men he had started sending to the US more than a year before fly planes into the twin towers in New York and the Pentagon near Washington DC, killing about 3,000 people. But he listened as shocked radio announcers broke the news.
Within days of the murderous assault, the then president, George W Bush, had begun framing the US response as a global “war on terror”, a clumsy, inappropriate and counterproductive strategic choice.
For those of us reporting on the ground during this period – watching US bombers over Afghan mountains and tanks in Baghdad streets, interviewing aspirant suicide bombers or the victims of attacks by extremist groups that proliferated from the UK to the Philippines – the errors and failures of this “war on terror” were glaring.
This unprecedented and indiscriminate series of campaigns would lead to invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, involve torture, renditions and alliances with dubious regimes, cost huge amounts of money, destabilise swathes of the Middle East and bring suffering to millions of people.
As the United States commemorates the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks, in which nearly 3,000 people were killed in New York City, Washington DC and Pennsylvania, the Guardian asked American readers to share how the attacks affected their day-to-day lives and the country at large.
Many readers shared their feeling of patriotism in the days following the attacks while also highlighting how the government’s response to 9/11 expanded government surveillance and fueled Islamophobia in the country. For those who were adults at the time of the attacks, the day marked a cataclysmic shift. For those too young to remember it, it served as the context for the complicated and violent world they grew up in.
“When 9/11 first happened, everyone became your friend. We were all together in this loss, and the country felt like home everywhere. Driving down a suburban street every house displayed an American flag,” wrote Jennifer Jasensky, a 55-year-old paralegal based in Milford, Connecticut. “It was a beautiful sight, like something out of a book or Hallmark movie.”
Elizabeth Zorko, a retired election administrator in Omaha, Nebraska, recalled a similar phenomenon: “I remember meeting the eyes of total strangers and there was a look that wasn’t there before, as if a deep personal connection had been forged by this shared horrific experience.”
That feeling of unity soon gave way to anger and division, in large part due to the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, begun by the George W Bush administration and framed as necessary conflicts to help the US win the war on terror.
A generation of spies had lost an enemy but not yet found a role. Then came 9/11.
A decade after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, al-Qaida’s devastating attacks on New York and Washington on 11 September 2001 announced to the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) that the long era of battling communism, for which it had been founded, was officially at an end.
It was to be replaced by a no-holds-barred “war on terror” that would leave the CIA with a soiled reputation over falsified intelligence that led to the invasion and occupation of Iraq, and an extraordinary rendition program in which suspects were subjected to “enhanced interrogations” at secret sites that official US inquiries subsequently defined as torture.
The US intelligence community was dramatically transformed after two planes flew into the World Trade Center, a third smashed into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in the Pennsylvania countryside after passengers overcame the hijackers.
Accounts of what unfolded inside the CIA’s headquarters in Langley, Virginia, suggests an organization unprepared for the drastically changed world the attacks ushered in, despite an awareness among some in the intelligence community that al-Qaida and its leader, Osama bin Laden, represented a clear and present danger.
Anna Sweeney Rossman was only five years old when her mother, flight attendant Madeline Amy Sweeney, died onboard an airliner that terrorists hijacked and deliberately flew into the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. And for years, she said in an interview on Wednesday, Rossman’s grief primarily centered on her mother’s absence from certain milestones in her life.
She recalled how planning her 2023 wedding – particularly shopping for a dress – hit her especially hard without her mom there. And Rossman said it was as much a blow to not have her mom there for the birth of her daughters, each younger than two, as the US prepared to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks on Friday.
Rossman furthermore admitted that it was “really scary” to think about how she was approaching the age her mother was when she was killed: 35.
Nonetheless, in remarks arriving as hundreds of millions across the US sought ways to pay tribute to those taken by the deadliest terrorist attack in the country, Rossman said she has drawn strength to confront her circumstances from the valor her mom showed in her final moments on American Airlines flight 11.
Officials credit Rossman’s mother, who also went by just Amy Sweeney, with helping authorities on the ground identify the flight’s hijackers by telephoning details about them to her supervisor. She did shortly before becoming one of nearly 3,000 people killed that day as terrorists crashed planes into New York City’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon in Washington DC and a field in Pennsylvania.
It’s been 25 years since the terrorist attacks of September 11, and during this time Muslim Americans have learned how to live in that dangerous space between other Americans’ fears and their ignorance.
The fear was clear from the beginning. Immediately following 9/11, Muslim Americans faced what Human Rights Watch called “a severe wave of backlash violence”.
A tide of hate rose up against ordinary Muslims and those who appeared to be Muslim, including at least three murders in the immediate backlash after the attacks.
The federal government, for its part, began targeting Muslim immigrants in a massive surge of repression that legal experts soon compared with the Palmer Raids of the 1920s.
The ignorance was just as evident. Even Oprah Winfrey did her part to allay it, dedicating an episode of her show in October 2001 to “Islam 101”. The Qur’an leapt on to the New York Times bestseller list that fall.
Yet despite these early efforts at education, most Americans still learned little about Islam and Muslims.
One 2006 study found that only a third of those polled realized that Muslims worship the same God as Christians and Jews do. Close to 10% of respondents thought Muslims worship a “moon god”.
Trump to commemorate 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks at the Pentagon
President Donald Trump is set to observe today’s 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks by attending a ceremony at the Pentagon.
It’s the second year in a row for Trump to mark the day at the Pentagon. The president, who is originally from New York, last attended the ground zero ceremony there in 2024.
During last year’s commemoration at the Pentagon , Trump delivered remarks recounting moments from the day of the attacks, including snippets of conversations from passengers who were aboard the hijacked airplanes.
At a Tuesday event at the Ellipse just outside the White House, Trump vowed to “never forget” victims, noting that the attacks were one of few moments in history that “divide time into really what came before” and after.
For the first time, this year’s ceremony will add a silent moment to honor people who were exposed to the clouds of toxic dust released by the twin towers’ collapse and have since died of cancer and other illnesses.
Questions remain about how many people developed health problems linked to the dust.
It’s a reminder of how the attacks’ long shadow has reached into many corners of life in the US and beyond.
Police officer Casey Kloepfer plans to spend time today at the Brooklyn station house where his father, officer Ronald Kloepfer, reported to work that day before being called to the World Trade Center. He didn’t make it home.
Casey Kloepfer was only four, but he grew up hearing about his father’s affinity for helping people and for a job that enabled him to do so. He became an officer this past June, AP reported
“It’s big footsteps to fill, but it’s definitely something that I take very seriously and want to continue to honor him and be the best police officer I can,” he said by phone this week.
The 29-year-old wears his father’s badge number and even has joined the New York Police Department lacrosse team, which his dad founded.
As clear as that cloudless September morning, Jenna Jacobs McPartland remembers the moment everything changed. “I was cleaning the bathroom and watching the Today show in the background and nine months pregnant,” the 52-year-old recalls by phone. “I think they were showing ‘Today throws a wedding’ when the news broke in.”
A plane had hit the north tower of the World Trade Center in New York. McPartland did not know that her husband, Ariel Jacobs, was attending a conference at its Windows on the World restaurant.“I called his office to say, ‘Hey, turn on the TV. Do you guys know what’s going on?’ His assistant said, ‘Oh my God, Jenna, he’s there.’ The whole world disappeared and there was this sort of hollow collapsing feeling.”
Ariel Jacobs did not live to see his son, Gabriel, born six days after September 11, 2001. McPartland, then living in Briarcliff Manor, New York, would marry twice more, set up a grief support charity, and become a chef and restaurateur. Each 9/11 anniversary, she has a picnic at the cemetery where a few pieces of bone from her late husband are buried.
Speaking from Fairfield, Connecticut, McPartland says: “Ari was an incredibly joyful person who cherished his life. I made a conscious choice to honour him by living as joyfully as I can. It’s not always easy. I still cry pretty frequently. If there’s a movie with a building getting blown up, or if I’m reading a book and they casually mention ‘post 9-11 this’ or whatever, it catches me off guard. The grief finds a place to live in the heart, and you visit it.”
McPartland and other victims’ families have learned to live with that grief over the past 25 years. But America writ large has struggled to carry the weight of the worst terrorist attack in its history. The world’s most powerful nation responded by inflicting terror of its own, betraying its history as a safe harbour for immigrants, and pitting Americans against one another. The initial heroism, goodwill and unity of 9/11 gave way to discord at home and diminished moral authority abroad.
McPartland adds: “It makes me incredibly sad and bordering on angry that the death of my husband has been invoked to cause more violence. It is the othering of people that got him killed in the first place and, when we Americans fail to learn that lesson and choose collectively as a nation to other people, whether it’s immigrants or other nations, that is a deepening of that tragedy that is sickening and unfathomable to me.”
It is the 25th anniversary of 9/11, as Americans come together to remember and commemorate the devastating effects of the attacks, which claimed the lives of 2,977 victims.
Today’s milestone anniversary will bring memorial rituals – wreath-laying, flag-flying, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names - and volunteer projects in tribute to the day.
“In the course of history, there are a few moments that divide time into, really, what came before” and after, president Donald Trump said at a 9/11 remembrance in Washington this week.
The Republican, who was in New York on 11 September 2001, has often recounted his memories and said he plans to attend the Pentagon’s anniversary ceremony later today.
Vice-president JD Vance is expected to attend the observance at the National September 11 Memorial in New York, while other administration officials are headed to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania.
Planned remembrances extend far beyond the attack sites, from beams of light projecting from New Hampshire’s Mount Washington to a stair climb at Mississippi State University’s football stadium to a ceremony at Honolulu’s 9/11 memorial.
In other developments elsewhere today:
Donald Trump doubled down on his pledge to pay all US adults $5,000 if Republicans hold on to control of Congress in the midterm elections. He’s one of the few people to actually mention the pledge tonight, as many lawmakers and officials – including his vice-president, JD Vance – avoided mentioning the so-called “dividend” altogether. Trump defended his plan: “We can do that because our country has never done better. We’re taking in trillions, trillions of dollars.”
In a shorter address to voters than his nearly two-hour speech on Wednesday, Trump again pleaded with voters to “pretend I’m on the ticket” in November. In an improvised pledge of allegiance to himself, Trump directed the audience to commit to voting in the midterm elections at all costs. The president asked Republicans in the arena to repeat: “I don’t care if I’m registered or not. I’m going to try. And cheat like hell like they do.” Trump also told those gathered in Dallas that they would “go to hell” if they didn’t vote.
Earlier, JD Vanceurged Republicans who may oppose parts of the Trump administration’s agenda not to abandon the party in November’s congressional races. The vice-president pointed to Charlie Kirk – the conservative activist killed a year ago today – to argue that voters shouldn’t “throw the baby out with the bathwater” over “a policy issue here or there”, an apparent nod to dissent over the Iran war that he avoided naming.
Vance’s speech, in many ways, was an audition for a possible 2028 presidential run. He spent much of his time on stage setting out the threats of the so-called “far left”, listing the administration’s greatest hits and slamming Joe Biden’s tenure in office.
Meanwhile, dozens of demonstrators gathered outside the arena to protest Trump’s policy agenda. Dallas police said that two people were taken into custody after an alleged assault involving a counter-protester and for blocking a roadway.
summary: As the United States marks the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks, families and officials are gathering at memorial sites including the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and the Flight 93 National Memorial. The milestone anniversary brings nationwide tributes, reflections on survivors, and remembrances of the 2,977 victims who died. The attacks profoundly altered American society, leading to the global 'war on terror,' major shifts in intelligence and surveillance, and enduring personal grief for families of victims.
key_points: The 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks is marked by memorial events, wreath-laying, and moments of silence at attack sites and across the country.
Nearly 3,000 victims lost their lives when hijacked airliners struck the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and crashed in Pennsylvania.
The aftermath of the attacks led the US government to launch the 'war on terror,' resulting in wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and significant changes to intelligence agencies.
Families of victims and survivors continue to share their personal stories and grapple with the generational impact of the tragedy.

title: Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast
author: Patrick Wintour
content:
Houthi forces in Yemen are making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the Iran-aligned group closer to full control of a key shipping route.
Seizure of the coast and some of the islands in the sea would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two choke points for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandab at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz.
Baraa Shiban, the Royal United Services Institute’s (Rusi) Yemen specialist, a London-based security thinktank, said the situation in the country was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope of putting more pressure on their forces than they could withstand. But in the past 48 hours the Houthis had major advances south, down Yemen’s west coast, taking them closer to the high ground overlooking the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait.
![A screen grab from video footage released by Saudi-backed forces shows a rocket being fired during fighting west of the city of Taiz.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c0317f00d206162ab154fc163ad64b52050d1c01/82_0_2500_2000/master/2500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen.
By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to use a new lever to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war with Iran to end before the US midterm elections at the start of November.
The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September.
![A partially sunken boat lists near a debris-strewn dock after strikes on Mocha, Yemen](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0dced1a06c18db533f6e3a0c9c9408bbd02df06e/472_0_2516_2014/master/2516.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested its forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land.
