The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. Analysts claimed that the effectiveness of Yemen’s government forces was weakened by internal divisions, as well as external pressure from Saudi Arabia.
![A satellite image shows smoke billowing from an Aramco oil depot in a desert landscape](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/39f915bb625ebf800468932212bfb60ad98cc3f0/0_0_4780_3825/master/4780.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The latter, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged Houthi ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish.
The clashes have raged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis were forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers.
The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region.
![A screen grab from video footage released by the Saudi-backed forces shows a fighter firing at Houthi forces in Taiz province.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/612da6d22d20639357ae749e9cf99f67812ed9ae/0_0_2500_2000/master/2500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.”
He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.”
The head of the Houthis’ national delegating negotiating team, Muhammad Abdul Salam, insisted non-Saudi commercial shipping would not be attacked.
The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.
![A screen grab of video footage reportedly showing Houthi attacks on Saudi-backed forces in al-Jawf province.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/23489f80538a039c160cba0de33ce2c15ff62bc3/333_0_3333_2667/master/3333.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The escalation to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior delegation of the Houthi group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a.
The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni group described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August.
Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz as a result of US-Israeli attacks.
summary: Houthi forces in Yemen have claimed control of the key port of Mocha and made major advances along the Red Sea coast in the most intense fighting since the 2022 ceasefire. The offensive threatens to give the Iran-aligned group control over strategic shipping choke points like the Bab al-Mandab strait, prompting heavy Saudi airstrikes and escalating regional tensions. The renewed conflict has driven oil prices above $100 a barrel and raised questions about the stability of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
key_points: Houthi forces seized the key port of Mocha, the city of Hays, and a major military camp in a drive down Yemen's west coast.
The advance brings the Houthis closer to controlling the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, posing a major concern for Saudi Arabia and the US.
Saudi Arabia responded to Houthi drone and missile attacks with numerous airstrikes, contributing to hundreds of reported fatalities.
Yemeni government forces organized a strategic retreat, hindered by internal divisions and a lack of integrated military resources.
The escalating conflict has pushed global oil prices above $100 a barrel.

title: Swiss Alps coach crash kills several people, local police say
author: Patrick Jackson
content:
![Emergency responders at the scene of an accident involving a travel coach in Susch in the canton of Grisons, Switzerland, 10 September 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/d79c/live/94f7da60-ad56-11f1-8128-99eda56e535a.png)
The coach was carrying dozens of Dutch nationals
- Published
A tourist coach has crashed in the south-eastern Swiss Alps, leaving several people dead and several injured, local police say.
The bus overturned between Susch and Zernez in the GraubÃ¼nden - also known as Grisons - region late on Thursday afternoon.
A large team of rescuers equipped with several helicopters was deployed to the scene.
Some 48 Dutch passengers were on board the bus, according to a spokeswoman for the General Dutch Association of Travel Companies on behalf of tour operator OAD.
The spokesperson told Dutch newspaper De Telegraaf they could not yet say how many people had been killed or injured.
Images on Swiss news sites show a coach lying on its side beside a narrow country road on which stand numerous ambulances while groups of rescuers work at the scene.
The coach reportedly left the Netherlands on Monday and was on a day trip to Switzerland from Austria when the crash happened.
Zernez is the entry point for visitors to the Swiss National Park, a vast Alpine reserve stretching more than 100 sq km (40 sq miles) across the mountainous Engadine valley.
summary: A tourist coach carrying 48 Dutch nationals crashed and overturned in the south-eastern Swiss Alps, resulting in several deaths and injuries. The accident occurred late Thursday afternoon on a road between Susch and Zernez in the Graubünden region. A large rescue operation involving multiple helicopters and ambulances was deployed to the scene.
key_points: A tourist coach crashed and overturned in the Swiss Alps, causing several fatalities and injuries.
The bus was carrying 48 Dutch passengers on a day trip from Austria.
The accident took place between Susch and Zernez in the Graubünden region late on Thursday afternoon.
Emergency responders deployed a large team equipped with several helicopters and ambulances to the scene.

title: Several dead as Dutch tourist coach overturns in Switzerland
author: Simon Ormiston
content:
A coach believed to be carrying tourists through one of Switzerland's most scenic Alpine valleys has overturned near the entrance to the country's national park.
A tour coach has overturned on a mountain road in the eastern Swiss canton of Graubünden, leaving several people dead and a number of others injured, authorities have confirmed.
The crash took place on Thursday on the stretch of road linking the villages of Susch and Zernez, deep in the Engadine valley.
Local police confirmed the fatalities via a post on X, though they have not yet released the number of victims, their nationalities, or any explanation for what caused the vehicle to leave the road.
The Dutch Federation of Travel Agencies (ANVR) told AFP that the coach belonged to the tour company Oad and was carrying 48 passengers, all of them from the Netherlands.
Television footage from Swiss broadcasters showed emergency crews swarming the scene, working around the coach as it lay overturned on an embankment beside the carriageway. Helicopters were seen landing nearby to assist with the response.
A police spokesman told AFP that the force did not wish to provide a more detailed toll until the victims' families had been informed.
According to the ANVR, the coach left the Netherlands on Monday and was on a day trip to Switzerland from Austria when the crash happened.
Zernez sits at the gateway to the Swiss National Park, a rugged Alpine reserve covering more than 100 square kilometres across the Engadine region, and is a popular starting point for visitors exploring the region.
Police say the investigation into the cause of the crash is ongoing.
summary: A tour coach carrying 48 Dutch passengers overturned on a mountain road in the eastern Swiss canton of Graubünden, resulting in several fatalities and multiple injuries. The crash occurred on Thursday on a stretch of road between Susch and Zernez in the Engadine valley while the vehicle was on a day trip from Austria. Local authorities and police are investigating the cause of the accident, with the exact death toll being withheld until families are notified.
key_points: A coach carrying 48 passengers from the Netherlands overturned on a mountain road in eastern Switzerland.
The crash occurred on Thursday between the villages of Susch and Zernez in the Engadine valley.
Authorities confirmed multiple fatalities and injuries, but withheld exact numbers pending family notifications.
The vehicle belonged to the Dutch tour company Oad and was on a day trip from Austria.
Police have launched an ongoing investigation into the cause of the accident.

title: Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’
author: George Chidi
content:
Donald Trump’s promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery.
“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said during the unprecedented Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump dividend.”
It comes amid extreme concern over the US national debt, which exceeded $40tn for the first time in August.
Speaking to Politico, Chip Roy, the Republican US representative from Texas, sounded skeptical. “Well – I would like to know how they would plan to pay for … back of envelope … well over $1tn,” he said.
In the moments after Trump made the announcement, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X that “this would cost about $1.2 TRILLION in just one year. That’s more than ALL THREE ROUNDS of COVID relief checks, despite no recessions. The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.”
The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting the cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt.
“The 10-year [treasury bond is] approaching 5%,” Goldwein said on Thursday morning. “Inflation is not under control. We spend more on interest than we spend on defense or on Medicare at this point. Social security is six years from insolvency. Just about the last thing we need is to borrow another trillion dollars to send checks to everybody.”
Spending like this risked an economic sugar high followed by a recessionary crash, he said. But Goldwein was most concerned about what might happen if Trump’s gambit is effective.
“If this works, the lesson for every future politician is going to be: if you want to win an election, promise a trillion dollars. And multiply a trillion dollars times the number of elections we have coming up, that is a recipe for bankruptcy.”
Democratic political leaders reacted with blunt condemnation.
“After making you sicker and poorer with his war, Donald Trump now wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.”
The Democratic National Committee (DNC) pointed to Trump’s record on similar pledges, from $5,000 stimulus checks as a result of the work of the so-called department of government efficiency (Doge) to $2,000 stimulus checks from revenue from tariffs.
“Donald Trump and Republicans are once again offering empty promises to Americans,” said Kendall Witmer, the committee’s rapid response director. “The only people reaping the benefits of Trump’s economy are himself, his family, and his ultra-rich elite donors. Meanwhile, working families get nothing except sky-high receipts at the grocery store and the pump, unaffordable healthcare premiums, and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation.”
The Bipartisan Policy Center has been tracking tariff revenue since Trump began raising rates in 2025. As of 8 September, the US has collected about $210bn in tariff and excise tax revenue in 2026. At a rate of $21bn a month, the US federal government would have to collect tariffs for nearly five years to cover a $5,000 payment, assuming every dollar of tariff revenue went to the payment, and discounting tariff payments refunded to retailers in legal challenges.
Peter Schiff, chief economist for Euro Pacific Asset Management, said that Trump’s pledge had already begun rippling through financial markets.
“Even though bond investors know that, even in the unlikely event Republicans retain control of the House, Trump’s promise to borrow over $1 trillion more to buy votes won’t be kept,” Schiff wrote in a post on X. “The promise itself is so reckless that they’re dumping Treasuries, sending yields to new highs …
“Making his promise even worse, Trump referred to his $5,000 bribes as ‘dividends’, as if his policies had been so successful that the US now has surpluses to share. Instead, his reckless policies have produced massive deficits. Trump needs to send Americans bills, not checks.”
JD Vance appeared to walk back Trump’s pledge, suggesting that the benefit would be means-tested.
But the US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, promised support for Trump’s idea. “I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” Moreno wrote on X.
summary: Donald Trump promised a $5,000 "Trump dividend" for US citizens if Republicans retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections, drawing accusations of bribery and widespread criticism over its staggering projected $1.2tn cost. Critics, economists, and Democrats warned the plan would dangerously spike the national deficit and inflation rates, while some Republicans also expressed skepticism or attempted to walk back the pledge. Proponents like Senator Bernie Moreno, however, voiced support and promised to introduce a bill to pass the dividend.
key_points: Donald Trump proposed a $5,000 "Trump dividend" for US citizens contingent on Republicans winning control of Congress in the midterm elections.
Experts estimate the payout would cost roughly $1.2 trillion, threatening to dramatically increase the national deficit and inflation.
Democratic leaders and various economists strongly condemned the promise, labeling it as bribery and warning of severe economic consequences.
Some Republicans, including Chip Roy and JD Vance, expressed skepticism or suggested the plan would be means-tested, while others like Bernie Moreno pledged immediate legislative support.

title: Twenty-five dead after fire erupts on cargo ship in Qingdao, eastern China - state media
author: Phelan Chatterjee
content:
Watch: Thick plumes of smoke rise from cargo ship fire in Qingdao, China
- Published
Twenty-five people have been killed in a fire on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked at a port in eastern China, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
Of the 42 people on board, 17 were were evacuated of which five are in hospital in stable condition, CCTV reports.
The vessel was undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in the city of Qingdao when the blaze erupted at around 11:15 local time (03:15 GMT). It was put out just over three hours later, according to CCTV.
Photos released by state media showed the vessel to be the Ocean Melody, a 190m (623ft) long Liberia-flagged carrier which arrived in Qingdao on 31 August, according to tracking site MarineTraffic.
![Large boat undergoing maintenance](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/893/cpsprodpb/77c8/live/9d308770-acfe-11f1-beae-535b95a24b3e.jpg)
China's Premier Li Qiang urged the rescue of people trapped on board the ship
Qingdao is a major trading hub and ranks among the world's busiest ports.
It is unclear what caused the fire. An eyewitness told the AFP news agency there was thick smoke rising from the ship, but he heard no explosion.
The country's leader Xi Jinping earlier called for "all-out" search and rescue efforts while Premier Li Qiang stressed the need to "prevent secondary disasters".
The fire comes nearly a month after a shipyard explosion in the south-eastern Chinese province of Fujian killed a rescue worker and injured 12 others.
![Emergency vehicles seen on the road to the docked ship](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1008/cpsprodpb/9f5e/live/c697ea50-ad11-11f1-826f-933990eae6f0.jpg)
summary: A fire on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked at a shipyard in Qingdao, eastern China, has left 25 people dead. The blaze erupted during maintenance work and was extinguished just over three hours later. Out of the 42 people on board, 17 were evacuated, with five currently hospitalized in stable condition.
key_points: Twenty-five people were killed in a fire aboard the Liberia-flagged cargo ship Ocean Melody.
The vessel was undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in Qingdao when the fire started.
Seventeen of the 42 people on board were successfully evacuated.
The cause of the fire remains unclear, though state leaders called for all-out rescue efforts.

title: Vance appears to walk back Trump’s offer of $5,000 ‘dividend’ if Republicans win midterms – US politics live
author: Tom Ambrose; Shrai Popat
content:
Vance appears to walk back Trump’s offer of $5,000 ‘dividend’ if Republicans win midterms – US politics live
Vice-president suggests payment would not go to all and would be paid for by tariff revenues despite supreme court rulings against much of Trump’s program
Vice-president JD Vance appeared to partially row back on Donald Trump’s outlandish claims that every adult citizen in the US would receive $5,000 if the Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
“If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told a roaring crowd, during a nearly two-hour long speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which he also urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”.
But Vance, speaking after the president, suggested the so-called dividend payments would not go to the wealthy and that it could be paid for by US tariff revenues – though the suggested payment dwarfs what the US has taken in through the protectionist measures.
Congress would need to approve or otherwise acquiesce to the payment. The sum would far exceed US tariff revenues even before the Supreme Court tossed much of the president’s tariff program last year.
The White House has yet to release details on Trump’s announcement.
Surrounded by supporters waving American flag placards, Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”, but devoted much of his speech to fearmongering about what would happen should Democrats win the House or the Senate for the final two years of his presidency.
“There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America.”
The president and Republicans are gambling that throwing a midterm convention – the first the GOP has ever held – can buoy the party, which is predicted to lose control of the House. Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in competitive races skipped the two-day confab entirely.
In a nearly two-hour speech, Donald Trump capped off his first night remarks at the GOP midterm convention by pleading with Republicans to “pretend that I’m running”. The president centered himself in the battle to control Congress, and acknowledged that candidates are more successful when he is on the ballot. He offered an ominous outlook if Republicans fail to retain power.
Throughout his remarks, Trump also tried to campaign on behalf of Republicans in competitive midterm races. While he made fun of Ken Paxton’s clothing choices and the way he speaks, he praised the Republican nominee for US Senate in Texas as “the single greatest attorney general” in the state’s history, while also branding his opponent James Talarico as a “disaster”.
Earlier, Democratic senator John Fetterman made a surprise virtual appearance at the Republican midterm convention, delivering a video address supporting Dave McCormick, a Republican senator in Pennsylvania. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his party since his election in 2022, said in the video that he would always reject “extremes and socialism”, repeating an oft-used Republican critique of the Democratic party’s increasingly popular left wing.
Meanwhile, several Republicans who are facing tough races have chosen not to attend the convention in Dallas. This include Susan Collins, the five-term incumbent senator from Maine, and Dan Sullivan – the Republican senator from Alaska who is facing a tough contest against former Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola.
Talk show host Jimmy Kimmel said his interview with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico will not air on ABC tomorrow following threats from the FCC.
Kimmel said the FCC had threatened him, his show, ABC, its affiliates, and local stations over “simple traditional editorial decisions” and guest bookings.
He said the full interview will be shared on YouTube instead.
Democrat John Fetterman makes surprise appearance at Republican convention
Shrai Popat
Democratic senator John Fetterman made a surprise virtual appearance at the Republican midterm convention, delivering a video address supporting Dave McCormick, a Republican senator in Pennsylvania.
Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his party since his election in 2022, said in the video that he would always reject “extremes and socialism”, repeating an oft-used Republican critique of the Democratic party’s increasingly popular left wing.
The video message will do little to dampen speculation that the renegade senator, who is now more popular among Republican voters in Pennsylvania than the Democrats who helped elect him, is preparing to switch political parties. Fetterman has repeatedly said that is not his plan, though he recently suggested he would be forced to formally break with the Democratic party if it ever became “the anti-Israel party”.
Democrats currently hold 47 seats in the US Senate. Despite the long odds, Democrats believe discontent with the economy and Trump’s low approval ratings have given them a rare opportunity to retake control of the upper chamber. A defection would jeopardize their already narrow path to a majority.
Yet if Fetterman remains a Democrat, he would hold outsized influence, effectively wielding veto power in a 51-49 majority.
Marc Goldwein, the senior policy director at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a think tank in Washington, said Donald Trump has no authority send money to Americans without approval from Congress.
Goldwein added that dividends are something that companies pay when there’s a surplus, but the US is running $2tn annual deficits and has $40tn in debt.
“The idea that we’ve had fiscal success is backwards and bordering on laughable,” he said. “We don’t have surpluses to give away.”
Congress would need to approve or otherwise acquiesce to the payment. The sum would far exceed US tariff revenues even before the Supreme Court tossed much of the president’s tariff program last year.
The move was reminiscent of billionaire Elon Musk’s efforts to buy votes in last year’s Wisconsin state Supreme Court race, where he handed out million-dollar checks to voters to try to boost a candidate who ultimately lost.
Trump’s proposal would be legal because the payment would go to everyone regardless of how they voted, or whether they voted at all, said New Mexico-based attorney John Day.
“This is a campaign promise,” Day said. “It’s not a payment to individuals to try to get them to vote in a particular way.”
Vice-president JD Vance appeared to partially row back on Donald Trump’s outlandish claims that every adult citizen in the US would receive $5,000 if the Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
“If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told a roaring crowd, during a nearly two-hour long speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which he also urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”.
But Vance, speaking after the president, suggested the so-called dividend payments would not go to the wealthy and that it could be paid for by US tariff revenues – though the suggested payment dwarfs what the US has taken in through the protectionist measures.
Congress would need to approve or otherwise acquiesce to the payment. The sum would far exceed US tariff revenues even before the Supreme Court tossed much of the president’s tariff program last year.
The White House has yet to release details on Trump’s announcement.
Surrounded by supporters waving American flag placards, Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”, but devoted much of his speech to fearmongering about what would happen should Democrats win the House or the Senate for the final two years of his presidency.
“There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America.”
The president and Republicans are gambling that throwing a midterm convention – the first the GOP has ever held – can buoy the party, which is predicted to lose control of the House. Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in competitive races skipped the two-day confab entirely.
In a nearly two-hour speech, Donald Trump capped off his first night remarks at the GOP midterm convention by pleading with Republicans to “pretend that I’m running”. The president centered himself in the battle to control Congress, and acknowledged that candidates are more successful when he is on the ballot. He offered an ominous outlook if Republicans fail to retain power.
Throughout his remarks, Trump also tried to campaign on behalf of Republicans in competitive midterm races. While he made fun of Ken Paxton’s clothing choices and the way he speaks, he praised the Republican nominee for US Senate in Texas as “the single greatest attorney general” in the state’s history, while also branding his opponent James Talarico as a “disaster”.
Earlier, Democratic senator John Fetterman made a surprise virtual appearance at the Republican midterm convention, delivering a video address supporting Dave McCormick, a Republican senator in Pennsylvania. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his party since his election in 2022, said in the video that he would always reject “extremes and socialism”, repeating an oft-used Republican critique of the Democratic party’s increasingly popular left wing.
Meanwhile, several Republicans who are facing tough races have chosen not to attend the convention in Dallas. This include Susan Collins, the five-term incumbent senator from Maine, and Dan Sullivan – the Republican senator from Alaska who is facing a tough contest against former Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola.
summary: Vice-President JD Vance appeared to qualify Donald Trump's campaign promise of a $5,000 dividend for adult citizens if Republicans win the midterms, suggesting the money would exclude the wealthy and be funded by tariff revenues. Experts and critics noted that such payments require congressional approval and would vastly exceed actual tariff revenues, while the US runs high national deficits. The announcement came during the first-ever Republican midterm convention in Dallas, an event skipped by several vulnerable GOP candidates amid Trump's low approval ratings.
key_points: Donald Trump promised a $5,000 dividend to adult citizens if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate.
JD Vance suggested the payments would not go to the wealthy and would be funded by tariff revenues.
Experts pointed out that the proposed payouts would far exceed US tariff revenues and require congressional approval.
Several vulnerable Republican candidates in competitive races chose to skip the GOP midterm convention.
Democratic senator John Fetterman made a surprise virtual appearance at the convention to support a Republican candidate.

title: Five dead and 86 missing as fire breaks out on ferry in the Philippines
author: Virma Simonette Rivera; Kelly Ng
content:
Watch: What we know about the fatal Philippines ferry fire
- Published
At least five people have died and 86 are missing after a fire broke out on a ferry in the Philippines, the country's coastguard said.
The MV June Aster, which set off from Manila ferrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron when it caught fire.
The blaze, which erupted at 18:45 local time (10:45 GMT) Wednesday, was still burning as of 11:00 on Thursday. The strong currents and thick smoke were a challenge to those working to extinguish it, the coastguard said.
A survivor says he was in the sea for two hours before he got rescued. "It was cold. If the rescue was delayed, I would definitely have died," Roland Lerma told the BBC.
![Flames engulf a ferry as a fire erupted in the night](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/c2bd/live/40eb11a0-acc8-11f1-950e-0d3c5642d8c0.png)
The fire broke out as the vessel nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron in Palawan
Video clips shared by the coastguard on Wednesday night showed the vessel engulfed in flames and people being pulled out of the water into rescue boats.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation, the coastguard said.
The coastguard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest the fire started in the cargo hold, which is the compartment where containers and or goods are stored, the coastguard said. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.
Forty-three people have been rescued but it is unclear how many have sustained injuries.
Seven of the survivors were taken to a hospital in Culion, a larger neighbouring island, which has higher bed capacity and more comprehensive healthcare services.
A first responder told the BBC they had never seen such a disaster in Coron, calling it "really heartbreaking".
"I was one of the people who carried and transported the casualties to the hospital last night," they said, adding that the ferry was an hour away from its destination.
The survivors were taken to an evacuation centre in Barangay Turda, which sits just north of Marcilla. The state of their injuries is unclear.
Anelyn Magbanua is among those anxiously waiting for news of their loved ones.
Her husband Marlon had spent a few days in Manila visiting their two children, who were going to school in the capital city.
Magbanua last heard from him while the ferry was passing through a village about two hours from the port in Coron, she tells the BBC.
"I was expecting that the ferry will arrive at the pier at between 18:00 and 19:00 yesterday," she said, adding that she had gone to bed early but was awakened by a cousin who told her the ferry Marlon was on had caught fire.
"I couldn't describe what I am feeling right now. I have been crying and praying since last night," Magbanua says.
She'd travelled to a hospital in Coron, hoping to find Marlon among the survivors â but he remains unaccounted for.
"My two-year-old son and I are outside the hospital as we speak. We have nothing but ourselves," she says.
![MV June Aster burns as flames and smoke rise after a fire broke out on the ferry](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/800/cpsprodpb/d767/live/5b775ff0-acc9-11f1-8a98-f947b5bcd52b.jpg)
Footage from the coastguard show the vessel engulfed in flames
Rai Garcia has three family friends among those missing.
Mae Lorraine Galera-Navoa, who is the sister of Garcia's brother-in-law, had travelled to Luzon to attend her father's funeral, accompanied by her husband Elyzer Navoa and their three-year-old daughter Hiraya Joy.
They had been travelling home to El Nido in Palawan on board the vessel when it caught fire.
"We haven't received any news yet. That's why we had to comment on local news threads just to receive updates," Garcia says.
"We still hope and pray for their safety."
Garcia and his family made a poster to appeal for information of the family of three using a photo Mae had taken on the ferry and shared with immediate relatives.
Others have posted on the Philippine Coast Guard's Facebook page asking for information of their missing loved ones. "Please can you find my sibling," read one comment.
Maritime accidents are common in the Philippines, an archipelago of 7,100 islands.
Inter-island ferries are a cheap way to move people and cargo between islands, some of which are inaccessible by air.
But there is always the risk of severe weather, monsoon rains and typhoons which can cause turbulent conditions. The country is affected by an average of 20 typhoons every year.
Past accidents have also been blamed on poor maintenance and uneven enforcement of safety laws.
In 2023, 31 people died after a fire broke out at a passenger ferry in the country's south-western tip. The MV Lady Mary Joy 3 was on its way to Basilan island from Zamboanga city, a major port in the main southern island of Mindanao.
But with 86 still missing, this ferry disaster could prove to be among the worst to have happened in the Philippines in recent years.
Additional reporting by Joel Guinto
summary: At least five people have died and 86 are missing following a fire on the MV June Aster ferry in the Philippines. The vessel, carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members, caught fire as it neared its destination in Coron. Coastguard officials stated that strong currents, thick smoke, and challenges such as passengers not wearing life vests complicated rescue efforts.
key_points: Five people died, 43 were rescued, and 86 remain missing after the MV June Aster caught fire.
The ferry was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members when the blaze broke out near Coron.
Preliminary survivor interviews suggest the fire started in the cargo hold.
Maritime accidents are common in the Philippines due to factors including weather and safety enforcement issues.

title: Muted US response to UK's West Bank sanctions may reflect simmering frustration
author: Tom Bateman
content:
![Trump and Netanyahu shaking hands in July at the White House](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/966/cpsprodpb/3dfe/live/ef7217b0-ac7c-11f1-994b-c7df927931ed.jpg)
- Published
As the UK unveiled sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, Israel responded with fury, declaring it would shutter Britain's diplomatic mission to the Palestinians, kick out UK military staff from an international coordination base near Gaza and ban nearly a dozen left-wing British members of parliament from entering Israel.
It was a blaring signal of defiance and a remarkable diplomatic escalation.
The UK had taken the action arguing it had a moral imperative to stop the "destruction" of the two-state solution - a future independent Palestinian state - at the hands of the Israeli government. It accused Israel's government of turning a blind eye to the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians by settlers.
The standoff, which by the afternoon extended to a further 11 mostly European countries set to join the settlement trade ban, raised a crucial question: When Israel becomes isolated, the US as its superpower backer often steps in to provide a diplomatic shield. Was the US, too, going to condemn Britain's policy?
Such a reprimand had been previewed by some observers. It felt even more likely when the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, appeared on the BBC before the UK announcement suggesting American "sanctions, repercussions or retaliations" could be coming for Britain, albeit that he didn't know what these were and hadn't spoken to President Trump.
But as Tuesday wore on, Washington's response was notably muted.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked about the UK move by reporters on the way to Colombia, said: "Obviously, we're not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today but I don't have any comment on it right now."
He added that Britain had notified the administration ahead of time (most likely during a phone call Trump had with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Monday) and said the US shared "the goal of stability" at a tense time in the region and didn't "want to see some uptick in violenceâ¦ in the West Bank".
It was hardly a withering rebuke of the British move, let alone any kind of punishment. In fact, Washington seemed to be sharing some of the concerns that motivated the move.
Asked about it on Wednesday, Trump said he would be speaking to Israel to understand their thinking, adding: "I understand exactly what's going on, but I want to find out why all of a sudden has that happened."
My understanding is that discussions about the US response were taking place at a high level within the administration on Tuesday. The baseline position appeared to be against any moves that could negatively impact American companies.
Fears for children's safety in West Bank school as settler attacks rise
Huckabee, who has longstanding views based on biblical justifications for Jewish settlement in the West Bank, appeared to be speaking off the cuff in some of his public remarks - a feature now common for some Trump-appointed ambassadors.
Staunchly pro-Israel Republicans in Congress were very publicly arguing for actions against Britain; pointing out that US states like Florida have punitive laws against companies that boycott Israel. But from the White House and State Department, more targeted criticism of the UK did not materialise.
It is still possible the administration will come out with some condemnation of the British move in the coming days. But the lack of any urgent pushback is likely to reflect current frustrations within the Trump administration at the Israeli leadership.
Trump's biggest foreign policy priority currently is trying to prevent the crisis worsening in the Strait of Hormuz, now the focal point of his stalemated war with Iran. His joint attack with the Israelis has left numerous friction points in his complex relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
At critical moments when Trump tried to reach a deal with Tehran, Netanyahu escalated fighting against Hezbollah in Lebanon. Israel has said it was acting against threats to security, but the moves had the potential to derail US diplomacy.
Meanwhile, Trump wants progress on his Gaza peace initiative, involving disarmament of Hamas and Israeli military withdrawal. Netanyahu has publicly rejected the plan in its current formulation.
Officially, the State Department referred me to Rubio's comments in Miami in relation to the UK announcement. But all told, Trump appears unwilling to come out to bat for Netanyahu currently.
This has extended to him so far not endorsing Netanyahu in the upcoming Israeli election. The administration, aware of splits within Trump's base of support on Israel, has also itself grown irritated at the extent of settler violence in the West Bank, given the lack of action by the Israeli government to meaningfully punish it. This is embarrassing for the White House.
West Bank violence against Palestinians is frequently the subject of protests from Trump's Gulf Arab allies - the countries mediating on Gaza, who Trump needs to pressure Hamas. They wonder how the US can draw concessions from the Israelis in relation to this if it can't on settler violence in the West Bank.
Trump eyes a legacy prize in both defeating Iran and moving forward with his Gaza peace plan - so batting for Israel against Europe over West Bank settlements seems to be, for Trump - so far, at least - juice that is not worth the squeeze.
  - Published23 hours ago
 ![Ed Miliband in the House of Commons](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/6cd1/live/8d1d81e0-aba9-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
- ![Palestinian kids walk to school. They are wearing blue school uniforms.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/1697/live/fa2ce530-ab47-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
summary: The UK and several European countries implemented sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank, prompting a furious diplomatic escalation and retaliation from Israel. Despite preliminary suggestions of potential American pushback from some officials, the US response from the White House and State Department remained notably muted. This lack of urgent condemnation likely reflects simmering frustration within the Trump administration regarding Israeli leadership, ongoing friction over Iran and Gaza diplomacy, and concerns over rising settler violence.
key_points: The UK introduced sanctions over West Bank settlements to protect the two-state solution, leading Israel to shut down a UK diplomatic mission, expel military staff, and ban certain British MPs.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered a muted response, stating the US would not take the same action as the UK but shared a goal of regional stability and avoiding increased violence.
President Trump's primary foreign policy focuses include managing the crisis involving Iran and pursuing a Gaza peace initiative, which Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has resisted.
The Trump administration has grown irritated by settler violence in the West Bank and the lack of action by the Israeli government to punish it.
Trump's reluctance to defend Israel against European sanctions also stems from pressure by Gulf Arab allies who are mediating on Gaza.

title: Tens of thousands line the streets as Norway bids farewell to King Harald V
author: Jon Henley
content:
Norway has observed a minute’s silence as it takes leave of King Harald V in a series of ceremonies, bringing to a close 13 days of national mourning that followed the popular monarch’s death last month at the age of 89.
Tens of thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo and foreign heads of state and government converged on the Norwegian capital for the funeral of the late king, a light-touch and unassuming reformer who ruled for more than three decades.
With the king’s casket carried on an artillery carriage, draped in Norway’s red royal banner and topped with white flowers, the funeral cortege made its way on foot along Oslo’s main avenue from royal palace to the cathedral, as a 21-gun salute rang out from the Akershus fortress.
![Norway’s Prince Sverre Magnus, King Haakon VIII, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Princess Martha Louise walk behind the coffin of Norway’s King Harald V, Oslo, Norway, 9 September 2026.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1eebcec78cce6de3c9a118098320e598a7fdaaa5/226_0_5764_4619/master/5764.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
King Haakon VIII, who succeeded his father on Harald’s death, and other royal family members walked in the cortege, with Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, 89, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, who is recovering from a lung transplant in June, following in a car.
![funeral cortege](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/057f871dd5bfac3a99929d11eef504067933473c/0_0_6938_5163/master/6938.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The procession was followed by a church ceremony attended by royals including Britain’s Prince William and Princess Anne; Spain’s King Felipe and Queen Letizia; Sweden’s royal family; Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary; the Netherlands’ King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima; and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and political leaders and dignitaries from more than 20 countries were at the service, at which the speaker of Norway’s parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, recalled a monarch who was “not afraid to meet his people with his rubber boots on”.
![William, Prince of Wales and Princess Anne, Princess Royal leave the funeral service of Norway’s King Harald, Oslo, Norway, 9 September 2026.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/b26f25f7d09951d25ed9ff09442b2b8e7cd4dc56/94_138_3074_2206/master/3074.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said Harald “struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth. He made Norway greater. He spoke of a ‘we’ in Norway where everyone is there for each other.”
After the service four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral, one breaking away to symbolise the king’s passing. The casket was then carried to the Akershus fortress where it was due to be lowered into the royal crypt, next to Harald’s parents and grandparents, in a private ceremony.
![A painted portrait of Norway’s King Harald V is displayed among flowers and Norwegian flags at a makeshift memorial outside the Royal Palace in Oslo, Norway.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a5ac8b3d091b792defcd9a86eae1f57b59f6234e/0_0_6949_4633/master/6949.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Norwegian police said securing the funeral had been the largest planned operation in the force’s history. More than 46,000 Norwegians have filed past the king’s casket in the past week and schoolchildren were allowed to miss classes for the occasion.
after newsletter promotion
Harald’s death came at a time of numerous crises for the Norwegian royal family, with Mette-Marit, 53, in particular coming under heavy criticism – including from the prime minister – for her association with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
![Marius Borg Hoiby](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4bfa199600d8175b19928e4022cc5f5d904ee766/0_0_1120_1140/master/1120.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The new queen’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest and wearing an ankle monitor pending his appeal against a conviction for rape and domestic violence, was given permission to attend the funeral and was a pallbearer during the transfer to the royal chapel.
Despite its recent scandals, however, the monarchy remains broadly popular: 72% of Norwegians support it, while 20% favour a republic or another form of government, according to a poll for the public broadcaster NRK.
![The casket of King Harald V leaves the Royal Palace for Oslo Cathedral, Norway, 9 September 2026.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d1dcca80f338ffecd2c8aee5cd36c0a2a8cf6f86/0_0_8116_5410/master/8116.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
summary: Tens of thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo for the funeral of Norway's King Harald V, concluding 13 days of national mourning following the monarch's death at age 89. Foreign heads of state, international royals, and dignitaries from more than 20 countries attended the service at Oslo Cathedral. The late king was remembered as an unassuming reformer, and his casket was later taken to the Akershus fortress for a private burial in the royal crypt.
key_points: King Harald V died at the age of 89 after ruling for more than three decades.
The funeral procession featured a 21-gun salute, a foot cortege from the royal palace to the cathedral, and a flyover by F-35 fighter jets.
Foreign royals and political leaders, including Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, attended the service.
Securing the funeral was the largest planned operation in Norwegian police history.
A recent poll for NRK showed that 72% of Norwegians support the monarchy despite recent family scandals.

title: Israel sanctions will not hurt intelligence sharing between spy agencies, says Miliband
author: Patrick Wintour
content:
British intelligence has been given assurances by its Israeli counterpart that information sharing with the UK will continue as before, Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has said.
The disclosure counters predictions that his decision to impose a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements would lead to a collapse in cooperation between the agencies.
The exchanges of information are seen as mutually beneficial and it is understood that Israeli intelligence was never willing to become mired in any political dispute between the two governments.
Miliband insists the intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
Miliband also expressed confidence that the US shared some of his exasperation with Israel’s reluctance to constrain the settlers in the West Bank, or to engage fully with the 20-point plan for Gaza set out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace.
As yet there has been no explicit criticism of the UK’s actions by the White House.
Trump avoided taking a hard stance when pressed about the coalition of countries, including the UK, France, and Canada, that have imposed new sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
“I’ll be speaking to Israel, I’ll be speaking to them, and I’ll find out what’s their thinking,” he said on Wednesday.
Trump, now locked in fighting midterm elections, appears reluctant to leap to the aid of Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, who persuaded him to go to war against Iran. That decision has pushed oil prices beyond $100 a barrel, helping to swell a threatened “blue wave” that could leave the Democrats in charge of both the House and the Senate.
There is also cross-party concern in the US at the violent tactics adopted by some Israeli settlers.
Miliband said on Sky News on Wednesday: “We obviously talked to the Americans in advance of our announcement. I think the whole international community, let me say this, has been quite frustrated, to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government.
“I think there is real concern about what is happening … underlying so much of the conflicts in the Middle East is this failure to really grasp the situation between Israel and Palestine.
“It’s in our interest to act not just because it’s standing up for our values, but because it’s in our interests to have this two-state solution as a rock of stability in the Middle East.”
The US decision not to oppose the UK over its sanctions and ban on trade with the Israeli settlements follows conversations between Trump and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, on Monday, as well as previous diplomatic exchanges at lower levels.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, was careful not to endorse the UK sanctions, but affirmed he shared the objective of securing greater stability.
Miliband can also claim credit for persuading Canada and France to join the trade ban, the surprise element in the package announced on Tuesday.
The agreement came together late in the process. Eight other European countries have announced their intention to introduce such measures or to support the measures within the EU, a statement of solidarity that represents probably less of a shift than headlines might suggest.
Some of the signatory countries had already taken steps independent of the EU, or had long been advocating for measures such as suspension of the Israel-EU trade agreement.
For France, the decision to join the British initiative was formalised relatively late during Emmanuel Macron’s trip to London, when he met Burnham on 3 September and celebrated the display of the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum.
France acted after a Franco-Swedish proposal made to the EU27 in April appeared to be making little progress.
The French plan aimed to establish an embargo or tariff on products from the occupied territories, but resistance from a constellation of countries including Germany, Italy and Bulgaria blocked progress. The commission also appeared to raise objections.
Paris last year had led the push to recognise the state of Palestine as critical to the two-state solution, but much of the French diplomatic energy had subsequently drifted. The UK, along with Jordan, will hold a meeting concerning improving humanitarian supplies into Gaza at the UN general assembly later this month.
In advance of Miliband’s statement, Trump had been hinting that he might support the Argentinian claim to sovereignty over the Falklands, a proposal mooted by Netanyahu’s son.
But in a little-noticed move likely to please Washington, Miliband this week supplemented the action against Israel by announcing fresh nuclear-related sanctions against Iran, including targeting Iranian ships involved in “malign behaviour”.
The UK also said it was backing a motion to be put to the UN stating Iran was in breach of its obligations on nuclear proliferation.
The new sanctions are extended to cover energy, software, metals, gold and related activities such as shipping, insurance and banking. Most Iranian aircraft will be prohibited from landing in the UK.
In response to the UK ban on goods, not due to come into force for at least six months, Israel has said it will: close the British consulate in in occupied East Jerusalem; remove British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel; terminate the UK’s role in training Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank; and deny 12 mainly leftwing MPs entry to Israel.
summary: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has stated that British intelligence has received assurances that information sharing with Israel will continue despite the UK's trade ban on illegal Israeli settlements. The UK-led initiative, which has also drawn in Canada and France, stems from international frustration over Israeli settlement actions and the lack of progress toward a two-state solution. In response to the UK's measures, Israel announced actions including closing the British consulate in East Jerusalem and denying entry to certain British MPs.
key_points: Israeli intelligence assured the UK that bilateral information sharing will continue despite the new trade ban on illegal settlements.
The UK trade ban on settlements was developed alongside Canada and France following frustrations with Israeli government actions.
The White House has not explicitly criticized the UK's actions, and the US shares concerns regarding violent settler tactics.

In response to the UK sanctions, Israel announced retaliatory measures including closing the British consulate in East Jerusalem and terminating the UK's role in training Palestinian Authority forces.

title: Miliband rejects chief rabbi’s claim that West Bank sanctions put UK Jews at risk
author: Aletha Adu
content:
Ed Miliband has rejected warnings from the UK’s chief rabbi that the government’s sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements will make British Jews less safe, as he emphasised ministers can confront the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government while also fighting antisemitism.
The foreign secretary announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, with the government taking the position that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory was unlawful.
The measures were coordinated with France, Canada and nine other countries that were also introducing sanctions on Israel over the increasing expansion of settlements, which the UK government says is threatening the future of a Palestinian state.
In a joint statement, leaders including Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and Mark Carney said: “The time has come to take further action to uphold our commitment to protect the two-state solution, our interests and to stand up for our values, before it is too late.”
The chief rabbi, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, called the UK sanctions a “dark day for British Jews” and said they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”.
Milliband, who describes himself as a “proud British Jew”, said he did not agree with Mirvis. Asked on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme whether he was saying the chief rabbi was wrong, Miliband replied: “Yes, I am saying I don’t agree with the chief rabbi, somebody over whom I have great respect.”
He added: “I just want to be very, very clear. As I said it in my statement yesterday, anyone who holds British Jews, or indeed Jews around the world, responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is engaging in antisemitism, pure and simple.
“And it must be possible to stand up in our society for British values of freedom, dignity, and against oppression and injustice, and do so as I believe I did yesterday in a way that calls out antisemitism.”
![Ephraim Mirvis](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/fe684eaf53f0c0d69c179cb9c307d58909d8ae45/0_0_4687_3265/master/4687.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The foreign secretary was pressed on the chief rabbi’s fear that British Jews could feel less safe as a result of the sanctions and was challenged by the BBC presenter, Justin Webb, who suggested Mirvis’s claim could mean less to Miliband because he did not attend synagogue.
“No, I don’t agree with that,” said Miliband, adding: “Antisemitism is a scourge and an evil … I want Jews, I want people of all faiths and none to feel safe in our country.”
NEW Burnham told MPs at PMQs that it was vital to take the decision before the Israeli elections because of the tenders for the E1 settlement plans were being finalised soon – and the sanctions would affect the practicality of those plans being carried out.
“Words from any politician about a two-state solution will be only words if it’s not backed with action, and leadership is about taking action where there is injustice, where we need to correct unfairness, people being driven out of their homes, losing their homes, being intimidated in their daily lives,” he said.
“Britain has to stand for something. Britain has to show leadership. Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice, where people are being bullied out of their homes, intimidated. We will always stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them.” NEW ENDS
Tuesday’s sanctions announcement also prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel.
Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised.
Miliband told Sky News he would “let our American friends speak for themselves” but insisted the international community had been “quite frustrated to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government”.
The foreign secretary said he regretted what the Israeli government had announced but was “proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do”.
Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance if this”.
The government is set to enact:
- 
  An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories and a new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.
- 
  A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements and a ban on advertising them in the UK.
- 
  Personal sanctions against the main individuals accused of promoting settler violence.
- 
  A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.
Miliband made an impassioned statement in the Commons on Tuesday, recounting the horrific tales he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank, whose homes had been destroyed, and doctors in Gaza who saw children dying while waiting for treatment.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the sanctions were “the right thing to do” and emphasised they were aimed “not at the Israeli people”. Burnham is due to face MPs over this issue at prime minister’s questions.
summary: Ed Miliband has rejected warnings from the UK’s chief rabbi that government sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank will endanger British Jews. The UK, coordinating with several other nations, introduced the trade and personal sanctions to protect the two-state solution and oppose illegal settlement expansion. In response to the measures, Israel ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering the country.
key_points: Ed Miliband disagreed with Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis's claim that West Bank sanctions put British Jews at risk.
The UK government announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements, coordinated with France, Canada, and nine other countries.
The measures include import bans on settlement goods, service restrictions, and personal sanctions against individuals accused of promoting settler violence.
Israel retaliated against the UK's actions by ordering the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banning 12 British individuals from entering Israel.

title: Miliband defends sanctions on Israeli settlements and pushes back against chief rabbi’s criticism – UK politics live
author: Andrew Sparrow
content:
Miliband defends sanctions on Israeli settlements and pushes back against chief rabbi’s criticism
Good morning. Yesterday Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, made what may turn out to be one of the most important Commons statements of the year. Here is our overnight report by Pippa Crerar, Jessica Elgot and Kiran Stacey.
It starts: “Rarely in recent years has the Commons felt like the cockpit of history. On Tuesday it did.”
Ministers were worried about a backlash from Donald Trump. So far, that has not happened, and in the US Axios is reporting that, when Andy Burnham spoke to Trump on Monday, “two sources with knowledge of the call said Trump didn’t push back or ask Burnham to change course”. In his report for Axios, Barak Ravid says: “US officials told their British counterparts they shared their concerns about the Netanyahu government’s West Bank policy, even if they disagreed with these specific sanctions, sources say.”
But in the UK some of the leading organisations representing the Jewish community have strongly condemned the decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and Sir Ephraim Mirvis, the chief rabbi, described yesterday as “truly a dark day for British Jews”. The rightwing papers are all leading their coverage on his remarks.
Mail splash Photograph: Daily Mail
Miliband has been giving interviews this morning, and he has said he does not agree.
Asked about the chief rabbi’s statement, Miliband told Sky News:
Well, I’m a proud British Jew, and I don’t agree with the chief rabbi.
I have great respect for the chief rabbi, but I don’t agree with him, and I believe that it must be possible to do what we did yesterday, which is to stand up for British values of the rule of law, of dignity for people, of the prevention of injustice, and do so in a way, as I did yesterday, to say to anyone in our country who holds British Jews responsible for the actions of the Israeli government, that is antisemitism, pure and simple.
We will hear from Andy Burnham on this later at PMQs.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9am: Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, speaks at the Wild Summit in Bristol. Words and video planned
From 9am: David Anderson and Jonathan Hall, the former and current independent reviewer of terror legislation respectively, are among those giving evidence to phase two of the Southport inquiry, looking at Prevent’s role in managing violence-fixated individuals.
10am: Prof Alexis Jay, chair of the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA), is among the experts giving evidence to the London assembly’s police and crime committee on grooming gangs.
After 12.30pm: Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, may make a Commons statement on the air traffic control chaos. She is also opening the second reading debate on the civil aviation bill.
Deputy Tory leader Alex Burghart accuses Labour of 'hypocrisy', saying it is not taking similar action against China
Alex Burghart, the deputy Tory leader, was giving interviews this morning. On Israel, he opened up a new line of attack against the government, accusing it of hypocrisy. This is what he told GB News.
At the same time that Labour were saying all these things about Israel in the House of Commons, they put out a communique.
They put out an account of a conversation that Andy Burnham has had with the Chinese president, and it said how constructive they wanted to be with China, how they wanted to work with China, and what a great relationship we have.
Now, I’m not saying we should put sanctions on China, but I would point out that the Chinese over the past few decades have been guilty of some of the very worst human rights violations that we’ve seen anywhere, and yet Labour’s hypocrisy is capable of allowing it to have these two totally different approaches at the same time. I think that this is madness.
Reform UK insists National Rally agreed migrant policy after backlash in France
Reform UK has insisted its deal with France’s far-right National Rally to return migrants back across the Channel was fully approved by the party and signed off by its president, Jordan Bardella, amid a furious backlash in France. Rowena Mason and Angelique Chrisafis have the story.
Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar thanks Badenoch for her 'firm opposition' to UK sanctions
Gideon Saar, the Israeli foreign minister, has thanked Kemi Badenoch for her “firm opposition” to the government’s sanctions against his country. They spoke last night and afterward he posted this on social media.
Great conversation this evening with UK Opposition Leader @KemiBadenoch and Shadow Foreign Secretary @TomTugendhat.
I thanked them for their firm opposition to the hostile Labour Government’s announcement today and its series of anti-Israel policies since taking office.
I welcomed their support for the friendship with Israel and their commitment for the future relations between our countries. We know that we have many friends in the UK, but unfortunately we are faced with the ongoing hostility of the current Labour government.
I also thanked Kemi for her warm wishes ahead of the Jewish New Year.
Miliband says he is 'confident' that security cooperation with Israel will continue despite backlash over sanctions
In his interview on the Today programme, Ed Miliband also said that he was “confident our security cooperation with Israel will continue” despite the sanctions.
Asked why he was confident that there would not be a problem, “given how angry [the Israelis] are”, Miliband replied:
I won’t go into the details of this, but we have important intelligence and security relationships with Israel and I’m confident they will continue.
And I was very clear yesterday that we do believe in working with our Israeli partners when it comes to the threats they face from Iran. For example, I announced new sanctions on Iran yesterday.
She explained that, while the most obvious part of the announcement relates to the ban on the import of goods produced in settlements, the measures relating to financial services are potentially much more significant.
She said:
Miliband highlighted that the Israeli settler population in occupied Palestine had almost tripled over the past three decades, from 270,000 in 1993 to 770,000 today.
That expansion is underpinned by large government subsidies. A trade ban alone would be unlikely to have much impact on the viability of construction that is a government priority, or on the broader Israeli economy.
However, plans to place sanctions on any company that finances or facilitates settlement expansion could force Israel’s main banks and insurance companies to choose between their business interests in the UK and those in occupied Palestine.
Miliband has not provided details of the new measures, which he said would take between six and nine months to put in place. But they have the potential to slow or stop construction.
The activist Yehuda Shaul wrote in a social media post about new building projects: “Companies that bid for tenders on government-led projects, including settlement expansion, must have a financial guarantor. Without the backing of Israeli financial institutions, these projects cannot occur.”
Some Israeli commentators have expressed doubts as to whether, in practice, these sanctions really will cover mainstream Israeli banks. But, in his interview on the Today programme this morning, Miliband insisted they could.
He said:
I also make this wider point, because this is about a substantive intervention to make a difference to the facts on the ground.
With our sanctions regime, we are also seeking to cut off the supply of the supply lines of British finance, British construction, for settlement expansion. This is about a clear purpose, which is to draw a line in the sand and to stop this infinite, ever-expanding settlement expansion.
Asked if Israeli banks would be covered too, Miliband replied:
The way this works is that we sanction companies, and we don’t name the companies in advance. We sanction companies that might be engaging in the occupied territories. And then it is about the relationship with British citizens and British companies.
When Justin Webb, the presenter, put it to Miliband that this meant the sanctions would go much wider than just applying to people “selling dates”, and that they would apply to companies in Israel with relationships with settler companies, Miliband replied:
Yes, because this is about seeking to have an impact on the services that are provided to expand the occupation.
And we are very serious about making a substantive difference and using the power of our sanctions regime to make a difference to the facts on the ground.
Ed Miliband leaving Millbank studios this morning. Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty Images
A spokesperson for the Israeli embassy in London has accused the UK of deploying a diplomatic “nuclear option” against his country.
In an interview with the Today programme this morning, Alex Gandler said:
A response and a conversation between friends is something that is wanted.
Operating a nuclear option of sanction between democratic countries, especially towards a country that is at war for the past few years and is fighting a shared enemy in Iran, is something that is unheard of.
Hence, our assessment that this has nothing to do with realities on the ground and everything to do with the fact that there’s politics involved.
Gandler also claimed the timing of the announcement was particularly bad.
The timing couldn’t be worse than it is regarding Israel, as we are less than 50 days away from elections in the country, days away from our high holidays in Israel.
It definitely does not promote the relationship between Israel and the United Kingdom, that is for sure, and it does create an atmosphere for violence against Jews.
The BBC’s Tom Bateman has posted this on social media. It is the sign outside the UK consulate in Jerusalem that Israel is now closing. (See 9.21am.)
Sign outside UK consulate in Jerusalem Photograph: Tom Bateman
Bateman says:
The very long standing sign that used to be on the wall in the British consulate in East Jerusalem. Israel has said it will close the consulate in retaliation for the UK’s trade ban on settlements
In his interview with Sky News this morning, Miliband sidestepped a question about what Washington is telling the UK government about its decision to impose sanctions on Israel relating to the illegal West Bank settlements.
Miliband said:
I’ll let our American friends speak for themselves.
We obviously talked to them in advance of our announcement.
You know, I think the whole international community has been quite frustrated, to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government.
I will let them say what they feel, but I think there is real concern about what is happening … Underlying so many of the conflicts in the Middle East is this failure to really grasp the situation between Israel and Palestine, and this is why it’s in our interest to act.
Miliband plays down significance of Israel's retaliatory measures, saying UK sanctions still 'right thing to do'
In his interview with Sky News this morning, Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, said that he regretted the fact that Israel is ordering the UK to close its consulate in Jerusalem in response to the UK sanctions. But he said the government had weighed up “the costs and benefits” of its move in advance.
He said:
I regret what the Israeli government has announced, but I’m proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do.
It will be damaging, that’s true, but we weighed up the costs and the benefits in advance of this.
And we did something very important. We talked to the representatives of the Palestinian people, the Palestinian prime minister, the representative here, and they both said to us with a very clear voice, you need to act from our point of view.
He added:
I would prefer that Israel hadn’t announced what it did, but overall, I strongly believe that what we did, along with other international allies, was absolutely the right thing to do.
Ed Miliband leaving the Millbank broadcasting studios at Westminster this morning, after doing TV and radio interviews. Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty Images

In his report for Axios, Barak Ravid says: “US officials told their British counterparts they shared their concerns about the Netanyahu government’s West Bank policy, even if they disagreed with these specific sanctions, sources say.”
But in the UK some of the leading organisations representing the Jewish community have strongly condemned the decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and Sir Ephraim Mirvis, the chief rabbi, described yesterday as “truly a dark day for British Jews”. We will hear from Andy Burnham on this later at PMQs.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9am: Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, speaks at the Wild Summit in Bristol. Words and video planned
From 9am: David Anderson and Jonathan Hall, the former and current independent reviewer of terror legislation respectively, are among those giving evidence to phase two of the Southport inquiry, looking at Prevent’s role in managing violence-fixated individuals.
10am: Prof Alexis Jay, chair of the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA), is among the experts giving evidence to the London assembly’s police and crime committee on grooming gangs.
After 12.30pm: Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, may make a Commons statement on the air traffic control chaos. She is also opening the second reading debate on the civil aviation bill.
