summary: A Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in the murder case against Lindsay Clancy after the jury deadlocked following seven days of deliberations. Clancy does not deny killing her three children in 2023, but her defense argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible. Prosecutors will determine their next steps, which could include a new trial or a plea agreement, at a hearing scheduled for September 29.
key_points: A judge declared a mistrial after the jury deadlocked and could not reach a unanimous verdict after a week of deliberations.
Clancy pleaded not guilty to three first-degree murder charges for the 2023 deaths of her children, with her defense arguing she suffered from postpartum psychosis.
Clancy remains held on murder charges and will continue to stay in a mental health facility.
A hearing is scheduled for September 29 to determine the next steps for prosecutors, which may include holding another trial or pursuing a plea agreement.

title: Witkoff and Kushner will travel to ‘end’ Russia’s war in Ukraine: Trump
author: Evan Semones
content:
![US President Donald Trump speaks before signing executive orders releated to beef processing and cattle ranchers, in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on September 4, 2026. (Photo by Kent NISHIMURA / AFP)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/afp_6a9b20f0e9ec-1788551408.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
United States President Donald Trump said that US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are travelling this weekend in an attempt to revive peace talks between Ukraine and Russia.
On Friday, while speaking at the White House, Trump said Witkoff and his son-in-law Kushner, who are preparing to travel to Kyiv and Moscow this weekend, are bringing a proposal to “end the war”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Ten injured in Ukraine as Kyiv expects talks with US envoys in coming days
- list 2 of 3US envoys headed to Russia and Ukraine to relaunch mediation
- list 3 of 3Russian drone strikes Ukraine’s security service headquarters
“I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner … to see whether or not we can get something done,” Trump said. “And there may be a good chance that we’ll do it.”
“We have an idea for peace,” Trump added without mentioning any specifics about his administration’s plan.
According to Russian state news agency TASS, Witkoff and Kushner will be in Moscow on Saturday and Sunday, their first visit since January.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said the duo would be in Ukraine on Sunday, marking their first visit to the country since Trump returned to power.
Russian President Vladimir Putin recently said negotiations were “frozen”. But this weekend’s expected talks come as both sides continue to ramp up air attacks, with Russia hitting the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU security services on Friday.
At least 12 people were injured in the strike, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said that while people weren’t shocked the SBU building was hit, it has made them wonder what target might be next.
“It’s not so much that people never expected the SBU to be hit, but it really raises the question of if Russia can hit this, what else can it hit?” she said. “Some people here are wondering whether this attack, for example, could be aimed at possibly dissuading” the US envoys’ trips to Ukraine.
Trump told reporters Friday that a peace deal in the more than four-year conflict has remained elusive due to what he described as a “personality problem” between both sides.
“President Zelenskyy and President Putin truly hate each other,” Trump said. “They have serious hate, and it’s getting in the way.”
While exact figures are unknown, a study released in July by the Center for Strategic and International Studies says the war has cost Russia some 450,000 lives. Ukraine is estimated to have endured between 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities.
summary: US President Donald Trump announced that US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are traveling to Kyiv and Moscow to revive peace talks and propose a plan to end the Russia-Ukraine war. The weekend visit marks the envoys' first trip to both countries since Trump returned to power, coming amid ongoing air attacks and a recent Russian strike on Ukraine's security service headquarters. Trump attributed the difficulty in reaching a peace deal partly to a severe personal animosity between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
key_points: US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are traveling to Kyiv and Moscow to attempt to relaunch peace negotiations.
President Donald Trump stated the envoys are bringing a proposal to end the war, though specific details were not disclosed.
The diplomatic visit coincides with intensified air attacks, including a Russian strike on Ukraine's SBU security service headquarters in Kyiv that injured at least 12 people.
Trump cited a deep personal hatred between Presidents Zelenskyy and Putin as a major obstacle that has kept a peace deal elusive.

title: Trump's peace envoys to visit Moscow and Kyiv over weekend
author: Jaroslav Lukiv
content:
![US negotiators Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff. Photo: April 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/0e39/live/bcf0df00-a86d-11f1-bbad-43eaf67b94b6.jpg)
Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law (left), and Steve Witkoff are expected to hold separate meetings with the presidents of Russia and Ukraine
- Published
US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend, as efforts to end the war appear to be gathering pace.
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed he will meet the envoys on Sunday, after they visit Moscow on Saturday to hold talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Witkoff and Kushner have led US President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal, but a gulf remains between the two warring sides.
"They are bringing with them a proposal to end the war," Trump told reporters when asked about the visits.
Earlier on Friday, Zelensky said a Russian drone hit the office of Ukraine's security chief Oleksandr Poklad in Kyiv. Poklad appears to be unharmed.
In a post on social media, Zelensky said he had ordered Poklad, who head the SBU security service, to respond "adequately" to the attack.
Witkoff and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, have visited Russia multiple times, but the purported talks will be the first in Ukraine.
Zelensky said he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to do the same for Ukraine.
Russia's state news agency Tass said Witkoff and Kushner were "expected to arrive in Moscow and then to Kyiv... on 5-6 September", quoting a source.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later told reporters: "I wouldn't announce anything, but when these contacts take place, we will inform you."
Meanwhile, Putin told an international economic forum on Thursday that "there are chances" a peace deal could be reached.
"First of all, Moscow and Kyiv must agree between themselves," he said.
But he showed no sign of backing down from his maximalist demands, which included more territorial concessions from Ukraine.
Kyiv and its European allies have repeatedly rejected Putin's terms saying they are tantamount to capitulation.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and currently controls about 20% of its territory.

summary: US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are scheduled to visit Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend to hold separate meetings with the presidents of Russia and Ukraine. US President Donald Trump stated that the envoys are bringing a proposal to end the war, although significant gulfs remain between the two warring sides. The upcoming discussions follow recent developments, including a Russian drone strike in Kyiv and ongoing talks regarding potential peace terms.
key_points: US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow on Saturday and Kyiv on Sunday.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed he will meet with the US envoys.
President Donald Trump stated that the envoys are carrying a proposal to end the war.
A Russian drone recently hit the office of Ukraine's security chief Oleksandr Poklad, who was unharmed.
Russian President Vladimir Putin stated there are chances for a peace deal but maintained his demands for territorial concessions.

title: Norway seizes Russian ship over Ukraine's $4.2bn Crimea claim
author: Quirino Mealha
content:
Norwegian authorities have impounded a Russian-owned expedition cruise vessel in Svalbard on behalf of Ukraine's state energy company, Naftogaz, which is hunting Russian assets worldwide to collect on an arbitration award stemming from Russia’s illegal annexation of Crimea.
Norwegian officials seized the Russian state-owned ship named "Professor Molchanov" on Wednesday at the port of Barentsburg in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard.
The authorities acted on an application from Ukraine's state energy company, Naftogaz, which is pursuing compensation for energy assets Russia expropriated when it illegally annexed Crimea in 2014.
The seizure followed an order from the Norwegian Nord-Troms and Senja District Court issued on Monday.
Svalbard's governor, Lars Fause, whose office carried out the operation as the local enforcement authority, said the vessel may not leave its current location. Passengers who were aboard are being dealt with separately by Norwegian authorities.
At the time of writing, the Kremlin has not made a statement regarding the situation.
A $4.2 billion bill that Moscow will not settle
An arbitration tribunal at the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled in 2023 that Russia must compensate Naftogaz and six associated companies for unlawfully seizing their Crimean assets, including gas fields, pipelines and the Black Sea producer Chornomornaftogaz.
The outstanding principal stands at roughly $4.22 billion (€3.64bn), before interest and costs which could drive the amount to around $5 billion (€4.31bn).
Russia has declined to pay.
Naftogaz has therefore been petitioning courts in countries where Russian commercial property can be found, and the award had already been recognised as enforceable in Norway before this week's order.
"Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz' acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko, calling the seizure "another important step towards restoring justice."
Fedorenko added that the company would "continue to pursue Russian assets around the world" until the money is paid.
In Norway, Naftogaz is represented by the law firm Wikborg Rein, alongside international counsel Covington & Burling.
Part of a widening hunt
The Arctic operation is not an isolated one.
Enforcement proceedings in the Crimea case are active in around ten jurisdictions, with Russian assets already seized in Finland and France.
Barentsburg is a Russian coal-mining settlement sitting on Norwegian territory, a legacy of the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, which confirmed Norwegian sovereignty over the archipelago while granting signatory states, Russia among them, equal rights to commercial activity there.
The "Professor Molchanov", owned by the Russian Federation, runs commercial expedition cruises including voyages to Svalbard itself.

![Department store windows display the Danish flag and the Danish crown in Copenhagen, 13 January, 2024](https://images.euronews.com/articles/stories/09/89/98/09/480x270_cmsv2_8b7a6ac3-24cb-5c95-8654-fee7619ccd18-9899809.jpg)

summary: Norwegian authorities have seized a Russian-owned expedition cruise vessel in Svalbard at the request of Ukraine's state energy company, Naftogaz. The action aims to enforce a $4.2 billion arbitration award against Russia for the expropriation of energy assets in Crimea following its 2014 annexation. Naftogaz is actively pursuing Russian commercial assets across approximately ten jurisdictions worldwide to collect the unpaid compensation.
key_points: Norwegian officials impounded the Russian state-owned ship "Professor Molchanov" at the port of Barentsburg in Svalbard.
The seizure was executed following an order from the Norwegian Nord-Troms and Senja District Court on behalf of Naftogaz.
A 2023 tribunal ruling ordered Russia to pay roughly $4.22 billion for unlawfully seizing Crimean energy assets, a payment Russia has refused to make.
Similar enforcement proceedings and asset seizures by Naftogaz are active in other jurisdictions, including Finland and France.

title: UN votes to adopt new world map to reflect Africa's true size
author: Thomas Mukhwana; Wycliffe Muia
content:
![Side-by-side maps of Africa comparing two map projections. The Mercator projection on the left makes Africa appear smaller in comparison with Europe to its north. The Equal Earth projection on the right shows a longer, more proportionally accurate shape of the continent.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/722b/live/e7c4b610-a873-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png)
The Mercator projection is the map widely used across the globe but inaccurately depicts the sizes of countries and continents
- Published
The UN General Assembly has voted to replace the traditional world map with one that more accurately reflects the size of Africa.
The "Correct the Map" resolution, sponsored by Togo and backed by African Union (AU) members, passed with the support of 164 nations, including France and the UK. The United States was the only nation to vote against it - and there were six abstentions.
The UN vote is non-binding but will see changes to the maps used by institutions around the world.
The Mercator map, which has been in common use since the 16th Century, has come in for criticism as it shows Africa as similar in size to Greenland, even though it is 14 times larger.
Critics say this leads to the development needs and potential for countries near the equator to be minimised.
The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the world.
The distortion of his map is a result of the fact that it is impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.
Whenever a map of the world is drawn, compromises need to be made.
The Mercator map shows the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing bigger.
In an effort to correct this, a team of cartographers in 2018 created an equal area map they called the Equal Earth projection.
In February, the AU's 54 member states adopted it, and said it "more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa".
Online campaign group #CorrectTheMap said: "You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare."
Ahead of Friday's vote, Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the Reuters news agency: "A fair world begins with a fair map."
Earlier he had told a UN briefing: "A map is never neutral. It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood."
He had the backing of the French Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot, who said his ministry was going to stop using the Mercator map, external.
"Changing the map obviously doesn't change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth," he said.
But Yaryna Ferencevych, a US representative at the UN, said the resolution mocked the work and purpose of the UN General Assembly, external.
"Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th Century, and their role in promoting reparations and 'cognitive justice'," she said.
In March, the US was also critical when a resolution was adopted declaring the transatlantic slave trade "the gravest crime against humanity".
![Why does Africa appear so small? comparing the Mercator and Equal Earth map projections. The top section explains that projections like Mercator distort land areas near the poles. Annotations note that Greenland appears as large as Africa in this projection, despite Greenland covering about 2.2 million square kilometres and Africa about 30.4 million square kilometres, roughly 14 times more. The lower section shows an Equal Earth map projection, which presents the relative sizes and shapes of continents more accurately, making Africa appear substantially larger than Greenland.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/9787/live/a8e18490-a883-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
"Africa's misrepresentation on world maps is not just a cartographic error - it's a narrative issue," Lerato Mogoatlhe from Africa No Filter, one of the groups behind the campaign to ditch the Mercator map, told the BBC.
It was part of efforts to stop the "world's longest misinformation and disinformation" about Africa, she said.
For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, the Mercator map has implicitly downplayed the African continent's vast resources, population and investment opportunities.
"Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.
More BBC news from Africa:
![To the right of the banner a woman with sunglasses on her head and wearing a denim jacket and yellow T-shirt looks down at her mobile phone. A graphic for BBC News Africa in black and red is on the left of the image which has a pale golden brown background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/a743/live/681bd460-6ee0-11f1-8e1d-bbbb1017d210.png)
summary: The UN General Assembly has voted to adopt a new world map that more accurately reflects the true size of Africa, replacing the traditional Mercator projection. Sponsored by Togo and backed by African Union members, the non-binding resolution passed with 164 votes in favor, while the United States was the only nation to vote against it. The 16th-century Mercator map has been criticized for making regions near the equator, such as Africa, appear much smaller than they actually are.
key_points: The UN General Assembly voted to replace the traditional Mercator map with an equal-area projection that correctly shows Africa's size.
The resolution passed with 164 votes in support, with the US as the sole opposing vote and six abstentions.
The Mercator map, created in 1569, makes Africa appear similar in size to Greenland even though Africa is roughly 14 times larger.
African Union members and campaign groups argued that the Mercator projection minimized the continent's development needs, resources, and global standing.

title: Lindsay Clancy's case ended in a mistrial - what happens next?
author: Madeline Halpert; Sareen Habeshian
content:
Watch moment judge in Clancy case says a mistrial likely
- Published
After a week of mulling Lindsay Clancy's fate, a judge has declared a mistrial in the case of the US mother accused of murdering her three young children.
It came after the jury said they could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether Clancy was guilty of murder.
The declaration opens the door to a host of possibilities about what happens next.
Clancy, who faced three counts of first-degree murder, does not deny killing her children in 2023 but pleaded not guilty, with her lawyers arguing she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible.
The prosecution said she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them.
What is a mistrial?
Under US law, the jury must unanimously reach a conclusion "beyond a reasonable doubt". If they cannot, the judge can call a mistrial, which ends the trial with no verdict.
Jurors in Clancy's trial had been deadlocked for days, and told the judge three times that they were unable to come to a unanimous decision.
Sullivan, who is overseeing the trial, previously urged them to continue deliberating until there is no possible chance of a decision.
In a last-ditch effort he issued additional instructions, known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge in the state, encouraging the panel to consider all perspectives and ensuring jurors were questioning and examining their own views in the case.
The jury continued to indicate they could not come to a consensus, leading the judge to say he had no choice but to declare a mistrial.
This does not mean prosecutors have proven their case, nor does it mean the defendant is not guilty.
Now, the prosecution could either refile and restart with a new jury or negotiate a plea agreement.
Alternatively, prosecutors could dismiss the charges altogether.
Watch: BBC's Ione Wells explains how the Lindsay Clancy trial could end
Will Lindsay Clancy go free?
Not immediately. Clancy will remain held under the same murder charges in the mental health facility where she is currently housed as lawyers weigh their next steps.
If a new trial is planned, Clancy will remain in that facility until it begins - though her lawyers could ask for a review of her bail situation, said Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law.
Even as a new trial is being prepared, prosecutors could still negotiate with Clancy's team over a plea agreement, Cucolo said.
Will prosecutors ask for a new trial?
In serious felony cases like these, prosecutors often ask for a retrial.
If they do, the jury selection process will take place once again and a new trial will be scheduled with a new set of jurors.
The time it could take to schedule another trial will depend on factors including the court schedule, any legal requests either side may file, and how long it may take to line up expert witnesses.
The six-week trial in Massachusetts captured significant public interest, with crowds sometimes gathering outside.
"A case like this that obviously has been so high profile, and there is so much of an emotional response to this to the facts of this case, I think it's very likely that the prosecutor will ask for a retrial," Cucolo said.
![Clancy's children Cora Clancy (left), 8-month-old Callan (centre) and three-year-old Dawson](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/620/cpsprodpb/a102/live/ff5d77d0-a87d-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Clancy's children Cora (left), eight-month-old Callan (centre) and three-year-old Dawson
Why was the jury deadlocked?
That is unclear, but it's been a complex case with each side presenting a huge amount of expert testimony.
The identities of the nine women and three men on the jury has not been made public, and the judge banned any photographing or filming of them to retain their anonymity.
But once the case is over, a juror can choose whether or not to speak publicly about the case and their deliberations.
Following other high-profile trials, jurors have in some instances come forward to discuss the case, even writing books or doing media interviews.
So while it remains unknown to the public what has gone on behind closed doors, more could be revealed in the coming days or weeks.
If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.
In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline
  - Published8 hours ago
 ![Lindsay Clancy in court](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/e0d0/live/d392c020-a241-11f1-804a-af7f2afa0e85.jpg)
summary: A judge declared a mistrial in the case of Lindsay Clancy after the jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict on charges that she murdered her three children in 2023. Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors argued her actions were intentional. Clancy will remain held in a mental health facility while prosecutors weigh their options, which include seeking a retrial, negotiating a plea agreement, or dismissing the charges.
key_points: A mistrial was declared after the jury remained deadlocked and unable to reach a unanimous verdict after days of deliberations.
Clancy does not deny killing her three children in 2023 but pleaded not guilty, with her defense arguing she suffered from postpartum psychosis.
The prosecution claimed Clancy made a calculated and intentional decision to kill her children.
Clancy will remain housed in a mental health facility under her current murder charges while legal teams determine their next steps.
Prosecutors can choose to refile and restart with a new jury, negotiate a plea agreement, or dismiss the charges altogether.

title: Russian Conscripts Increasingly Blocked From Leaving Country Amid Mobilization Fears
author: Kyiv Post; Alisa Orlova
content:
Russian conscripts are increasingly being stopped at the border as authorities tighten restrictions on leaving the country, with the latest cases fueling fears that Moscow may be preparing for another mobilization.
Between Aug. 18 and 31, Russia’s human rights project “Idite Lesom” (Get Lost) received reports from 73 conscripts who tried to leave the country. Fifty managed to cross the border, while 23 were denied exit. In several cases, the travel bans appeared only during border checks.
One conscript who had lived in Indonesia for years returned to Russia for a two-week visit but was unable to leave again. His registry record showed a travel ban.
Another was stopped at a Moscow airport despite saying he had never received a draft notice. He learned about the restriction only when he reached border control.
In another case, a conscript checked the electronic registry before a Moscow-Yerevan flight and found no restrictions. Border officers nevertheless told him he was barred from leaving. Minutes later, the ban appeared in the registry.
A conscript from Novosibirsk discovered he had received a draft notice only after being stopped at the airport. Although the military enlistment office later canceled the restriction, border guards stopped him again two days later because the ban remained in their system.
Still, not every conscript is being blocked.
One man with a draft notice for a medical examination and a valid deferment was able to fly to Yerevan because no travel ban was listed. Others successfully left Russia despite having paper draft notices. One conscript even crossed into Kazakhstan despite his registry showing a travel ban and other restrictions.
![ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 3, 2026](https://static.kyivpost.com/storage/2026/09/04/a1df3e0404db8c0c8b2a79977ef6f88c.webp?w=420&f=webp) 
Belarus is also becoming a less reliable route out. Of 11 conscripts who contacted “Idite Lesom” after attempting to leave through Belarus, four succeeded and seven were stopped.
Putin denies new mobilization plans
The tightening restrictions come as speculation grows that the Kremlin could announce another mobilization following September’s State Duma elections.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly dismissed such reports, most recently calling them an “information attack” aimed at disrupting the elections.
“There is no scenario today that would require mobilization,” Putin said Thursday at the Eastern Economic Forum. He described the reports as a planned information operation.
A day earlier, Putin called reports of a possible post-election mobilization “nonsense” and again rejected the possibility of a new mass call-up.
Putin has insisted that Russia does not need another mobilization, claiming that Russians continue to join the military voluntarily by signing contracts with the Defense Ministry.
He also claimed Russia has “no problems” recruiting troops for the war against Ukraine, while alleging that Ukraine’s armed forces are losing 8,000 to 12,000 personnel each month. He provided no evidence for the figure.
Despite the Kremlin’s repeated denials, speculation about a new mobilization has intensified since the summer.
Russian pro-war Z-channels reported in July that a potential forced call-up could involve as many as 1.2 million people. Western intelligence agencies have separately assessed that Russia is preparing military infrastructure to receive and equip additional recruits.
The Institute for the Study of War has also reported signs of preparations for a potential new mobilization. Western intelligence officials and several European officials who spoke to The Washington Post have not ruled one out, citing Russia’s heavy battlefield losses.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates that Russian forces have suffered at least 1.4 million casualties in Ukraine, including severely wounded troops who cannot return to service.
Russia tightens the exit
Russia’s electronic draft system has already been used to restrict travel. After the electronic draft-notice registry was fully launched in March, Russians began reporting that failure to appear at military enlistment offices could trigger bans on leaving the country.
Authorities have also tightened coordination with Belarus. In April, a St. Petersburg conscript was stopped while attempting to leave Russia through Belarus, prompting the Movement of Conscientious Objectors to warn that border authorities in the two countries may have begun exchanging data from their military registration systems.
Meanwhile, Russians appear to be rushing to leave through other routes.
Amid the mobilization rumors, traffic through the Upper Lars border crossing between Russia and Georgia surged to record levels.
From Aug. 15 to 18, more than 19,000–20,000 people crossed the border each day, according to Russia’s Federal Customs Service – significantly more than during comparable periods in previous years.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter
summary: Russian authorities are increasingly blocking conscripts from leaving the country, fueling fears of a potential new mobilization amid tightening border restrictions and electronic registry bans. Between August 18 and 31, the human rights project "Idite Lesom" recorded 23 cases of conscripts being denied exit out of 73 reported attempts. While Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly dismissed reports of an upcoming mobilization as "nonsense" and an "information attack," intelligence assessments and growing border traffic indicate widespread public concern.
key_points: Russian human rights project "Idite Lesom" received reports of 23 conscripts being denied exit from the country between August 18 and 31.
Travel bans frequently appeared unexpectedly during border checks or were applied to electronic registries in real-time.
President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly denied plans for a new mobilization, calling such reports an information attack.
Despite Kremlin denials, Western intelligence, think tanks, and pro-war channels have pointed to signs of potential mobilization preparations driven by heavy battlefield casualties.

title: Higher education regulator apologises for imposing £585,000 fine on university
author: Richard Adams
content:
England’s higher education regulator has apologised for a string of mistakes in its decision to punish the University of Sussex with a record fine that was later overturned by the high court.
The Office for Students (OfS) tried to impose a £585,000 fine against Sussex last year after claiming the university breached free speech regulations involving its former professor Kathleen Stock. It was forced to back down in April after a judicial review initiated by Sussex found the OfS “had closed its mind” and acted with bias.
In a statement, the regulator said: “The OfS made mistakes in the Sussex case, which we regret. The actions we are announcing today show our continuing commitment to learning the lessons from this case with humility and honesty.”
Among the changes promised by the OfS in a “lessons learned” report were “ensuring respectful relationships with higher education providers” and in the future using “alternative forms of intervention where possible to effect change” before taking enforcement action such as fines.
Prof Sasha Roseneil, Sussex’s vice-chancellor, said she welcomed the OfS’s acknowledgement of its mistakes but was concerned that its plans for reform “fell short” in a number of areas.
Roseneil said: “[The report] reveals deep cultural problems within the OfS in relation to freedom of expression and internal challenge, and it is heartening to see the new leadership setting different expectations for the organisation, expectations that are more appropriate for a public institution, trusted to regulate one of the most important sectors in a democratic society.
“However, the report does not fully reflect the breadth or the seriousness of the high court’s findings or all the lessons that could be learned from the case.
![Sasha Roseneil.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/612ca20eee49624fd15ff5d606294cba2a51fb0b/1113_289_3835_4794/master/3835.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“It is also disappointing that the review missed the opportunity to engage with the University of Sussex when their lack of engagement was roundly criticised by the high court.”
The high court’s findings were backed up by an internal review by KPMG commissioned by the OfS, published in summary on Thursday. KPMG’s findings criticised the regulator for being adversarial, allowing gaps in its written records, and lacking clear accountability.
“It appears that insufficient emphasis was placed on maintaining constructive engagement and dialogue with higher education providers, which contributed to relationships becoming increasingly adversarial,” according to the review’s summary.
![Kathleen Stock, a British philosopher and writer.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6e3603237777003f483003bc705fbf82ecd1db7c/2673_790_1246_1557/master/1246.jpg?width=120&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
KPMG also criticised the OfS’s leadership at the time for becoming blinkered: “The investigation team was made up of particularly senior staff, reflecting the case’s novelty, complexity and profile.
“However, the concentration of decision making and delivery responsibilities within a relatively small group reduced the opportunity for independent challenge and fresh perspectives.”
The OfS’s chair, Edward Peck, and chief executives Ruth Hannant and Polly Payne, thanked the University of Sussex’s leadership “for the frank discussions and insightful commentary leading to this point”.
Hannant and Payne took over as the OfS’s chief executives in June and had no prior involvement with the decision to fine Sussex. The OfS investigation began after Stock’s resignation from Sussex in 2021, following campus protests for her views on transgender rights and gender identity.
summary: England's higher education regulator, the Office for Students (OfS), has apologized for mistakes and bias in attempting to impose a record £585,000 fine on the University of Sussex over free speech regulations. A high court judicial review previously overturned the fine, and an internal KPMG review criticized the OfS for acting in an adversarial manner with poor accountability. In response, the OfS published a lessons-learned report outlining planned reforms, though Sussex vice-chancellor Sasha Roseneil stated the changes fall short in several areas.
key_points: The OfS apologized for errors in trying to fine the University of Sussex £585,000 over free speech issues related to former professor Kathleen Stock.
A high court judicial review previously forced the OfS to back down after finding it acted with bias and closed its mind.
An independent KPMG review criticized the regulator for being adversarial, lacking record-keeping, and having a concentration of decision-making power.
The OfS issued a report promising changes, such as fostering respectful relationships and using alternative interventions before imposing fines.
Sussex vice-chancellor Sasha Roseneil welcomed the apology but stated that the proposed reforms failed to fully reflect the seriousness of the high court's findings.

title: Nepal-Tibet flash flood: Two workers pulled alive from hydropower tunnel nine days after disaster
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen; Gaurav Pokharel
content:
Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after deadly flash floods buried the projects in deep mud and left them trapped.
The workers were rescued during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a hydropower project in one of the areas worst-affected by last week’s deadly Nepal floods, according to army spokesperson Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet.
Sanjay Shah was the first to be rescued and was taken to the Nepal Army barracks in Trishuli. Subsequently, another person, identified as Kabir Maharjan, was also rescued from the tunnel. They were rescued from a depth of 170 metres inside the tunnel, confirmed Basnet.
Sanjay Shah was foreman at Upper Trishuli 3A and Kabir Maharjan was a supervisor.
Nepal’s army released images of Shah being pulled from the small dark entrance of a tunnel. He emerged covered in mud but conscious and was carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.
Officials said the two men were in stable condition and have been flown to a hospital in Kathmandu.
Speaking to army officials after he was rescued, Shah’s first question was: “what day is it?”.
Describing his ordeal to rescuers, Shah said he had been in the tunnel’s control room at the time of the flood.
“Usually there would be only five or six people there but at this time there must have been around 40 to 45 people inside,” he said. “Since I was in the control room, my responsibility was to save everyone’s lives. After such an accident, I couldn’t just run away by myself. I had to save everyone.
“While trying to get everyone out, I told them that there had been a major accident at the dam and urged everyone to run. In doing so, I lost time. In the end, I couldn’t get out myself.”
To keep himself calm in the darkness of the tunnel, Shah said he spent his time chanting mantras. He said that while trapped inside the tunnel, he had only been communicating with three or four others.
“They were communicating by shouting to each other from nearby. There could also be people inside the powerhouse. Some of them may not have been able to escape,” he said.
Nepal’s communication minister Bikram Timilsina said officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued. “We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,” Timilsina wrote on social media.
Most of the hydropower projects along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the valley last week, triggered by the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
![A survivor is carried out after being rescued from inside a tunnel](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/db4cb8002d8ff5c389774138e2f706493280eedb/0_0_1280_853/master/1280.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters
At least 1,259 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country’s disaster management agency.
Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on the hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued across several projects.
Large boulders and flood waters had deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels.
Army and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try and clear debris from the tunnel entrance. It was confirmed that voices of multiple people had been heard inside after a breakthrough was made on early Friday morning.
After the rescue team called out, “Don’t panic, we are rescuing you,” they received a response from inside: “Okay.”
At least 557 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.
Families of those missing in the tunnels have been gathering at the hospitals in Kathmandu and at the Nepal electricity office for nine days, desperate for answers about their relatives. Posters of workers missing in Trishuli 3A and other projects line the wall of Tribhuvan University teaching hospital in Nepal’s capital.
In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels.
Rescue efforts have also been focused on Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant where Nepal authorities said they are confident that 46 workers trapped in an underground chamber in the plant are still alive.
summary: Two workers were rescued alive from a deep hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after flash floods triggered by a melting glacier buried the projects in mud. Sanjay Shah and Kabir Maharjan were pulled from a depth of 170 metres and flown to a Kathmandu hospital in stable condition. Officials and rescue teams continue operations, hoping to find more survivors trapped in the tunnels.
key_points: Two workers, Sanjay Shah and Kabir Maharjan, were rescued alive from the Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel after nine days.
The flash floods were triggered by a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
Both rescued men were found at a depth of 170 metres and have been flown to a hospital in Kathmandu in stable condition.
Authorities and rescue teams are continuing round-the-clock operations, believing more workers may have survived in air pockets inside the tunnels.

title: Hillary Clinton leads tributes to Gloria Steinem: ‘Her activism was rooted in optimism’
author: Richard Luscombe
content:
Leading figures from politics, entertainment and wider society led glowing tributes to Gloria Steinem on Thursday, with Hillary Clinton hailing the American feminist icon who died at 92 at home in New York City as “one of the architects of the entire structure of women’s equality”.
Clinton, a former US secretary of state, presidential candidate and first lady, was among the first to jump in with praise early on Thursday when she appeared on the CBS Mornings TV show to share her respect and gratitude for Steinem.
Clinton urged younger generations to use Steinem as a role model in supporting each other in promoting the causes she championed.
“I’m hoping that young women realize that the fight is worth it,” she said. “It is exhilarating.”
Kamala Harris, the former US vice-president, hailed Steinem as a “trailblazing activist, organizer, and journalist – an icon in so many ways”, in a post on X.
“To know her as a person is to know someone who was kind, sharp, and witty. She was invested in young women and keeping the door open for the next generation of leaders,” Harris wrote.
“I will always be grateful for her encouragement and support in my campaign for the presidency. A campaign that was made possible, in no small part, because of her activism and so many other giants upon whose shoulders we stand.”
Others who eulogized Steinem included Nancy Pelosi, the Democratic former House speaker, who called her “a fearless trailblazer who transformed the fight for equality in America”. Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, added her voice to call Steinem her “friend and mentor”, while the music icon Patti Smith referred to her as “the greatest”.
Broadcaster Oprah Winfrey called Steinem a “formidable reformer who shaped American thought and culture”. And Billie Jean King, the athlete who led the fight for equality for female tennis players, said in a Facebook post that “the world has lost a true giant and a dynamic voice”.
“She lit a torch many years ago. It is now our responsibility to keep it lifted into the future. May she rest in power,” King wrote.
Jill Biden, another former first lady, released a statement in which she said she and former US president Joe Biden “are holding Gloria’s loved ones in our hearts”.
Biden wrote: “Gloria Steinem understood that women’s equality begins with the freedom to make decisions about our own bodies, health, and futures. For decades, she fought to make that freedom real for generations of women and girls.
“She spoke up when it was difficult, listened to those whose voices too often went unheard, and never stopped pushing our country forward. Her voice changed our country, and her courage will continue to inspire us to keep fighting for the freedoms she spent her life defending.”
Steinem had supported Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign as the Democratic nominee running against Republican Donald Trump, which was ultimately unsuccessful as Trump prevailed in an election that would have given the United States its first female president. Clinton said on Thursday she was “heartsick” at news of the death of her feminist friend and ally.
“Everyone who not only knew her but followed her, was inspired and challenged by her,” she said.
“I think back to my first awareness of Gloria way back in the 1960s into the 70s, when all of a sudden this incredibly smart, beautiful, talented woman began talking about how women should have equal opportunity, how we should aim for the stars, be able to pursue our own dreams.
“I knew there were, back when I was a young woman, schools that wouldn’t take women, jobs that wouldn’t take women, scholarships that weren’t open to women. I lived it.
“But the lived experience became much more real and applicable to our entire society when Gloria began to point it out.”
Clinton noted Steinem’s distaste at what politics had become in recent years, and said she had “the most incredible conversation” with her during a visit to Steinem’s home last year.
“Even though we’re facing some challenges and pushback here in this country and around the world to women’s full participation and equality, Gloria was at heart an optimist,” she said. “Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that’s a moral choice, and she made it every day.”
Pelosi paid tribute in a post on X that said: “Gloria Steinem was a fearless trailblazer who transformed the fight for equality in America and inspired generations of women to know their power.
“Her voice, courage and relentless advocacy helped break down barriers and open doors once firmly closed to women. May it be a comfort to all of us who loved Gloria that her extraordinary legacy will live on in every generation that carries her fight forward.”
Markle posted her memories on Instagram. “Celebrating the life and legacy of my friend and mentor, and also grateful to know that in these last few weeks and days she knew exactly how loved and admired she was,” she wrote.
“My very favorite story about GLO is when she was out one day in NY, and a woman approached her in absolute awe and said she wanted to introduce her young daughter to her (though she was embarrassed to say the young girl may not know who she was).”
The post continued: “Gloria replied: ‘It doesn’t matter if she knows who I am. What matters is that she knows who SHE is’. Rest in peace, and rest in pride.”
Smith, who shared a similar path to Steinem as a cultural revolutionary icon emerging from New York in the 1960s and 70s, posted a brief tribute on Instagram. “This is the greatest Gloria. All are grateful for her revolutionary spirit; a lifetime of service,” she wrote.
The Oscar-winning actor Julianne Moore played Steinem in the 2020 biopic The Glorias. She said on Instagram: “The time I spent studying Gloria in order to play her was one of the most edifying of my life.
“Everything I watched, everything I read, everything I observed about her gave me a template for how I wanted to behave. Her honesty, her tolerance, her patience, and her insistence on humanism and inclusion as she moved through the world offers us all a moral roadmap.”
Others who paid tribute on Thursday also recalled Steinem’s trailblazing.
“Gloria was one of a kind. Genuine, generous, curious, thoughtful. She lived a staggering life and her passing is a staggering loss tempered only by the ferocity of her legacy,” Roxane Gay, the prominent social commentator and author of Bad Feminist, commented on the Instagram post announcing Steinem’s death.
Winfrey, on her own Oprah Daily website, said Steinem “challenged a culture that often told us who we could be, what we could do, and how much space we were allowed to take up, and then spent her life making that space wider for all of us”.
Alongside a picture of Winfrey and Steinem together, the TV host added: “She never wanted the movement to be about her. She understood that real change happens when one woman finds her voice and then uses it to help another woman find hers.”
summary: American feminist icon Gloria Steinem has died at her home in New York City at the age of 92. Prominent figures from politics, entertainment, and sports—including Hillary Clinton, Kamala Harris, Nancy Pelosi, and Oprah Winfrey—paid glowing tributes to her legacy. Tributes highlighted her decades of trailblazing activism, her support for women's equality, and her enduring optimism.
key_points: Gloria Steinem passed away at her home in New York City at the age of 92.
Hillary Clinton praised Steinem as an architect of women's equality whose activism was rooted in optimism.
Kamala Harris, Nancy Pelosi, Oprah Winfrey, and Jill Biden also shared tributes celebrating Steinem's lifelong dedication to civil rights and women's freedom.
Figures like Meghan Markle and Julianne Moore remembered Steinem as a mentor, friend, and moral roadmap for women.

title: El Nino: A phenomenon supercharged by climate change
author: Nick Clark
content:
![A farmer loads dried leaves and other crop residue from a completely drought-damaged cornfield onto a truck in Tecoluca, San Vicente department, El Salvador, on August 26, 2026.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/afp_6a983f13bf2a-1788362515.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Anchovies are an unlikely bellwether for a building climatic event, but their disappearance from the coast of South America is heralding one of the biggest El Ninos in living memory.
These small fish usually live in colossal shoals along the Pacific coast of South America, feeding in the cold, nutrient-rich waters. Fishermen in Peru and Chile eagerly await the fishing season every year, but every now and then, it does not come as planned. This is one of those years.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Panama Canal restricts traffic amid Hormuz crisis: Why this matters
- list 2 of 3UN warns El Nino could be ‘off the charts’, strongest in decades
- list 3 of 3How wildfires are scorching France’s wine industry
Some years the easterly trade winds in the Pacific weaken or even reverse. The trigger for this remains uncertain, but it causes a warm ocean current to flow east to the coast of South America. This replaces the nutrient-rich cold water, causing the anchovies to disappear.
Because the warm waters arrive around Christmas time, Peruvian fishermen named the phenomenon El Nino de Navidad (The Christmas Child).
The impact of El Nino, a natural weather pattern, spreads much further than South America, and can bring drought or floods to millions in affected areas. This year it comes supercharged by climate change, which is worrying many scientists, governments and aid workers.
Stephanie Roe, lead climate scientist with the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), told Al Jazeera that this “super El Nino” is a stark reminder of how climate change can intensify pressures on both people and the natural world.
“El Nino can bring devastating climate extremes on its own, but it’s unfolding today on a much warmer planet, increasing the likelihood that heat, drought, floods and fires will push communities and ecosystems beyond anything they have experienced before,” Roe said.
Drought and floods
As it develops in the Pacific, this year’s El Nino is combining with an ongoing, massive marine heatwave, further adding to the impacts of human-induced global warming. Its effects will be felt through food systems and biodiversity, impacting the livelihoods of fishermen and farmers, and the billions around the world reliant on the agricultural industry for their food.
El Nino’s development is being closely monitored from both space and sea, using satellites and a network of buoys. The devices in the Pacific Ocean continuously transmit data on ocean temperatures, currents and winds, helping scientists assess how powerful the event could become. Indications currently suggest the 2026-27 El Nino could be the strongest on record.
Research by the Met Office, the United Kingdom’s national weather and climate service, shows that a typical El Nino episode leads to temperature rises of between 1 and 2 degrees Celsius in the equatorial Pacific Ocean. But projections now indicate that when El Nino fully bites in late 2026 or early 2027, temperatures could spike by 3C.
“We should be clear this is an unprecedented event. I have never seen an El Nino signal this intense in our forecasts,” Adam Scaife, professor and the Met Office’s head of long-range forecasting, told Al Jazeera.
“This implies that if the forecast is accurate – and other forecast systems show similar extreme values – then this will far exceed our recent experience of El Nino and its worldwide climate influences,” Scaife said.
What are the implications?
Scientists know that the weather is never certain, but an El Nino ramped up by global warming spells trouble. United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has compared it to “pouring fuel on the fire of a warming world”.
The effects will be felt by billions across the world, bringing droughts to some regions and severe flooding to others. In some cases, it can bring both.
Southeast Asia and South America will be particularly badly affected by this phenomenon, according to Carbon Brief, a United Kingdom-based website specialising in climate issues. There might be drought in Southern Africa, but flooding in the east of the continent. El Nino could also bring extreme heat that would weaken summer monsoons, leading to drought.
According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, this super El Nino demands exceptional preparation and response. “Never before in the 50-year history of the WMO have we launched such a major mobilisation delivering forecasts and services to save lives and livelihoods,” she said.
Uneven effects
El Ninos can reduce the number and size of Atlantic hurricanes and provide welcome rainfall to drought-stricken areas. Models indicate that the peak will be from December to February, which coincides with the main planting season and crop-development period in South America.
Investment bank Morgan Stanley said that wetter conditions could benefit agricultural yields in Argentina and southern Brazil, but other parts of Brazil might face more irregular rainfall and delayed planting.
Overall, the outlook is grim, with crop failures caused by El Nino and the climate crisis rippling through supply chains and leading to billions of dollars in damage to the global economy. One group of economists at Citigroup investment bank have estimated that a super El Nino could inflict as much as $7 trillion in global economic losses over five years, as its effects leave lasting scars on gross domestic product (GDP) growth.
“Most El Nino years are a nuisance, but this one has the makings of a shock, as weather patterns shift across key growing regions,” said Julia Rizzo, Morgan Stanley’s commodities strategist for Latin America.
“The effects may extend far beyond local forecasts and into supply chains, prices and investment returns.”
The World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that El Nino could hit as global food systems face systemic challenges due to high energy and fertiliser prices, brought about by the United States’ war on Iran.
“Together these factors increase the risk that climate shocks could push more people into hunger,” the WFP told Al Jazeera.
The United Nations agency forecasts that 274 million people will be facing acute hunger by the end of 2027, an increase of 49 million from current levels.
Outbreaks of disease, like malaria and dengue fever, could be another consequence, particularly in places where sanitation and health systems are already under pressure.
John Nairn, WMO’s senior extreme heat adviser, said extreme heat is the most direct concern.
“Where pre-existing drought exists, heatwaves intensify and compound other hazards such as water scarcity, dust, wildfires, smoke and flash floods,” Nairn said. “Each carries its own burden, ranging from heat mortality and respiratory impacts to waterborne disease.”
It is also feared that the compounding effects of El Nino will put highly stressed ecosystems under more pressure.
In the Pacific region, the loss of baitfish, including anchovies and sardines, is having a knock-on effect up the food chain and could cause deaths among seals and sea lions. Thousands of seabirds have also already washed up dead on Eastern Pacific coasts from California to Ecuador.
“Our recent surveys have been reporting seabird strandings and deaths every day, but it started to explode in June. It showcases the magnitude of this El Nino over such a large expanse of the Pacific,” said Sebastian Cruz of the American Bird Conservancy.
And perhaps most alarming of all for scientists is the likely increase in global temperatures.
“During large El Nino events, significantly more heat is released from the ocean to the atmosphere, leading to an increase in global average temperature,” said Met Office climate scientist Nick Dunstone. “So 2027 is very likely to replace 2024 as the hottest year on record.”
summary: The disappearance of anchovies off the coast of South America is signaling the arrival of an exceptionally strong El Nino event, intensified by climate change and an ongoing marine heatwave. Scientists warn that this unprecedented phenomenon could cause global temperature spikes, severe droughts, and heavy floods, potentially resulting in trillions of dollars in economic losses. The compounding impacts threaten global food systems, heighten the risk of acute hunger for millions, and put additional pressure on vulnerable ecosystems and wildlife.
key_points: The 2026-27 El Nino is projected to be the strongest on record, potentially pushing equatorial Pacific temperatures up by 3 degrees Celsius.
The natural weather pattern is amplified by climate change and an ongoing marine heatwave, raising concerns over extreme heat, droughts, and floods worldwide.
Economists estimate that the super El Nino could cause up to $7 trillion in global economic losses over five years due to crop failures and supply chain disruptions.
The United Nations forecasts that climate shocks combined with other factors could push the number of people facing acute hunger to 274 million by the end of 2027.
Ecosystems are already suffering, evidenced by mass strandings of dead seabirds and the disappearance of baitfish like anchovies along the Pacific coast.

title: Gloria Steinem, chic feminist writer who brought women’s rights to the mass market
author: Telegraph Obituaries
content:
![Gloria Steinem in 1965: witty and trenchant, she contradicted the stereotypical image of the dour feminist](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000500546848_17884315737550_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqhnpZDwl738N_2PZHYpB61v-izaxkYgR5SyePioJ2Z1I.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Gloria Steinem in 1965: witty and trenchant, she contradicted the stereotypical image of the dour feminist](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000500546848_17884315737550_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqhnpZDwl738N_2PZHYpB61v-izaxkYgR5SyePioJ2Z1I.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Gloria Steinem, the writer who has died aged 92, was America’s best-known feminist until the age of 66, when she signed up for marriage, an institution she had been famous for attacking.
With her movie-star good looks (Newsweek once described her as a “life-size counter-culture Barbie Doll”), Gloria Steinem emerged late on to the feminist scene, and her immediate promotion to its leadership was not appreciated by longer-serving members of the movement. But with her looks and her journalism, which was witty as well as trenchant, she contradicted the stereotype of the dour, boiler-suited man-hater and brought feminism to the mass market.
She came to public notice when she dressed up as a Playboy Bunny and wrote about the experience. Then, with Betty Friedan, she set up the National Women’s Political Caucus in 1971 and led campaigns for abortion rights, equal pay, equal representation, and an end to domestic violence. In 1972 she launched Ms magazine, which made feminism chic and added a new word to the English lexicon.
She had a talent for the pithy aphorism, though her most famous quotation, “A woman needs a man like a fish needs a bicycle,” was in fact misattributed to her (the phrase was originally Irina Dunn’s). She did, however, coin the term “reproductive freedom” as a battle cry for feminist demands for contraception and abortion rights. In a series of brilliant satires she challenged conventional views on women’s place in society.
![Gloria Steinem in 1967: Newsweek once described her as a 'lifesize counter-culture Barbie Doll'](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000500545889_17884309104050_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq7HVybmJHsiZ-in9phuBAJ6mP3TGOxk3If4w9zvP7RTg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
In “If Men Could Menstruate”, she suggested, “they would brag about how long and how much. Corporate consultants would charge double for greater intuitive powers in those sensitive days at the onset of their cycles.”
In “What If Freud Were Phyllis?” she charted the career of a certain Phyllis Freud, the mother of psychoanalysis, who is born into a world in which women are considered superior because of their ability to give birth. Phyllis makes insights into universal problems such as womb envy, clitoris envy, penis anxiety and breast-castration anxiety.
One of Gloria Steinem’s selling points was that no one could accuse her of turning to feminism because she could not get a man. The cast list of her lovers, including the film director Mike Nichols, the publishing and property tycoon Mort Zuckerman, the Kennedy speechwriter Ted Sorensen, the economist JK Galbraith, even the macho writer Norman Mailer (who instructively failed to perform), only added to her fame.
![Walking arm in arm with Mort Zuckerman in 1984](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000500545892_17884334188060_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqaHd6X3lW3lGv45Ug3tlONZ3XVdg1rRzimPdm_Jg3Voo.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Such, indeed, was the obsessive public interest in her sex life (she had, Americans were informed, experienced her first orgasm at a New York masturbation workshop), that in 1969 she felt obliged to issue a statement which read: “I am not now, and never have been, a girlfriend of Henry Kissinger.” She behaved badly but got away with it because she did so with panache.
She was an outspoken advocate of the notion that children are best off conceived out of wedlock and, at the height of her fame in the 1970s, persuaded hundreds of thousands of women to reject a social convention that she mocked as a “little death” or “an arrangement for one and a half people”.
In 1985, when her sister in arms, Betty Friedan, broke ranks and argued that the women’s movement had underestimated the importance of the family, Gloria Steinem denounced her, bringing an end to a beautiful friendship.
![Linda Lovelace, Gloria Steinem, Lindalee Tracy, and Bonnie Sherr Klein attend the premiere of 'Not A Love Story: A Film About Pornography' in New York (1982)](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000500545899_17884313119010_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Thus, in 2000, when she married David Bale, a South African businessman, there was outrage. The fact that the marriage was a Cherokee ceremony conducted by the activist Wilma Mankiller, the bride wore jeans and the couple referred to each other as “the friend I married”, did nothing to convince many of her sisters that she was anything but a traitor to their cause.
Gloria Steinem was born in Toledo, Ohio, a midwestern industrial town, on March 25 1934. Her father, Leo, was a travelling antiques dealer; her mother, Ruth, had been a successful newspaper reporter who wrote under a male pseudonym, but gave it up to raise her two daughters.
When Gloria was five, her mother had the first of a series of nervous breakdowns. When she was 10, her parents divorced and her adored father left. While her older sister went away to college, Gloria was left to care for her mother. They lived in a rat-infested basement.
Ruth was diagnosed as suffering from anxiety neurosis and doped up on chloral hydrate. Gloria fed her sandwiches, fought the rats and pretended things were just fine. In later life she often said that her own reluctance to have children came from having already mothered her mother.
![Gloria Steinem with opera conductor Sarah Caldwell in 1975](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000500545872_17884303525540_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqJH-rFL7fccQ_6RWVNgivMWS7_ypwhOWBnRvU8FozZxY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Somehow, she managed to continue her studies and won a place at Smith College (where she was briefly engaged). Afterwards, she spent two years in India working with Gandhi’s followers. She returned to America and became a freelance journalist in New York. By her mid-twenties, she was a columnist on The New Yorker and a writer for Esquire.
She came to fame in 1963 when she wrote an undercover exposé of life as a Playboy Bunny. She was 28, and did not then consider herself a feminist; even so, there was surprise when her claim that “Being a Playboy Bunny is rather like being hung on a meat hook” brought a deluge of letters from girls wondering where they could sign up.
From then on her journalism became more radical. She became involved in the civil rights and anti-war movements, though it was not until 1969 that she came out as a fighter in the feminist cause. The catalyst was a “speak-out” in Greenwich Village where dozens of women stood up and announced that they had had abortions. Although she did not join them, the “great blinding lightbulb of her life” came on.
The meeting made her aware of the context of her own struggles as an independent woman, and she subsequently spoke about an abortion she had had secretly in London in the 1950s. Her admission brought her saturation coverage in the press and she moved effortlessly into the role of feminist icon – and hate figure.
![As editor of Ms magazine, Gloria Steinem used shock tactics and satire to change men's attitudes](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000500545887_17884335527990_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqWZZ9520Qrn8RyVs0byqFfymqy_qNHx9smJQdyZJhsFQ.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Rush Limbaugh, the Right-wing radio talk-show host, referred to her as a “Feminazi”, and she was the target for attacks by Christian and anti-abortion groups who tended to portray her as a fascist or Marxist sociopath bent on the moral destruction of American society. But such barbs never seemed to worry her: “An actress friend of mine said she’d been married to one fascist and one Marxist and neither of them took the garbage out,” she joked.
As editor of Ms from 1972 to 1987, and as the author of such works as Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions, Gloria Steinem used shock tactics and satire to change men’s attitudes towards women and women’s attitudes to themselves. The debut issue of Ms contained a full-page petition for the legalisation and regulation of abortion; “Down with panties!” bellowed Germaine Greer in a subsequent issue.
If Gloria Steinem occasionally reached the realms of parody (“The architecture of Catholic churches mimics the female body,” she wrote. “The outer portals serve as the labia majora, the inner portals as labia minora, the side altars as ovaries, and the high altar the uterus at the heart of the swelling dome that holds the body of the faithful”), she was always readable and thought-provoking.
![Attending the Citymeals-on-Wheels Power Lunch for Women with Bill Clinton in 1992](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000500546108_17884314569390_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
One of her more attractive characteristics was her contempt for the therapy industry. “The examined life,” she wrote, “is not worth living.” But her attitudes to this and to other things began to change in the late 1980s: after the end of her affair with America’s richest bachelor, Mort Zuckerman, and a diagnosis of breast cancer, she began to wonder about the meaning of life and consulted a therapist.
A different woman emerged in Revolution from Within (1992), a cliché-ridden and mawkishly intimate book about her search for “self-esteem”, full of Einstein, the Upanishads and re-parenting the inner child. Her subsequent revelation that she had tried desperately to conceive in late middle age in order to please Zuckerman demonstrated beyond doubt that she was not so different from her weaker sisters after all.
She met David Bale in 1999 at a pro-abortion Voters for Choice rally in Los Angeles. When they married, the reaction of many feminists was withering: “Gloria Steinem’s marriage is proof positive of the emotional desperation of the ageing feminists who for more than 30 years worshipped the steely career woman and callously trashed stay-at-home moms,” thundered Camille Paglia.
![With the Duchess of Sussex in 2023](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/09/03/TELEMMGLPICT000500545897_17884307794940_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqEGnaGdKWTbTgcBBebr969kgS7S-ukhk48w-_KmtyACY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Gloria Steinem’s interpretation of her marriage was more homely and prosaic: “There’s a certain comfort in knowing that there’s a person who is going to be able to make medical decisions if you are incapacitated,” she observed. But her life as a married woman was all too short. David Bale, whose four children (including the actor Christian Bale) she became stepmother to, died in 2003.
Her activism continued, and in 2015 on International Women’s Day for Disarmament she was one of 30 women who linked arms with 10,000 Korean women on both sides of the demilitarised zone between North and South. That year she wrote an apologetic article for The Advocate backtracking on a 1977 piece she had written about the male-to-female tennis player Renée Richards, criticising transsexuals who “surgically mutilate their own bodies” in order to conform to gender stereotypes.
In 2013 she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by Barack Obama. Earlier this year she was asked by The New York Times if she had any advice for President Trump on his turning 80. “Resign,” she said.
Gloria Steinem, born March 25 1934, died September 2 2026
summary: Gloria Steinem, who has died at the age of 92, was America's most prominent feminist icon, journalist, and co-founder of Ms. magazine. Using her sharp wit, journalism, and cultural presence, she popularized women's rights and challenged traditional social stereotypes. Later in life, her marriage to David Bale in 2000 sparked controversy among some feminists who viewed it as a betrayal of her anti-marriage stance.
key_points: Gloria Steinem rose to fame after writing an undercover exposé as a Playboy Bunny in 1963 and co-founding Ms. magazine in 1972.
She campaigned for abortion rights, equal pay, equal representation, and coined the term "reproductive freedom."
She married South African businessman David Bale in 2000, which drew criticism from some fellow feminists.
She was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by Barack Obama in 2013.

title: BoM forecasts strongest El Niño on record as research points to ‘alarming’ climate change influence
author: Graham Readfearn
content:
The growing El Niño weather phenomenon to Australia’s east is already breaking heat records, with forecasts showing it will likely easily surpass previous events, according to Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology, as seperate research suggested climate change had greatly shortened the odds of the event hitting record extremes.
On Thursday the UN’s weather agency said the event in the Pacific was continuing to strengthen and would probably persist until early 2027, warning it had the “potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world”.
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”
In an update this week, the Bureau of Meteorology said the El Niño was now forecast to peak in late spring or summer and “reach levels above the warmest observed since reliable records began in 1950”.
El Niño events tend to mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east in winter and spring, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires.
El Niño strength is assessed by analysing sea surface temperatures in a region of the equatorial Pacific known as Niño 3.4. The bureau has said the strength of an El Niño does not necessarily mean stronger effects for the continent.
However, bureau analysis of the unfolding event suggested this El Niño had already broken records.
“We have been looking at the rate of warming observed in the last two months and it has been faster than any other event. Not only is it strong, but it has escalated rapidly,” said Felicity Gamble, a senior climatologist at the BoM.
Gamble said the relative sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region for the month of August were likely to be between 2.2C and 2.3C above average – higher than any previous August since 1950 (the year after which records are considered to be more reliable).
She said forecasts were suggesting relative sea surface temperatures in that region could peak over 3C above average, compared to the highest previous figure of 2.6C observed in January 1983.
Gamble said the relative sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region had warmed by more than 2C between February and July.
She said: “No other period in the historical record exceeds that. This is the first event where we have had that change exceed 2C in the space of six months.
“We could be seeing a record in terms of the strength, and also the rate of warming and the duration.”
after newsletter promotion
Climate experts have said El Niño will likely combine with climate change to push global temperatures to record highs next year.
Gamble said in the Pacific region, El Niño was already contributing to droughts in Papua New Guinea, with food and water shortages and major wildfires in Indonesia.
This winter was Australia’s third-warmest on record and the hottest on record for New South Wales, Tasmania and Victoria.
Scientists at the University of Melbourne have released preliminary research into the influence of climate change on the predicted peak of the El Niño. By analysing historical records and comparing climate models with and without the influence of greenhouse gas emissions, the scientists found climate change had made “an event of this magnitude” six times more likely.
The study has been submitted to a journal for peer review, but the authors said they had used a methodology common to many other published studies.
Dr Andrew King, one of the co-authors of the research, said: “This points to the fact that there is likely a climate change role here in the chance of having these extreme El Niño conditions. It seems likely there is a human fingerprint emerging in this event.
“We are seeing something that does not appear to have happened before and that is alarming.”
The bureau’s long range forecast for September to November points to an increased chance of below average rainfall for the south and east, but above average for most of the continent’s western half. Temperatures are also likely to be above average south of the tropics.
summary: Australia's Bureau of Meteorology forecasts that the developing El Niño weather phenomenon will surpass previous records, driven by unusually rapid warming in the equatorial Pacific. The UN weather agency warns the event will persist and impact global communities, while separate research indicates climate change has made such extreme conditions six times more likely. El Niño typically brings hotter, drier conditions, increasing risks of heatwaves, droughts, and bushfires.
key_points: The Bureau of Meteorology forecasts the current El Niño will reach levels above any observed since reliable records began in 1950.
August sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region are expected to be between 2.2C and 2.3C above average, with peaks potentially exceeding 3C.
The UN weather agency warned that the strengthening event will likely persist until early 2027.
Preliminary research from the University of Melbourne suggests climate change has made an El Niño event of this magnitude six times more likely.
El Niño is already contributing to droughts and food and water shortages in Papua New Guinea, as well as wildfires in Indonesia.

title: Gloria Steinem: Feminist activist and journalist dies, aged 92
author: Mallory Moench
content:
Watch: Gloria Steinem talks about her legacy in 2023 BBC interview
- Published
Gloria Steinem, who became a leader of the women's liberation movement in the US, has died aged 92.
In a post on Instagram, her foundation said she "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City on Wednesday, "surrounded by many who loved her".
Steinem, who was a writer and magazine editor, co-founded the Women's Action Alliance - a group dedicated to fighting sexism - more than 50 years ago.
She started her career as a journalist in New York and went on to co-found Ms. magazine, one of the first publications to focus on women's issues other than housekeeping and beauty.
During the 1970s, Steinem was a vocal campaigner for women's reproductive rights, among other causes.
She herself obtained an illegal abortion in London when she was 22 years old, and years later celebrated the US Supreme Court's 1973 ruling in the case of Roe v Wade, which granted women the constitutional right to abortion. Nearly half a century later she witnessed the reversal of this decision.
She also spoke out in favour of the legalisation of same-sex marriage, as well as equal rights and pay for women, and protested against the death penalty and female genital mutilation.
![Feminist Gloria Steinem speaking at Democratic National Convention.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/23c8/live/cf91da40-a784-11f1-b2d5-535b3b3d379f.jpg)
Steinem was one of the main voices campaigning for women's reproductive rights in the 1970s
Born on 25 March 1934 in Toledo, Ohio, she had a difficult childhood and did not go to school full-time until she was 12 years old.
After university in the late 1950s, she went to India on a research scholarship and spent two years in a variety of roles, including helping village women organise non-violent protests against government policies, which sparked her interest in grassroots activism.
