Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany is used by the Germany military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carries most of the country's aerial cargo.
The head of Nato, Mark Rutte, said the organisation "stands in full solidarity with Germany".
"The evidence is clear. And I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response," he wrote on X.
The issue was due to be discussed at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland later on Tuesday.
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression. We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security."
She added that the EU was preparing additional sanctions against Russia.
Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail."
Germany is one of several Nato member states to have reported drone sightings at airports, military and industrial sites over the last year.
Berlin has until now been tight-lipped about who may have been behind the Leipzig attack, except to say the "foreign powers" may have been involved.
US media had already reported that American officials had linked the incident to Russia.
Berlin has warned that the country is the "daily target" of hybrid warfare, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned last week that those who carried out hostile acts against Germany would "pay a price".
The government is looking to boost the powers of its intelligence services, which have long been criticised as relatively toothless, to counter such threats.
Germany is a key backer of Ukraine with Merz forthright in his support for Kyiv.
It is not hard to imagine why Ukrainian cargo planes at a key German logistics hub might be in Moscow's sights.
But this announcement comes at a delicate moment for Merz's government.
A key state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could propel the far-right Alternative fÃ¼r Deutschland (AfD) into power at a state-level for the very first time.
The AfD, which is Germany's biggest opposition party, wants to stop sending support to Ukraine and re-open ties with Russia.
In a separate development, German police say they are investigating the discovery of improvised explosive and incendiary devices at a power substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday.
A power line was damaged, which caused a temporary outage. It is not known who planted the devices.
  - Published21 August
 ![A German police officer standing next to a police vehicle. The officer wears an operational vest that reads "polizei".](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/787/cpsprodpb/3237/live/ba89ed70-9d72-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
- ![A police officer in dark protective clothing walks next to an explosive-disarming robot at Leipzig/Halle Airport on 5 August 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/963/cpsprodpb/4d1e/live/99257560-a09b-11f1-8a1f-314a01485cf4.png)
summary: Germany has officially blamed Russia for a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport that occurred on 4 August. In response, Berlin announced the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, terminated the contract for the Russian House in Berlin, and imposed tighter entry controls for Russian nationals. Moscow denied involvement and stated it would respond in a mirror-image fashion.
key_points: A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport on 4 August and failed to explode due to a faulty detonator.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt stated that equipment analysis and intelligence findings proved Russian involvement.
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul ordered the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and summoned the Russian ambassador.
Nato and EU leaders expressed full solidarity with Germany and announced preparations for additional sanctions against Russia.

title: Nepal-Tibet floods: warning signs visible before glacier collapse, report says, as death toll passes 1,000 – latest updates
author: Tom Ambrose; Yohannes Lowe; Damian Carrington; Cait Kelly
content:
A satellite image taken by Planet Labs and released on Saturday shows the glacier before its collapse, and, right, on 28 August. Composite: Planet Labs PBC/AFP via Getty Images
A satellite image taken by Planet Labs and released on Saturday shows the glacier before its collapse, and, right, on 28 August. Composite: Planet Labs PBC/AFP via Getty Images
Warning signs visible days before Nepal glacier collapse, report suggests
Three months before last week’s devastating floods, experts from China and Nepal met in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, on 27 May to discuss the risk of disasters in the border area and to coordinate on how best to monitor and respond to hazards such as floods, according to the Reuters news agency.
The participants called for joint risk-reduction measures, including inventories of glacial lakes and hazard mapping, but two Nepali officials told Reuters they did not receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels after the meeting.
Now, a rapid hazard assessment of the Nepal-Tibet disaster prepared by HiRISK, comprised of a group of scientists that produce risk data in the High Mountain Asia region and create guidelines for policymakers, said there were “pre-event indications” of the avalanche, raising more questions about the effectiveness of disaster preparedness.
The assessment was prepared by HiRISK on 28 August, according to ABC News (Australia), which first reported the findings. Jakob Steiner, a co-author of the report and a geoscientist with the University of Graz who has researched lake bursts in Nepal, told the outlet that early warning systems for construction workers were “very weak”.
The HiRISK report noted that no early warning system for glacier-related hazards had been established in the affected area.
“Given the rapid speed of the initial avalanche, warning time from conventional … systems would have been minimal and likely insufficient for successful evacuation at the Nepal-China border check point at Rasuwagadhi (Gyirong Port),” it said.
“Further downstream, with warning times of 10 minutes or more, comprehensive and well-capacitated systems could have saved a significant number of lives.”
It is unclear what data – if any – China had before the disaster of the conditions of the glaciers in the area, especially those lying outside its borders.
“No siren can outrun a mountainside collapsing in seconds,” says Prof Anjal Prakash, from Flame University in India. He blames a lack of political will to fight the climate crisis and to plan infrastructure for the devastating flood in Nepal and Tibet.
Prof Prakash said:
Nepal’s mountains have been sending warnings for a decade: thinning glaciers, retreating snowlines, permafrost turning to slush under roads and hydropower plants we kept building anyway. We didn’t lack the science, as researchers have tracked this decline for 50 years. We lacked the political will to act on it.
Early warning systems are being sold as the fix, but no siren can outrun a mountainside collapsing in seconds. The real failure sits upstream, in land-use decisions that pushed settlements and infrastructure onto riverbanks our ancestors deliberately avoided, and in a global economy still burning the fossil fuels that are cooking these glaciers from the inside out.
Every villager who watched that valley disappear paid for emissions decisions made thousands of kilometres away. Until governments treat the Himalayas as a climate frontline rather than a postcard backdrop, Rasuwa won’t be the last name we’re forced to memorise.
Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said:
For years, scientists and local communities have been warning that the Hindu Kush Himalayas are at huge risk from climate change. We also know a warming climate, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making tragedies like this one, and so many others around the world, much more likely, frequent and severe, with vulnerable communities often hardest hit.
But the solutions to global heating are equally clear – especially a faster global shift from fossil fuels to renewables and more investment in climate resilience.
Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.
Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.
In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues.
People search posters of those missing in Nepal flood
At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled.
Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims.
“Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.” You can read more here:
Nepal last week turned down foreign involvement in general search and rescue but said it needed specialised services and advanced technological support in areas such as life-detecting machines, large refrigerators and pre-fabricated bridges.
Aid worth more than $42m has poured into the country and Nepal is now working with experts from other countries to help with rescue operations.
But the apparent hesitance to accept immediate foreign help has come under scrutiny as the damage and scale of the disaster increasingly comes into view.
Nepal army soldiers work during a search and rescue operation near the Hydropower Project sites in the Rasuwa district of Nepal. Photograph: Nepal Army/Reuters
Speaking to NPR, Bhim Gautam, chief executive officer of the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal, said his country lacks “technology, equipment and expertise” to carry out effective rescue operations at hydropower projects.
“Our expertise is only in dealing with small flooding. We have never faced a situation like this before,” Gautam told the outlet, adding that his industry’s leaders had to “pressure the government” to allow in foreign rescue workers, a claim that we have not been able to independently verify.
“Late last week, the government approved rescue teams from China, India and Australia to come,” Gautam said. “But it is so late now.”
Death toll from floods rises to 1,010, with thousands still missing, Nepal's foreign ministry says
Lok Bahadur Chhetri, spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, has been holding a press briefing on the floods, providing updates on the search efforts and scale of the disaster. Here are some of the main points from what he said:
The national priority is to save lives, locate the missing, rescue survivors and provide urgent relief to those affected.
More than 21,000 personnel from Nepal’s army, police and armed police forces are engaged in search and rescue, relief and evacuation operations while the government coordinates with its neighbours and the international community, which is providing vital equipment and expertise.
1,010 bodies have been recovered, about 4,000 people are missing and more than 11,800 people have been rescued, including about 324 foreign nationals.
Approximately 590 foreign nationals from 39 countries remain missing – these figures continue to be updated.
Specialised tunnel rescue teams are working to find those feared to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites along the Trishuli River including at the Chilime, Langtang and Upper Trishuli 3A sites.
Nepal’s prime minister Balendra Shah said that the disaster highlighted the need for action to combat the climate crisis.
“This incident has indicated that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing with climate change,” Shah said in a social media post on Monday night.
“Therefore, this region must be alert, and at the same time, it is time for us to strongly raise the issue of disasters caused by climate change before the international community.”
China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China’s second batch of relief supplies for Nepal was expected to ship today, including drones, DNA testing and water purification equipment.
Chinese DNA testing experts will also help Nepal identity bodies, he said. Beijing has said it will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.
43,000 women and girls in Nepal need urgent humanitarian assistance, UN warns
An estimated 43,000 women and girls in Nepal are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance following the flood disaster last week, according to Christine Arab, UN Women regional director for Asia and the Pacific, who has been at a press briefing in Geneva.
Arab said women are running out of food, and safe water to drink, while facing exclusion from decisions that will shape their recovery even though they are likely to pick up more unpaid care work in the home.
She also highlighted how disasters increase the risk of trafficking, exploitation and gender-based violence while shrinking the availability of protection services for the most vulnerable.
“When there are no separate or safe latrines, adequate lighting or privacy, women and girls can face risks simply when using the toilet, bathing, sleeping, or moving around after dark,” Arab said.
“Women in the worst-affected areas tell us that food is their most urgent priority right now. Before the floods, women in Nepal were more likely to eat least and to eat last in their families, with serious consequences for their own health, particularly those who are pregnant or breastfeeding,” she added.
A woman walks among the ruins of flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot district on 1 September 2026. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images
Warning signs visible days before Nepal glacier collapse, report suggests
Three months before last week’s devastating floods, experts from China and Nepal met in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, on 27 May to discuss the risk of disasters in the border area and to coordinate on how best to monitor and respond to hazards such as floods, according to the Reuters news agency.
The participants called for joint risk-reduction measures, including inventories of glacial lakes and hazard mapping, but two Nepali officials told Reuters they did not receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels after the meeting.
Now, a rapid hazard assessment of the Nepal-Tibet disaster prepared by HiRISK, comprised of a group of scientists that produce risk data in the High Mountain Asia region and create guidelines for policymakers, said there were “pre-event indications” of the avalanche, raising more questions about the effectiveness of disaster preparedness.
The assessment was prepared by HiRISK on 28 August, according to ABC News (Australia), which first reported the findings. Jakob Steiner, a co-author of the report and a geoscientist with the University of Graz who has researched lake bursts in Nepal, told the outlet that early warning systems for construction workers were “very weak”.
The HiRISK report noted that no early warning system for glacier-related hazards had been established in the affected area.
“Given the rapid speed of the initial avalanche, warning time from conventional … systems would have been minimal and likely insufficient for successful evacuation at the Nepal-China border check point at Rasuwagadhi (Gyirong Port),” it said.
“Further downstream, with warning times of 10 minutes or more, comprehensive and well-capacitated systems could have saved a significant number of lives.”
It is unclear what data – if any – China had before the disaster of the conditions of the glaciers in the area, especially those lying outside its borders.
At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepalese authorities.
Emergency crews are using aircraft to reach stranded communities in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed by the flooding and landslides.
An aerial view shows the damaged Ghatbesi Bridge over the Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods in Nepal’s Dhading district. Photograph: Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/Getty Images
Nepal tourism department publishes list of names of missing people
Nepal’s tourism department published a list of the names of the people still missing, as of Sunday evening, after the catastrophic flooding in the district of Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit provinces in Nepal. It said there were 164 people from Nepal that remain unaccounted for and 25 from China.
It said a total of 583 foreigners were missing, with the highest number from India (183), followed by the US (64) and then Malaysia (55). There are 33 people from the UK that have been identified as missing.
Beijing’s state media reports that 16 people died in Tibet, with 546 missing, but advocacy groups have accused China of heavily underreporting the death toll from flooding in border regions with Nepal, raising questions about Beijing’s official account of the scale of the disaster.
The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.
The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state-run CCTV reported, saying it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.
Two Nepali officials said China had not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness.
Death toll from Nepal-China flood disaster exceeds 1,000, authorities say
The death toll from the catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China has passed 1,000 as of Tuesday morning, officials said, with authorities reportedly burying hundreds of unidentified victims after the flood disaster overwhelmed morgues.
Nepal’s disaster agency said in an update on Tuesday that 987deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreigners.
Chinese authorities, in their latest update on Sunday, reported 16 deaths and 546people still missing.
Armed police officers stand near bodies that are about to be transferred to the pit at the Devghat mass burial site in Chitwan, Nepal. Photograph: Adnan Abidi/Reuters
The initial 72 hours after a disaster are viewed as critical to a rescue operation and there are fading hopes that the missing will be found alive.
Rescue efforts nonetheless persist, but have been complicated by challenging terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather.
The devastating floods occurred last Wednesday when a huge section of a glacier in the Himalayas came loose and crashed on to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, unleashing a massive wall of water and mud that rushed down rivers and valleys.
The resulting floods obliterated villages and destroyed vital infrastructure such as power stations, roads and bridges.
Nepal army soldiers undertake a rescue operation at the site of a hydropower project in Upper Trishuli, Nepal. Photograph: Nepali Army/AP
Much of the rescue efforts are now focused on trying to reach the 900 or so missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 12hydropower projects in Nepal.
“A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told the Reuters news agency on Monday.
About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing, as my colleague notes in this story.
Many people are feared to still be trapped in the sprawling network of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower sites along the Trishuli River, which flows through central Nepal.
summary: Following a devastating glacier collapse and subsequent floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, the death toll has surpassed 1,000, with thousands remaining missing. A rapid hazard assessment by HiRISK revealed that pre-event warning signs were present, but the affected area lacked adequate early warning systems. Nepal has accepted international aid and specialized rescue teams as search and recovery operations continue.
key_points: The official death toll from the Nepal-Tibet floods has reached 1,010, with about 4,000 people missing.
A HiRISK report indicated there were pre-event signs of the avalanche, but early warning systems in the affected area were absent or very weak.
Over 21,000 security personnel and international rescue teams are engaged in recovery operations, utilizing foreign aid exceeding $42 million.
The disaster has severely impacted vulnerable populations, with the UN warning that approximately 43,000 women and girls urgently need humanitarian assistance.

title: Putin Arrives in Kyrgyzstan for SCO Summit - The Moscow Times
author: Moscow Times Reporter
content:
BISHKEK, Kyrgyzstan — President Vladimir Putin arrived in Kyrgyzstan on Monday to attend an annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), as well as a series of bilateral meetings with the leaders of China, India and other nations.
A Moscow Times reporter observed a heavy police presence and traffic jams in the capital Bishkek ahead of the Russian president’s arrival.
Putin will first meet Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss the long-delayed Power of Siberia 2 natural gas pipeline project, followed by a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Those first two meetings, as well as a third with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, are part of the Russian leader’s nine bilateral talks with foreign leaders that will extend through Tuesday.
Later on Monday, Putin will join other heads of state at the opening ceremony of the World Nomad Games, a biennial cultural and athletic event featuring traditional Central Asian sports such as horseback archery, falconry and mounted wrestling.
On the sidelines of the SCO summit, Putin will meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian for the first time since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in February 2026.
Putin will also discuss Black Sea security and the war in Ukraine with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. In addition, he will meet with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan to discuss Yerevan’s growing pivot toward the EU and the arrests of Armenia’s pro-Russian opposition figures.
Putin traveled to Bishkek with a “compact” seven-member delegation that includes Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk, presidential aides Maxim Oreshkin and Yury Ushakov, as well as Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, SCO coordinator Bakhtiyor Khakimov and Russian Ambassador to Kyrgyzstan Sergei Vakulov.
The 10-member SCO bloc was founded in 2001 by Russia and China to counter Western influence across Eurasia. Its other members include India, Iran, Pakistan, Belarus and four Central Asian republics.
Following the SCO’s final session and press conference in Bishkek, Putin is scheduled to fly directly to Vladivostok for the Eastern Economic Forum.
A Message from The Moscow Times:
Dear readers,
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.
We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help.
Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.
By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.
![paiment methods](https://static.themoscowtimes.com/img/contribute/payment_icons.png) 
Remind me later.
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Kyrgyzstan on Monday to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit and participate in a series of bilateral meetings. His schedule includes discussions with leaders such as China's Xi Jinping, India's Narendra Modi, and Turkey's Recep Tayyip Erdoğan regarding regional projects, security, and international relations. He is also slated to attend the opening ceremony of the World Nomad Games before traveling to Vladivostok for the Eastern Economic Forum.
key_points: President Vladimir Putin arrived in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the annual SCO summit.
Putin has scheduled nine bilateral talks with foreign leaders, including Xi Jinping and Narendra Modi.
Key agenda items include the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, Black Sea security, and the war in Ukraine.
Putin will attend the opening ceremony of the biennial World Nomad Games.
Following the summit, Putin is scheduled to fly directly to Vladivostok for the Eastern Economic Forum.

title: Ceredigion family's fear for hydropower worker missing after Nepal flood
author: Sara Down-Roberts
content:
![Jit Bahadur Chaudhary, ei wraig a'u plentyn](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/e6e7/live/97fa82a0-a4bc-11f1-984c-751457a03c14.jpg)
Jit Bahadur Chaudhary (left), pictured with his wife Gita and their 13-year-old son Karan, remains missing
- Published
A woman in Wales says she has "lost hope" as she awaits news of a family member in Nepal who is missing following the massive flash flood last week.
Jyoti Upadhyay, who is from Nepal but has lived in Tal-y-bont in Ceredigion for the past five years, said she and her husband had not been able to find out anything about the whereabouts of hydropower station worker Jit Bahadur Chaudhary.
Chaudhary, who is not a blood relation but is considered family by Upadhyay as he has lived with her mother-in-law for the past 25 years, was working at the Trishuli 3B site in the Bagmati Province.
"To be honest, since Saturday we have lost hope," said Upadhyay.
On Monday morning, 933 hydropower workers from sites across Nepal were missing - in total, 4,247 people were unaccounted for, with at least 903 known to have died.
![A large quarry area with mud and water, and people in high vis jackets dotted about.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/26bd/live/b745a770-a48f-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
More than 4,000 people are missing after a massive flash flood in Nepal on Wednesday
Authorities have said rescue efforts have been largey focussed on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites - hydropower projects with tunnels.
Nepali authorities are blasting into hillsides to try and reach those trapped, with a controlled blast carried out at the Trishuli site in an attempt to open up access in the early hours of Monday.
"It has been extremely difficult to reach the site. What we understand is that all the buildings are under meters of mud and it has been impossible to search for anyone there," Upadhyay told BBC Radio Cymru's Bwrw Golwg programme.
"Within 20 minutes the connections were all down. The phone signals have not been working and that is why it has been so difficult to hear anything.
"It took about three days for us to get any information. We have been looking at the news, trying local contacts and trying to see what the army and the police have been doing."
She continued: "We know that the only way to reach the site is by helicopter. You need special skills to be able to drive a helicopter in that area. It is an extremely difficult place. We have been waiting for special machines to be able to work through the mud.
"There is some good news from other stations along the river as some people were able to hide in tunnels within the hydropower stations .
"There's not a lot of hope for that particular site - but we don't know until someone can get in. At the moment everything is under mud."
![People in hardhats and high-vis drilling into boulders in a quarry.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/290a/live/63d4e010-a48f-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Rescue efforts are underway to try to find the thousands who remain missing
The disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS).
The collapsed glacier hit the bottom of a valley so powerfully that it registered a tremor with a magnitude of 5.2, according to the agency.
This caused "subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream" - powerful floodwaters and debris travelled some 62 miles (100km).
Upadhyay explained that some tourists were among those missing, because the "area is important for pilgrimage to many religions".
She added the region was used to natural disasters, but that no one had expected flooding on this scale.
"In Nepal, we know that earthquakes can happen [but] this is worse than what has happened before," she said, adding the main concern was rising temperatures causing "more cases of glaciers melting and collapsing".
summary: A Welsh resident originally from Nepal is awaiting news of her missing relative, Jit Bahadur Chaudhary, who worked at a hydropower station affected by massive flash floods. The disaster, triggered by a glacial collapse, has left thousands missing and dead, with rescue teams struggling to access buried sites. Local authorities are using controlled blasts and special machinery to reach trapped workers, though communications and site access remain severely hindered.
key_points: Jit Bahadur Chaudhary, a hydropower worker at the Trishuli 3B site, has been missing since a massive flash flood struck Nepal.
Jyoti Upadhyay, a relative living in Ceredigion, stated that her family has largely lost hope as buildings at the site remain buried under meters of mud.
The disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that triggered powerful downstream floods and debris travelling 62 miles.
Search and rescue operations are facing immense challenges due to downed phone signals, difficult terrain, and thick mud, requiring helicopters and special machinery.

title: Turkish deep-sea search vessel joins efforts to retrieve 20 still missing after Cyprus ferry disaster
author: Helena Smith
content:
A deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus as Turkey joins efforts to retrieve the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the island’s northern coast.
The TCG Isin will join the vast operation to find survivors after the high-speed ferry sank on Sunday barely four nautical miles outside the port town of Kyrenia.
Authorities confirmed late on Monday – the first of three days of national mourning in Turkish-held northern Cyprus – that the tragedy had claimed eight lives, increasing the number of passengers still unaccounted for from 17 to 20.
A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, bound for Taşucu on the Turkish mainland when it began to take on water, had been rescued, they said. Almost all were either Turkish or Turkish Cypriot.
![People wearing orange lifejackets get off a small boat on a quayside.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/566b0fcaf49a3521f4fb9a4d26d87e3ebaeecaf3/0_0_1355_900/master/1355.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
International sympathy for the victims was highlighted as the Anglo-Cypriot founder of easyJet, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, offered €260,000 (£223,000) in support for the families of the deceased and missing, in a move hailed by Turkish Cypriot officials.
Visiting Kyrenia’s new port, where relatives gathered for news of loved ones on Monday, Tufan Erhürman, the self-styled state’s president, vowed search efforts would “continue with the same intensity, with no interruption, through the day and night”.
The Isin, capable of searching up to 3,000 metres below the sea surface, was due to arrive on Tuesday, he said, as he comforted the families of those still missing.
The ship is expected to play a vital role in recovering the ferry’s voyage data recorder, or black box, now viewed as key in deciphering the cause of a maritime disaster not seen since the breakaway territory declared independence in 1983.
Turkish Cypriot officials told the Guardian it was likely “all those responsible” would be charged with gross negligence as the seaworthiness of the 26-year-old ferry was also questioned.
The owners and shareholders of the privately owned company operating the passenger vessel have also been ordered to appear in court.
![Tufan Erhürman, a grey-haired man wearing glasses and a dark blue jacket, leans over a woman wearing a headscarf who is sitting in a chair with his hand on her shoulder. Other people are sitting by.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1f9e3c83b61137851e0175ac90fc910ec4afaa4f/0_0_3923_2771/master/3923.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
It remained unclear whether those still missing had been trapped on board.
“Nobody is saying it publicly, but the hope of any survivors being found at this point is very slim,” one official confided. “Those who weren’t rescued very likely didn’t find a lifejacket. We believe many were elderly people and mothers with babies and young kids.”
In testimony – and video footage – that emerged on Monday, panic-stricken passengers could be seen desperately looking for lifejackets and screaming before the double-hulled ferry flipped over. One mother, Ayten Biçer, described feeling her 12-year-old daughter slip from her hands and disappear as the ferry capsized and sank in a matter of minutes. “She was saying, ‘Don’t let go.’ And I didn’t let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn’t let her go,” she sobbed. Two of Biçer’s other children are among the 20 still missing.
![Ayten and Hayri Biçer wait for news of their two missing children outside the port of Kyrenia.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/8c53781e39d45e333652f6054174e1b09fbf0abb/0_0_5339_3698/master/5339.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The captain of the ferry and seven crew members were detained on Monday as judicial authorities launched an inquiry into the tragedy amid claims they had been among the first to abandon ship.
Appearing before a local magistrate, the crew attributed the disaster to the bow of the catamaran-style ferry breaking apart in turbulent seas. But eyewitness accounts contradicted that version of events, with passengers telling officials that appeals to turn back to port had fallen on deaf ears as the ferry began to take on water.
Ünal Üstel, the northern Cyprus prime minister, told reporters the Filo Jet was lying on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres and that he foresaw the Turkish salvage ship “reaching [it] tomorrow afternoon”. Boats, helicopters, aircraft and other search and rescue teams had joined the operation, he said, adding that search efforts were continuing “on a 24-hour basis”.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when a coup aimed at union with Greece – engineered by the military junta then in power in Athens – prompted Turkey to invade and seize the island’s northern third. Ever since, as many as 45,000 mainland Turkish troops have been stationed in the north.
In 1983, the territory unilaterally declared independence, but in the absence of a settlement, decades of international isolation have ensued.
summary: A Turkish deep-sea search and rescue vessel is joining the ongoing operation to find 20 people still missing after the high-speed passenger ferry Filo Jet capsized off northern Cyprus. The disaster, which occurred as the vessel headed to Turkey, has claimed eight lives and led to three days of national mourning. Authorities have detained the captain and seven crew members as inquiries into gross negligence and the ferry's seaworthiness begin.
key_points: A Turkish deep-sea search vessel, the TCG Isin, is assisting in the retrieval of 20 missing people and the ferry's black box.
The high-speed ferry Filo Jet sank four nautical miles off Kyrenia after taking on water, resulting in eight deaths and 241 survivors.
The ferry's captain and seven crew members have been detained following an inquiry into the tragedy.
EasyJet founder Stelios Haji-Ioannou offered €260,000 to support the families of the deceased and missing.

title: Northern Cyprus ferry: Couple's children missing after vessel capsizes
author: James Gregory
content:
![Ayten Bicer and Hayri Bicer, whose two children are missing after a passenger boat capsized off the coast of Kyrenia,](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/78e7/live/97d65330-a548-11f1-8689-6589354d0f8e.png)
Ayten Bicer and Hayri Bicer's two children are missing
- Published
Ayten Bicer felt her 12-year-old daughter slip from her grasp and disappear as the ferry they were travelling on capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, killing eight people.
Her daughter Miray and six-year-old son Memhet Asaf are among 20 people still missing after the vessel sunk while en route to Turkey from the coastal town of Kyrenia, in the self-proclaimed Turkish republic on Cyprus.
She and her husband Hayri survived, and like many other families are waiting for news of their loved ones back in port as rescuers continue to search.
"She was saying, 'Don't let go'. And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go," Bicer told reporters through tears.
Bicer said a suitcase fell on top of her, which forced her daughter from her grip. She managed to grab hold of her daughter's foot, but her shoes were coated in engine oil from the overturned vessel and she slipped through her hands.
"It was slippery everywhere. It was like oil. She slipped out of my hand," she recalled.
The family was returning to Turkey after a holiday on the Mediterranean island.
"We couldn't intervene, we lost our children," Hayri Bicer said. "Two of my three children are gone. We left them. We are leaving them on this island as we go."
The vessel had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members. Nineteen passengers are currently being treated in hospitals in northern Cyprus, local authorities say.
The eight crew members, including the ship's captain, and one other man were formally arrested on Monday. They will be detained for three days, while warrants have been issued for several other people.
The privately owned ferry left the popular holiday resort of Kyrenia at about 12:30 (09:30 GMT), en route to the town of Tasucu in Turkey.
It had been scheduled to travel to Turkey on Saturday but its journey was delayed due to severe storms hitting the island. The seas were still rough on Sunday.
Some eyewitness accounts say the double-hulled ferry jolted violently before slamming onto the sea surface, with part of its bow bursting open on impact.
Ãnal Ãstel, prime minister of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is only recognised by Turkey, told local media the boat was hit by two waves before it capsized.
While the captain of the vessel was trying to recover from the first wave, a second wave hit and it began taking on water, he said.
![People wait for news of their relatives at Kyrenia port.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/af8b/live/abd720f0-a52d-11f1-8ebe-efa2c58ecfe9.png)
Survivors continue to wait for news of their missing relatives at the port in Kyrenia
The boat has completely sunk and is lying at a depth of 514m (1,686ft), officials say.
Debris remains scattered across the water, including a black wheelie suitcase bobbing on the surface and a sheet of steel that appeared to have broken away from the ferry.
Authorities are attempting to recover the vessel's black box recorder to establish what happened.
A ship will be arriving from Turkey on Tuesday to help with search efforts, TRNC President Tufan Erhurman said.
Meanwhile, a three-day period of national mourning began on Monday.
The ferry - a high-speed 40m long, 10m wide Filo Jet vessel - sails under the flag of Turkey, according to Marine Traffic.
Filo Denizcilik, the company which operates the capsized passenger boat, said it was "deeply saddened by the tragic accident".
The TRNC controls the northern third of the island of Cyprus, which has been divided since 1974.
![Map of the eastern Mediterranean showing the route of a vessel between northern Cyprus and southern Turkey. A label near Kyrenia on Cyprus's north coast states that the vessel departed at 11:58 on Sunday. Another label near Tasucu on Turkey's southern coast states it was due to arrive at 17:52 local time. A red marker in the sea between the two locations identifies the approximate location where the vessel was sinking. An inset globe highlights the region's position. The map includes labels for Cyprus, Turkey, Kyrenia and Tasucu, a scale bar showing 20km and 10 miles, and a BBC logo in the bottom right corner.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/e66f/live/41e7f4a0-a477-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png)
summary: A passenger ferry traveling from northern Cyprus to Turkey capsized off the coast of Kyrenia in rough seas, killing eight people and leaving 20 others missing, including the two children of survivors Ayten and Hayri Bicer. The vessel had been carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members when it was reportedly struck by two waves. Local authorities arrested eight crew members and the captain as rescue and recovery efforts continued, backed by a three-day period of national mourning.
key_points: A ferry traveling from Kyrenia to Turkey capsized off northern Cyprus after reportedly being hit by two waves.
The disaster killed eight people, with 20 others still missing, including the two children of survivors Ayten and Hayri Bicer.
The vessel was carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members, and 19 passengers were treated in local hospitals.
The captain, crew members, and one other man were formally arrested and detained for three days following the incident.
A three-day period of national mourning began on Monday as rescue operations and investigations continue.

title: Nepal-Tibet floods: rescuers race to reach 900 people believed trapped in hydropower tunnels
author: Cait Kelly
content:
Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 people thought to be trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of half a dozen hydropower projects in Nepal following the devastating flash floods, the country’s disaster management authority said on Monday.
The death toll from the unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris that crashed through valleys of Nepal on Wednesday last week has now risen to 903 people, with 16 more dead reported on the Tibet side of the border. More than 4,000 are missing in Nepal, with another 500 in Tibet.
Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, have been buried in shallow graves on the plains of the Himalayan region after being swept down the mountains by the torrent.
Nepali officials said on Monday the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from hydropower projects in the flood-hit region.
Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud to try to access the tunnels. “A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” said Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet.
Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers. “There is just mud everywhere,” he told the Guardian. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.”
On Sunday his team was trying to access Chilime Hydropower in Ruswana, in the worst-hit area.
Mountaineers improvised by grabbing planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as a makeshift bridge, along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe, he said.
“Walking in it is very difficult; at one point it was up to our chests,” Gurung said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 metres in. Inside that far, you could [see further in]; it looked like it was just bodies.”
![Ashish Gurung, left, a fellow rescue mountaineer Jenjen Lama at the Chilime Hydropower in Ruswana, Nepal.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/15e449981e46c56df7f20cae5dbb0ee77048047e/0_237_3024_3683/master/3024.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The hydro company had given his team a map and it looked like there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived by staying inside the internal infrastructure.
“They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.”
The Red Cross has estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China and some experts linked to the effects of the climate crisis.
Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and it remained challenging to compile a complete assessment of the damage.
“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday. Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations, besides civilian workers and volunteers, he added.
Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday that 903 deaths had been counted there, with 4,247 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. As of Sunday, Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, and Chinese state media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including over a hundred Nepalis.
China’s state-run CCTV reported that Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220m yuan ($33m) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.
![Rescuers use diggers on Monday to clear way to a tunnel of the Trishuli 3A Hydropower project, following deadly flash floods and a mudslide, in Nuwakot district, Nepal.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/09884d3a6f3669fdca64c5b00312f79991cf45aa/0_141_1530_1059/master/1530.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Nepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search and rescue operations, but it has leaned on neighbours India and China for their expertise in tunnel rescues.
Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers.
However, the weather was good on Monday and rescue work continued to pick up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hard-hit districts.
In the holy town of Devighat, on the banks of the Trishuli river that flooded, residents walked around the shells of what had once been homes, trying to salvage their belongings from the debris.
The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported, saying it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.
Two Nepali officials told Reuters that China had not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels following a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that a lack of data sharing could hamper future disaster preparedness.
China’s foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment on the meeting.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse
summary: Rescue teams in Nepal are racing to reach more than 900 people believed to be trapped in underground hydropower tunnels following unprecedented flash floods of ice, rock, mud, and debris. The disaster has resulted in hundreds of deaths and thousands of missing persons across Nepal and Tibet. Rescuers face severe challenges due to deep mud and blocked tunnels, while international aid and local security personnel continue relief efforts.
key_points: Rescue efforts are heavily focused on reaching over 900 people trapped in hydropower tunnels in Nepal.
The disaster death toll has risen to 903 in Nepal and 16 on the Tibet side of the border, with thousands still missing.
Rescuers face major challenges clearing deep mud and debris using heavy equipment, ropes, and makeshift bridges.
The Red Cross estimates that more than 90,000 people have been affected by the flooding.
China and various experts have linked the devastating flash floods to the effects of the climate crisis and glacier instability.

title: US strikes Iranian launchers in strait of Hormuz, sparking reprisal attack on airbases in Jordan
author: Guardian staff reporter
content:
Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month.
“I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak island,” a US official said on Sunday. “Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.”
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said the US attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens and would be met with a “response and punishment” from Tehran, Iranian state media reported.
In response, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities, and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV.
A spokesperson said the US would pay for the attack economically and militarily, according to the semi-official news agency Fars.
Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported the US attack was a drone strike.
On Sunday night, Reuters reported a US source as saying that all incoming missiles on US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact so far.
The exchange of strikes came shortly after the US-Iran war hit the six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.
The US said its attacks were aimed at preventing Iran from launching more sea mines into the strait, days after it announced it had completed clearing explosives from the strategic waterway.
Donald Trump said last week that all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait of Hormuz and Iran had been told that any ship or boat placing new mines would be destroyed.
The last known US strikes on Iran were in late July and the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks, with Washington threatening to impose costly sanctions on countries that support Iran.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. The Iran war has now crossed its six-month mark.
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war to no avail.
While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming and Washington has since declared “economic warfare” against Tehran.
US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions. Eighteen US service members have been killed in the conflict.
The war has led to the blockade of the strait of Hormuz, which before the conflict accounted for the transit of about a fifth of the world’s oil barrels consumed.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse
summary: The United States conducted a drone strike against two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the strait of Hormuz to prevent the deployment of sea mines. In retaliation, Iran's Revolutionary Guards launched ballistic missiles at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan. While Iranian media reported heavy damage and casualties, a US source stated that all incoming missiles were intercepted with no significant impact.
key_points: US forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the strait of Hormuz.
The US action aimed to stop Iran from placing sea mines in the strategic waterway.
Iran responded with ballistic missile strikes on the King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan.
A US source reported that all incoming missiles in Jordan were intercepted with no significant impact.
The exchange occurred as the US-Iran conflict marked its six-month anniversary.

title: Devastated by floods and overwhelmed by bodies, Nepalis weep for what remains of their homes
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
content:
The bodies continue to wash up. But the morgues have already run out of room.
Since the deadly floods coursed through the Himalayan valleys of Nepal and Tibet, the numbers of people killed have continued to rise. The bodies have surfaced in their hundreds and continue to be pulled from the thick, tar-like mud that engulfed everything after the flood waters receded. By Sunday, the death toll stood at 804 in Nepal and Tibet.
Morgues across Nepal are already overflowing. Authorities say they are overwhelmed with the task of trying to identify the dead, many mangled beyond recognition and turning up miles from home. As places to safely store the victims run out, mass burials have begun in the district of Bharatpur.
DNA samples were taken from each body before it was given a tag and a location number, wrapped in a plastic bag and then placed in a shallow grave. The hope, said the police, was that these bodies would eventually be identified by loved ones through DNA and retrieved for proper funeral rites.
In Chitwan, about 100 miles downstream from the region worst hit by the flash floods and mudslides, more than 250 bodies have washed up along the riverbanks. But they are in such a disfigured state that only nine have been successfully identified. Many will now be buried, at least temporarily, in the forest on the edge of the city.
In an effort to speed up the identification exercise, local officials have adopted a macabre approach of simply asking people to go through pictures of the bodies and look for identifying features: a necklace, a wedding ring, a tattoo, a scar. Photos of those recovered have been placed on to PowerPoint slideshows, for relatives to sit patiently through, and have been uploaded to the Nepal police website. Outside the morgue in the capital, Kathmandu, photographs of the dead inside have been posted on the walls.
Yet with more than 3,000 still reported missing in Nepal and Tibet, there are fears that the numbers of dead may still rise exponentially. Many of the worst-hit areas, where entire villages were wiped away by the tidal wave of mud, water and debris, are still inaccessible except by army helicopter. Speaking on Sunday, the foreign secretary, Amrit Bahadur Rai, said the Nepal government had requested “more than 1,000 freezer units” for safe storage of the dead.
![People looking though a mud-covered room](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/587bcefaa63584d390dd04884c33471d83fb5499/957_258_4432_3546/master/4432.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Even in areas lower down the river valley that were decimated by the floods but have remained accessible by road, search and rescue teams have struggled to retrieve all those killed and buried in the mud. On Sunday afternoon in Devighat, a sacred town on the Trishuli River that was left in ruins by the floods, police search and rescue teams prepared to pull another victim from the muddy ruins of a house. All that was visible through the thick mud was their feet.
“It is very tough work. We have retrieved 10 bodies from here so far, maybe there will be more,” said Amabadutta Bhatta, a police superintendent working as part of search and rescue in the city. “The floods destroyed the first and second storey of most homes here. When we finally clear all the mud, which may be many months, who knows what we might find.”
Those who survived the floods in Devighat have slowly come back to see the remains of their houses, many of which were wiped away altogether. Standing next to the carcass of her house, reduced to a few concrete blocks and twisted metal, Usha Nepali, 49, wept for the home where she had raised her four children and then her three grandchildren.
![Woman on muddy street carrying a chair](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/cefd083d6c76a311a284a8fee719d12f2d083425/0_2096_3791_3032/master/3791.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“I invested everything to build this house, so now I don’t know where to go and what to do,” said Nepali. “Nothing is left except this cloth on my back. I haven’t even been able to change clothes since the floods. How can we rebuild this house? This land is no longer safe but it’s the only land we have. The river has taken everything.”
The precariousness of living next to the Trishuli River was underlined on Sunday as the fast-moving waters again swelled dangerously high and rescuers urged people to get to higher ground quickly. Many in Devighat were packing up the few items they could find in their homes, never to return.
Jamuna Magar, 36, said her husband’s family had been living in Devighat for generations. She had come here when she got married and described it as “such a beautiful place”.
![Pile of bags and fuel cylinders outside a house](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/70b38991bc1edbfc5ca69e727ee03f876aa25a9d/0_643_4197_3357/master/4197.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In the minutes after they got warning of the flood, she had time to grab her gold but nothing else. As she stood by the ruins of her house, clutching the only thing she had been able to retrieve so far – a plastic vat of vegetable cooking oil – she said she did not see how they could ever live in Devighat again.
“We had experienced flooding before, but we never knew a flood like this could come and take our house,” she said. “Everything we owned was on the ground floor of the house and now it’s all lost. Even our refrigerator washed away. I’m too worried about my life, about my children’s lives to stay here any longer.”
She feared it would take “decades before they can rebuild Devighat again”.
summary: Deadly floods and mudslides across Nepal and Tibet have left a death toll of 804 by Sunday, with morgues overflowing and bodies washing up in rivers. Authorities have begun mass burials after taking DNA samples to help families identify victims later, while more than 3,000 people remain missing. Survivors have returned to find their homes destroyed, and ongoing rescue efforts are hampered by inaccessible areas and swelling river waters.
key_points: The death toll from the floods in Nepal and Tibet reached 804, with over 3,000 people still reported missing.
Overflowing morgues have forced authorities to begin mass burials of unidentified bodies after collecting DNA samples.
Officials are using PowerPoint slideshows, website uploads, and photographs on walls to help relatives identify the victims.
Many villages were completely wiped out by mud and debris, and thousands of survivors are left homeless with unsafe land.

title: Race to save hundreds of workers trapped in flooded tunnels in Nepal
author: Samaan Lateef
content:
Rescue workers in Nepal are wading through mounds of debris and mud to find more than 3,000 people still missing after Wednesday’s catastrophic floods.
Poor weather conditions have been hindering the painstaking rescue effort, with perhaps the most complicated mission being extricating the hundreds of workers trapped inside flooded hydropower tunnels.
The Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal said 898 people working on 11 hydropower sites, including some under construction, remained missing.
At a tunnel in Trishuli, a manhole was drilled allowing rescuers to abseil.
Rescuers had also begun “sending air” to possible survivors by drilling holes in the tunnel’s façade, said Sudan Gurung, the Nepali home minister.
Crews also sent cameras inside, where around 40 workers were believed to be trapped, to establish whether anyone remained alive.
A visibly empty space had raised hopes that the Upper Trishuli-3B tunnel might not be filled with sludge and debris, officials said.
summary: Rescue workers in Nepal are struggling to locate thousands of missing people following catastrophic floods, hampered by poor weather conditions. Among the most complex operations is the rescue of hundreds of workers trapped inside flooded hydropower tunnels. Officials have drilled holes in the Trishuli tunnel's facade to supply air and deployed cameras to search for survivors.
key_points: Over 3,000 people are missing following catastrophic floods in Nepal.
Poor weather conditions are severely hindering ongoing rescue operations.
The Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal reported 898 missing workers across 11 hydropower sites.
Rescuers have drilled holes into a flooded tunnel in Trishuli to supply air and send cameras inside to search for about 40 trapped workers.

title: Captain in custody after boat capsizes off northern Cyprus, local leader says, as eight reported dead
author: Live Reporting Edited by Angus Thompson; Ben Hatton
content:
![A helicopter flies over the sea. In the background a small boat pulls along two life rafts](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/8/30/92dd8450-6f3a-41a7-bed6-aa86d92b8eb8.jpg.webp) Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Eight people are reported to have died after a passenger boat capsized off northern Cyprus on Sunday.
Search and rescue efforts continue, with some people still thought to be missing.
The captain and seven crew have been taken into custody, according to Ãnal Ãstel, prime minister of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus.
There were 267 people on board when the vessel capsized, he says. In an update earlier in the day he said 237 had been rescued.
The reason for the boat capsizing are not yet clear, but Ãstel says it was hit by two waves beforehand, according to Turkish media.
We're ending our live coverage now - you can read more in our news story here.
summary: A passenger boat carrying 267 people capsized off northern Cyprus on Sunday, resulting in eight reported deaths. Search and rescue operations are ongoing as some individuals remain missing. The captain and seven crew members have been taken into custody following the incident.
key_points: Eight people are reported dead after a boat capsized off northern Cyprus.
There were 267 people on board the vessel, with 237 rescued earlier in the day.
The captain and seven crew members are in custody.
