title: Nepal-Tibet floods: death toll nears 800; air pipe inserted to tunnel where large group trapped – follow updates
author: Mabel Banfield-Nwachi; Yohannes Lowe
content:
The death toll in Nepal has risen to 781, Reuters reports, citing the disaster authority.
As we reported earlier, there are slightly different figures going around from different agencies and officials, and earlier we reported 788.
Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 dead in Tibet and 546 people missing following Wednesday’s disaster, taking the overall toll to 797 dead and 3,048 unaccounted for.
Here are some images of rescuers and army personnel in Nepal trying to locate the thousands of people who are still missing.
Army personnel conduct a search and rescue operation for flood victims along the Narayani river at Bharatpur in Nepal's Chitwan district. Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images
Thousands of people have been rescued since the catastrophic floods on Wednesday, with thousands still missing. Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images
About 85 Americans remain missing after a devastating flood swept through a remote region of the Himalayas, the state department said on Sunday.
State department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told ABC talkshow “This Week” that nine Americans have been evacuated and that he was unaware of any US nationals dying in the disaster.
Pigott said:
The remoteness of this location makes getting reliable information difficult. But our dedication remains, our commitment remains.
The death toll in Nepal has risen to 781, Reuters reports, citing the disaster authority.
As we reported earlier, there are slightly different figures going around from different agencies and officials, and earlier we reported 788.
Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 dead in Tibet and 546 people missing following Wednesday’s disaster, taking the overall toll to 797 dead and 3,048 unaccounted for.
Nepal begins mass burials of unidentified flood victims
Nepal’s Chitwan district has become the site of mass burials for hundreds of unidentified victims whose bodies were swept away by the devastating flash floods on Wednesday.
Authorities have dug hundreds of graves in the district’s Devghat forest, with the forest trials serving as a temporary burial ground for bodies too badly decomposed to be identified.
“We were left with no other option and had to take this step. Our concern was the risk to public health posed by the rapid decomposition of the bodies,” Ganesh Arya, chief district officer of Baratpur, the headquarters of Chitwan district, said.
According to the Reuters news agency, authorities buried 96 unidentified bodies in the forest yesterday and planned to bury over 100 others on Sunday, as recovery teams continue to retrieve victims from rivers and piles of debris.
Armed police officers wearing protective equipment prepare to transport bodies to the pit at Devghat mass burial site in Chitwan, Nepal. Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters
Nepal’s disaster agency has said in an update that the death toll has increased to 788 after the catastrophic flash flood. There are slightly different figures circulating from various agencies and officials.
Authorities have issued high-alert fresh water surge and flash flood warnings for the Trishuli Bazaar area in Nepal’s Nuwakot district following severe upstream glacial collapses and debris flows.
A drone view of the aftermath of flash flooding along the Trishuli river amid fresh water surge warning in the Trishuli Bazaar area of Nuwakot district, Nepal. Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP
Senator Penny Wong, Australian minister for foreign affairs, said Australia is deploying a further $3m in humanitarian assistance to flood-afflicted areasalong the Nepal-China border.
Wong announced that this would include “$2m in supplies and other humanitarian support to be delivered by the ADF in the coming days.”
She added that the government will provide a further $1m to the Emergency Action Alliance appeal (EAA appeal):
There has been an overwhelming response from the Australian people to the Emergency Action Alliance appeal, which has now reached over $1.4m in donations.
As a result, the government will provide a further $1m to the EAA appeal.
Wong highlighted that 42 Australians remain unaccounted for, and outlined the government’s promise to “continue to do everything we can to confirm their welfare and support their loved ones.”
Senator the Hon Penny Wong promised a further $3m in humanitarian assistance following the floods along the Nepal-China border. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images
Here are a few of the latest images that show some the damage and the ongoing desperate search to find missing people.
Student Uma Shah looks for his school bag inside the flood-damaged Bageshwori Secondary School, in Dhading district, Nepal. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA
A wall posted with photos of missing people outside a hospital in the capital city, in Kathmandu, Nepal. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images
An aerial view shows the damaged Ghatbesi Bridge over the Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods in Nepal’s Dhading district. Photograph: Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/Getty Images
A police officer stands near identification number tags for bodies at the Devghat mass burial site for victims of deadly flash floods and mudslides, in Chitwan, Nepal. Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters
Nepal said on Sunday it had begun burying some of the hundreds of bodies recovered after devastating floods, as the death toll rises to 752.
Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 people are dead in Tibet and 546 people are missing following Wednesday’s disaster, taking the overall toll to 768.
The dead are traditionally cremated on funeral pyres in Hindu-majority Nepal, so the burials are viewed as long-term storage until families can retrieve them. DNA samples have been taken and all of those buried have been carefully recorded, foreign secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai told reporters, according to AFP.
Authorities in Nepal warned of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River.
Flood warning notices were sent to people’s phones early Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst hit by Wednesday’s catastrophic floods. Latest figures suggest at least 760 people have been killed, though this figure has not yet been confirmed. More than 3,000 people remain missing in Nepal and Tibet.
Nepali rescuers trying to reach hydropower workers believed trapped in tunnels swamped by flood debris deployed heavy machinery on Sunday, after rain and rising river waters hampered earlier efforts.
“Drilling of four holes has been completed... preparations are now underway to enter the tunnel directly... and proceed with search and rescue operations,” Nepal’s energy ministry said in an update.
Rescue operations entered their fifth day since the floods, with teams battling difficult conditions at the disaster sites.
Nepal’s government says more than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside multiple tunnels at hydropower projects, with key rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites in the Himalayan river valley.
They are among 933 hydropower workers missing since a wall of mud and debris swept down on Wednesday morning, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
Army rescue teams using drills at Trishuli 3A first broke through into the upper part of a mud-swamped tunnel on Saturday evening, and began pumping air and sending in a camera.
Overnight rain and rising river levels hampered efforts early on Sunday, filling the excavation area with water, before conditions eased.
Welcome to our continuing coverage of the aftermath of the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Rescuers in Nepal and China are still trying to locate thousands of people who are missing days after a wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region.
The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to at least 750 dead and more than 3,000 people missing after China’s latest update on Sunday. Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, while Nepali officials confirmed 734 dead and 2,498 people missing. There were reports of some dead swept downstream as far away as India.
China said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were missing on the Tibetan side of a border crossing with Nepal: the highest number was from Nepal at 104, while 49 Indian, 33 Latvian, 18 American and 15 British citizens were also unaccounted for.
Soldiers search for bodies in Nepal as rescue operations shift into search and retrieval. Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images
In a breakthrough late on Saturday, the Nepali army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where workers are believed to be trapped.
“We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside,” said the home minister, Sudan Gurungd. More than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside such tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.
Here’s the other main developments:
Four days after the disaster, authorities said some bodies being recovered had decomposed beyond recognition. They would be buried after legal formalities because of health risks and a fear of disease outbreaks. “DNA samples will be collected, and the bodies will be buried in an open space,” the Chitwan district administration said in a notice.
The foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said Nepalrequired specialist assistance to rescue people trapped in tunnels; restore transport and communication lines where bridges had been destroyed; identify bodies; conduct DNA testing; and store bodies for longer periods.
A team of Indian tunnel experts arrived in Nepal on Saturday, Khanal said. China’s Xinhua news agency reported Beijing had dispatched five tunnel experts to support rescue efforts, with four more due to join them.
The US will provide $3.6m in humanitarian aid to Nepal, “including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households,” the state department said in a post on X.
summary: Catastrophic flash floods and mudslides along the Nepal-Tibet border have left hundreds dead and thousands missing, with overall death toll estimates nearing 800. Authorities have begun mass burials of severely decomposed, unidentified victims in Nepal's Chitwan district due to public health risks. Meanwhile, rescue teams are utilizing heavy machinery and drilled air pipes to reach over one hundred hydropower workers believed to be trapped inside mud-swamped tunnels.
key_points: The combined death toll in Nepal and Tibet has approached 800, with over 3,000 people remaining missing.
Nepal has begun mass burials of unidentified and badly decomposed bodies in the Devghat forest to prevent disease outbreaks, while collecting DNA samples for future identification.
Rescuers successfully drilled holes and inserted an air pipe into a blocked tunnel at a hydroelectric site where over 100 workers are believed to be trapped.
Australia and the United States announced millions of dollars in additional humanitarian assistance and supplies for the flood-affected regions.

title: Nepal-China floods: What’s the latest death toll, how many remain missing?
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![Nepal floods](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-2292292245-1788069574.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
The death toll from devastating floods near the border between Nepal and China has risen to at least 734, with thousands missing following Wednesday’s disaster.
Rescue efforts are under way to locate more than 900 missing workers at hydropower projects in central Nepal.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 38-year-old Nepal flood survivor reunited with mother after rescue
- list 2 of 3Before and after images show catastrophic impact of Nepal flash floods
- list 3 of 3Nepal and China resume flood rescue as death toll surpasses 600
Authorities from Nepal and the Tibet region of China have put the total number of missing at just over 3,000, with some bodies washing up in neighbouring India.
A glacier collapse high in the Himalaya mountains in Nepal near the border with Tibet triggered Wednesday’s catastrophic flooding and landslides, which buried villages and towns along the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi river systems.
On Friday, rising water levels in a new lake formed by the build-up of debris prompted a temporary halt to search efforts amid fears of a second flood. Rescue operations resumed after the lake threat was deemed manageable.
Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Beijing, said that Chinese authorities say the risk seems to have been reduced, but it has not disappeared.
“They are closely monitoring the barrier lake, located one km upstream at the port of Gyirong and the border area. They are closely monitoring using satellites, radars, and drones,” she said, adding that “authorities are confident that if the situation around the barrier lake should deteriorate, they will be able to give notice of about 30 minutes to rescuers below”.
Here’s what we know about the latest rescue efforts and the victims:
Where are the 900 workers missing?
As of Sunday morning, around 933 people are missing or unaccounted for, according to the country’s Independent Power Producers’ Association. They were working at 11 hydropower project sites and tunnels in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, which are among the worst-hit areas.
The workers include citizens of Nepal, India, South Korea and China. How many are trapped or missing at each individual hydropower site remains unclear.
“After complaints emerged that people were trapped inside the tunnel, the government prioritised the deployment of a rescue team and has been advancing the work to clear the entrance by removing debris and rubble,” Nepal’s prime minister’s office said late on Saturday.
“To expedite the digging of the tunnel entrance and the search operations, a joint team of 82 personnel – including 62 from the Nepali Army and 20 from the Armed Police Force Nepal and Nepal Police – has been continuously deployed since last night. However, with adverse weather conditions persisting in the area, the rescue efforts have become quite challenging,” the statement added.
Nepal’s Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai said that 19,000 security personnel and 16 helicopters have been mobilised in the search and rescue operations.
Videos on social media show Nepali soldiers wading through mud trying to rescue workers trapped at the 216-megawatt Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project. The army has rescued 254 workers there.
But rescue efforts have also proved challenging at other hydropower sites, such as the 22MW Chilime Hydropower project in Rasuwa district, 133 km (82 miles) north of the capital, Kathmandu.
“We have not been able to carry out a rescue. The tunnel is filled with mud and it is impossible to enter,” Baburaj Maharjan, executive director of Chilime Hydropower Company, told the Kathmandu Post. “We are working to mobilise a rock-climbing rescue team,” he added.
India has sent teams to help rescue trapped workers.
According to Indian media reports, an 11-member team of medical personnel and tunnel-rescue specialists reached Nepal on Saturday to begin aerial assessments in the Chilime and Langtang regions.
What else do we know about the victims and the missing?
According to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the death toll from the floods has risen to 734.
The Kathmandu Post reported that bodies are turning up far downstream and local morgues are running out of space to store others until they are identified.
Rojita Adhikari, a freelance journalist and filmmaker from Nepal, told Al Jazeera that authorities are facing a challenge.
“Yesterday [Saturday] I was at a press conference with Nepal’s foreign minister and he said the country is struggling to store and identify dead bodies – whose numbers are mounting. He said Nepal does not have enough refrigerators to store the dead bodies and identify and test their DNA,” she said.
Unidentified bodies have been sent to 21 hospitals in different districts for preservation and identification, says the Kathmandu Post.
Chinese authorities in Tibet told reporters that 16 people had died in Gyirong County, as of Saturday evening.
As of Sunday morning, 2,498 people remain missing in Nepal. They include 589 foreigners and 127 Nepali citizens travelling with them, 45 personnel from Nepal’s army, 27 from Nepal’s police and 13 from the armed police force.
Reporting from Nepal, Al Jazeera’s Samer Allawi said Nepal’s disaster management authorities have evacuated thousands of people, including foreign nationals, with the help of the army and police.
In China’s Tibet region, authorities said on Sunday that 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries are missing. They include 104 from Nepal, 49 from neighbouring India, as well as 33 Latvians, 18 Americans, 15 Britons, six from Canada, six from Australia, three each from Russia, Malaysia and Germany, 10 from the Netherlands, New Zealand, Estonia, France and Ireland and one each from Finland, Lithuania, Portugal, Ukraine, Spain, Hungary and Kazakhstan.
Al Jazeera’s Yu said that getting a picture of the full scale of the devastation on the Chinese side of the border is difficult because foreign journalists are not allowed to enter the area. “We are completely reliant on the government and state media,” she said.
“The government says teams have desperately been searching the worst-hit area of the port of Gyirong since teams arrived there late on Friday after days of trekking through the mountains,” she said, adding that they have “searched at least 90,000 square metres using life monitoring equipment, search dogs and drones”.
Chinese authorities say that a team of hundreds of technical operators are using heavy machinery to slowly repair roads as access to the port of Gyirong is blocked following the flooding and landslides.
![A soldier at a Nepali army training centre in Trishuli in Nuwakot district helps evacuate flood victims](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-30T062424Z_992674463_RC2T8NAEZDYS_RTRMADP_3_NEPAL-FLOODS-1788072931.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C515&quality=80)
What do we know about rescue efforts?
Nepal and China are working together to identify missing citizens and foreign nationals.
But the efforts have proven to be challenging, with roads and bridges destroyed.
On Sunday morning, water levels in the Trishuli River rose after more rain, prompting residents and rescue workers to seek higher ground, a Nepalese police official said.
Al Jazeera’s Allawi said authorities “have not yet moved to the second phase of relief operations, which includes humanitarian assistance and reopening roads”, because of “the rugged terrain and the lack of sufficient resources”.
He added that Nepal’s finance minister [Swarnim Wagle] estimated losses from the disaster at “more than $4bn”, while warnings remain in force for potential flooding along rivers in northern Nepal.
“Local relief efforts are also very limited because of the difficulty of reaching the affected areas,” he said, adding that “dozens of kilometres of roads have been destroyed, as well as bridges over rivers”.
Al Jazeera’s Minelle Fernandez, reporting from the Nepalese capital, said the government has requested specialist help from India and China to “fill gaps” in its rescue operations.
“The reason the [Nepalese] foreign ministry spokesman said that this decision has been taken is because lives are at stake and that it is very, very urgent,” she said.
“The reason that initially Nepal had said they didn’t want assistance is they didn’t want the chaos which comes with huge teams being fanned out in different areas.”
![An undated handout photo of rescue workers taking part in a rescue operation near the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project, following deadly flash floods and mudslides, in Rasuwa, Nepal](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-30T100622Z_520297392_RC2X8NAFC30J_RTRMADP_3_NEPAL-FLOODS-1788084465.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Nepali journalist Adhikari accused world leaders of not prioritising the threats posed by the climate crisis. “This catastrophe is not Nepal’s fault. The country is paying the price for how world leaders have been dealing with climate change.”
“Nepal has had floods and disasters like earthquakes before, but I have never seen anything like what happened on Wednesday. Entire families have been swept away. People are devastated and have lost everything – their property, their security, their lifelines. They have no homes to return to in the flood-affected areas.”
China has mobilised 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220 million yuan ($32.7m) to support relief efforts, according to CCTV news. Beijing is also using heavy-lift drones and helicopters to airdrop equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers near the border crossing.
International aid has arrived from the United Nations, the Red Cross Federation, Australia, India, South Korea and the United States.
The US and Canada said they would provide $3.6m each in humanitarian aid. The United Kingdom has offered $6.8m in aid, while the UN released $2.5m in emergency funding.
On Friday, the European Union pledged $2.3m and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said it had allocated more than $1m and launched an emergency appeal for $31m.
summary: A glacier collapse in the Himalayas triggered catastrophic floods and landslides near the border between Nepal and China, burying towns and river systems. The disaster has left at least 734 people dead and thousands missing, including workers at multiple hydropower project sites. Rescue operations by Nepal, China, and international teams continue to face significant challenges due to destroyed infrastructure, adverse weather, and the threat of barrier lakes.
key_points: A Himalayan glacier collapse caused devastating floods and landslides along the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi river systems near the Nepal-China border.
The death toll has risen to at least 734 people, with thousands remaining missing or unaccounted for.
Over 900 missing workers at multiple hydropower project sites in central Nepal are the focus of intense search and rescue operations.
Authorities from Nepal and China, along with international aid teams, are utilizing heavy machinery, helicopters, and drones despite hindered access from destroyed roads and bridges.
Nepal is struggling with a shortage of refrigerated storage for the mounting number of recovered bodies.

title: Ukraine war latest: Russia hits Kyiv with deadly strike as dozens killed in care home
author: Stuti Mishra; Harriette Boucher; Maira Butt
content:
Russian strikes have killed at least 37 people in Kyiv, most of them from a care home for the elderly, according to local Ukrainian officials.
It marks the deadliest attack on Ukraine’s capital this year, the Associated Press reports.
The strikes hit an ammunition depot, sparking a fire in the Bucha district overnight that spread to surrounding areas.
Dozens were injured with nearby infrastructure including residential buildings and the care facility for the elderly and people with disabilities suffering “significant damage”.
Volodymyr Zelensky has vowed to punish those responsible and said criminal cases had already been opened on charges of official negligence.
He described it as a “terrible situation and terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people”.
Meanwhile, Russia’s defence ministry said it had successfully tested a nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missile that could reach the US.
The missile, which has a range of more than 6,700km, was fired from the Arkhangelsk region and reached its designated target at the Kura test site in Kamchatka.
Two killed, 27 wounded in Russian strikes on Ukraine's Kherson region
Russian strikes hit homes and apartment blocks in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson on Saturday, killing two people and wounding 27 others, including a child, regional head Oleksandr Prokudin said in a statement.
Mr Prokudin had said earlier in the week that Russia had intensified its attacks on critical infrastructure in the region, about 70 per cent of which is under Russian control.
He urged tens of thousands of residents to move to safer regions, citing the possibility of prolonged power and heating outages this winter.
Russia claims Myla warehouse held drone components
Russia's defence ministry said it struck a warehouse in Myla, a village in Ukraine's Bucha district near Kyiv, that was storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones, conflicting with Ukraine's description of the site as holding shells, mines and other ammunition.
The warehouse was hit in a Russian drone strike on Friday night that sparked explosions and fires, killing 37 people, most of them residents of a nearby care home, in the deadliest attack of the war this year.
Ukrainian officials have said the site was a Defence Forces storage facility and have opened criminal proceedings on charges of official negligence over the storage of ammunition near homes.
The ministry also said it had attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, along with a logistics centre and warehouse facilities in the Kyiv region that it said stored parts for Ukraine's Flamingo cruise missiles
Myla residents recall panic as drone strike sparked fires that raced through homes
Residents of Myla described scenes of panic as a Russian drone strike hit a warehouse in the village on Friday night, sparking massive explosions and fires that swept through dozens of nearby homes and buildings and killed 37 people.
The Friday night attack on the warehouse in Myla, a village in the Bucha district, was the war's deadliest attack this year and came on the second of three days of nearly round-the-clock Russian strikes that have severely disrupted life in and around the Ukrainian capital.
The warehouse strike sparked fires that raced through homes and damaged at least 50 residential buildings, said Tymur Tkachenko, who heads the local regional military administration. He was later cited by local media as saying 34 of the people killed were residents of a care home for elderly and disabled people. More than 370 people were evacuated.
The blasts rocked Myla, causing people to frantically seek cover.
"At about 8pm, the drone hit a warehouse somewhere and then the detonation began," Oleksandr Vodolaz, a village resident, told the Associated Press. "No one knew that weapons were stored there."
Another local, Zhanna Kravchuk, said she had so many questions about what happened.
"Why are weapons like this ... in warehouses and not on the front lines where they would help?" she said.
![Rescuers look on near a damaged house at a site of a yesterday's Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the village of Myla, Kyiv region](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/29/18/2026-08-29T152818Z_937312472_RC2C8NAORPIZ_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-ATTACK-KYIV-REGION.JPG)
Ukraine PM says Myla warehouse tragedy repeats 'criminal negligence' seen in July's Vyshneve strike
Ukrainian prime minister Serhii Koretskyi said the Myla warehouse strike echoed a July attack on an ammunition depot in the Kyiv suburb of Vyshneve, which killed 22 people and set off similar detonations and fires in nearby homes.
"Unfortunately, we can already see that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve did not become a lesson," Mr Koretskyi said. "In the fifth year of a full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes is criminal negligence."
"And all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again," he said.
The 37 killed in Friday's strike surpassed the 31 who died in a 2 July attack on Kyiv, which had been the deadliest single attack of the war so far this year.
Zelensky opens probe over stored explosives
President Volodymyr Zelensky said criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence, suggesting local officials may have been responsible for storing explosives near homes in the Kyiv region village of Myla.
"There are regulations in place - ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," Mr Zelensky said in an online post.
"Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions," he said, adding that "all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again."
A drone strike on the warehouse, which officials say may have illegally stored munitions, sparked explosions and fires that damaged dozens of nearby homes and buildings in Myla, a village in the Bucha district.
Watch: Moment Putin launches nuclear-capable missile in warning to West
Navy tracks Russian warships in English Channel during ‘intense’ operation
A task group was shadowed by Type 45 destroyer HMS Duncan, Type 23 frigate HMS St Albans and patrol vessel HMS Severn as it made its way from the North Sea through the English Channel.
Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko was watched escorting sanctioned cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta, with a Merlin helicopter extending the UK’s surveillance as the ships approached the Strait of Dover.
In response to the tracking, Russia deployed other military resources including the Neustrashimy frigate to guard the illegal shipment, UK officials said.
First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said there was “no room for complacency” as shadow fleet vessels continue to pose “an unacceptable risk” to maritime security and the environment.
“Alongside our allies, this approach is forcing Moscow to divert Russian warships away from their core purpose. That is because Russia knows we stand ready to act again, should it be required,” he said.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/21/08/01K60KWBFHMY8EAGJ0B0503NKJ.jpg?trim=0,0,0,0&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
ICYMI: Putin thinks Trump is ‘weakened’ by Iran war, says report
Vladimir Putin believes Donald Trump has been “weakened” by the war in Iran and this could allow the Russian president to ramp up aggression in Europe, US intelligence has indicated.
While the details of CIA director John Ratcliffe’s trip to Moscow this week remain elusive, The Washington Post has reported that the meeting cautioned Moscow against banking on the US president being distracted by conflict with Tehran to escalate action against Ukraine.
For Putin, the ground war in Ukraine has not proved to be the quick victory he presented to the Russian public, where in 2014, he claimed he could, if he chose to take Kiev, do so “in two weeks.”
Instead, as the war drags into its fifth year, Moscow has faced growing levels of internal division, putting pressure on the Russian president.
Watch: The woman making Ukraine safe from landmines amid a brutal war
Russia hits Kyiv with deadly strike as dozens killed in care home
Russian strikes have killed at least 37 people in Kyiv, most of them from a care home for the elderly, according to local Ukrainian officials.
At least 27 of those killed are reported to have been in the facility.
The strikes hit an ammunition depot, sparking a fire in the Bucha district overnight.
Dozens were injured with nearby infrastructure including residential buildings and the care facility for the elderly and people with disabilities suffering “significant damage”.
Volodymyr Zelensky has vowed to punish those responsible and said criminal cases had already been opened on charges of official negligence.
He described it as a “terrible situation and terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people”.
summary: Russian drone strikes hit a military storage facility in the Myla village of Kyiv's Bucha district, sparking massive fires that killed at least 37 people, primarily residents of a nearby care home for the elderly and disabled. The incident marked the deadliest attack on the Ukrainian capital this year and prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to open criminal investigations into official negligence regarding the storage of munitions near residential areas. Meanwhile, separate Russian strikes in the Kherson region killed two people and injured 27 others.
key_points: A Russian drone strike on a storage facility in Myla killed 37 people, making it the deadliest attack on Kyiv this year.
Most of the victims were residents of a nearby care home for the elderly and people with disabilities.
Ukrainian officials and President Zelensky opened criminal investigations into official negligence for storing explosives near residential areas.
Separate Russian strikes in the southern Kherson region killed two people and wounded 27 others.

title: Iceland's EU referendum: first partial results show razor-thin margin
author: Luca Bertuzzi
content:
Iceland's EU referendum is on a knife-edge, with the 'Yes' camp at 51.2% and the 'No' at 48.8%. 40% of the votes have already been scrutinised. As expected, rural constituencies are leaning decisively for the 'No' while Reykjavík's two constituencies lean solidly 'Yes'.
The partial results show a neck-to-neck race with the 'Yes' at 51.2% and the 'No' at 48.8%, with over 87,000 votes scrutinised.
In line with the opinion polls, the 'No' is heading toward 60% in more rural regions, whereas initial results from the capital Reykjavík point to around 58% for the 'Yes'.
The first nearly 10,000 votes scrutinised for the Southern Constituency give 'No' a significant advantage with 59.8% of the votes, against 40.2% for 'Yes'. The Southwest Constituency was equally split with 9,900 votes for 'Yes', and 9,900 for 'No'.
Similarly, with a little less than 6,000 votes counted, the initial results from the Northwest Constituency see the Eurosceptic camp at 60.8%, and the 'Yes' camp at 39.2%, whilst the Northeast Constituency with nearly 10,000 votes has the 'No' at 56% and the 'Yes' at 44%.
By contrast, the initial results for Reykjavík's south constituency with over 20,000 votes scrutinised have the 'Yes' at 55.9% and 'No' at 44.1%. The capital's north constituency has nearly 21,000 votes scrutinised, with the 'Yes' at 59.4% and the 'No' at 40.6%.
The partial results are consistent with expectations, as rural areas are expected to be more Eurosceptic due to concerns related to fisheries and farming, whilst the capital Reykjavík is expected to be more pro-EU.
Polling stations closed at 10:00 pm local time on Saturday for Iceland's high-stakes EU referendum.
On Saturday, Icelanders were called to vote on whether to resume accession negotiations with the European Union or abandon any prospect of joining the bloc for the foreseeable future. Around 272,000 individuals were eligible to vote.
According to preliminary figures, voter turnout was higher than, or at least comparable to, the 2024 parliamentary elections, when it reached 80%, according to local media.
Until a few days before the vote, polls suggested a neck-and-neck race, with the pro-European camp's advantage steadily eroding.
"Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?" was the question on the ballot.
Iceland applied for EU membership following the 2009 financial crisis, but froze the talks after the election of a Eurosceptic government in 2013.
Further results are expected through the night as counting continues.
This is a developing story.
summary: First partial results from Iceland's EU referendum show a razor-thin margin, with the 'Yes' camp at 51.2% and the 'No' camp at 48.8% after 40% of the votes were scrutinized. Voting patterns align with expectations, as rural constituencies heavily favor the 'No' side while Reykjavík leans solidly toward 'Yes'. The referendum asks citizens whether to resume accession negotiations with the European Union.
key_points: Over 87,000 votes have been scrutinized, representing about 40% of the total.
Rural regions are leaning toward 'No' by up to 60.8%, driven by concerns over fisheries and farming.
Reykjavík's constituencies are showing strong support for 'Yes', reaching up to 59.4%.
Voter turnout is reported to be high, comparable to or exceeding the 80% turnout in the 2024 parliamentary elections.
Iceland previously applied for EU membership in 2009 before freezing talks in 2013 under a Eurosceptic government.

title: Death was staring at us, says family trapped on balcony by Nepal floods
author: Samaan Lateef
content:
First, she heard the sound of stones breaking. Then the screams followed.
When she saw the torrents rushing towards her house, there was little else Laxmi Pandey Pyakurel could do.
The mother, 42, could only gather with her family on the balcony as they watched the floodwaters tear through their neighbourhood in Nepal.
She stood with her husband, their two children, her parents-in-law and a neighbour as the Trishuli river surged, with seemingly everything, apart from their house, destroyed in its wake.
“We saw death very closely. Death was staring at every one of us. We thought these were our final moments. I told everyone that if we had to die, we would die together,” Laxmi told The Telegraph on Saturday.
Remarkable footage of the family stranded in the middle of the gushing water was widely shared after Nepal was devastated by the glacier collapse, which triggered a huge flood in the landlocked country.
The family had been in a liquor shop, a few metres from their home, when people began shouting that the river was flooding.
summary: Laxmi Pandey Pyakurel and her family were trapped on their balcony as devastating floods from a glacier collapse surged through their neighborhood in Nepal. The family of seven watched as the Trishuli river destroyed everything around their house, believing they were facing their final moments. Viral footage captured the family stranded in the middle of the gushing water before they were able to survive the ordeal.
key_points: A glacier collapse in Nepal triggered massive floods that destroyed the neighborhood.
Laxmi Pandey Pyakurel, her family, and a neighbor were trapped on their house balcony.
The surging Trishuli river destroyed nearly everything around them.
Footage of the stranded family was widely shared online.

title: ‘The world needs to pay attention’: Nepalis and Tibetans in New York respond to the Himalayan disaster
author: Lok Darjee
content:
Geeta Tamang was getting ready for bed when her aunts shared news that upended her world.
“My aunts came into my room and told me what had happened,” said Tamang, a 24-year-old computer science student at Queens College. She lives in Jackson Heights, home to one of the largest Nepali and Tibetan communities in New York City.
Tamang’s family village lies in Rasuwa near the Nepal-Tibet border, where a Himalayan glacier collapsed on Wednesday. The torrent of water, mud and rock tore through communities downstream, sweeping away most of the village where Tamang grew up.
As her calls to relatives went unanswered, the uncertainty only fueled her fears. Those she did reach were largely unaware of the disaster that had unfolded. From her bedroom in Queens, Tamang found herself breaking the news to her own family, one call at a time.
Across New York’s Nepali and Tibetan diaspora, the flood has stirred grief and fear for relatives back home, and desperation to help in any way possible.
More than 600 people have been confirmed dead, and almost 3,000 remain missing, including Tamang’s grandmother’s sister.
“My grandmother’s sister, she’s really like a grandmother to me,” Tamang said, her voice trembling. “I don’t think there’s any chance she survived.”
Across the border in Tibet, Chinese authorities have reported at least seven deaths. But the official toll has been met with deep suspicion among some Tibetans living abroad, including Sonam Tshiring, 58, a Tibetan refugee who settled in Queens three decades ago who believes the number of people killed in Tibet is far higher than Chinese authorities have acknowledged.
![A young woman stands outside a restaurant.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4f11c25ac293efd26062fecae6e81f8315de5b8e/0_1229_4284_3426/master/4284.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
For Nepali and Tibetan communities thousands of miles away in New York and across the US, the catastrophe is about more than relatives missing and villages destroyed. It has sharpened the focus on an urgent injustice: who is being forced to bear the consequences of a warming planet, and why should communities that contributed so little to the climate crisis bear some of its greatest costs? Nepal is responsible for only a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet its Himalayan communities face mounting dangers as temperatures rise and glaciers retreat.
The disaster has also arrived at a particularly fraught political moment, as the US has retreated from international climate commitments while dramatically reducing foreign aid and humanitarian assistance, leaving vulnerable countries with fewer resources to prepare for and recover from disasters.
The anxiety has reached a younger generation of Nepali Americans, some of whom have spent much of their lives moving between Nepal and New York.
Ninima Rai, 19, lived in Nepal before moving to New York when she was 11. She was still a child when a devastating earthquake struck Nepal in 2015. This time, she watched a catastrophe in her homeland from thousands of miles away.
Her relatives in Nepal were safe, she said, though communications had been disrupted. From New York, she and other young Nepalis have been following updates, sharing information and supporting organizations that are assisting flood victims.
“It’s hard to see how we can support them from so far away,” Rai said.
![A phone displays a picture of two older people in traditional Nepali clothing.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/76d648846c7caf3623d301894afae61c3fe304c4/0_0_4284_5712/master/4284.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Tashi Sherpa, 16, was born in the United States but spent four formative years of her childhood in Nepal after her parents worried she might lose touch with their culture. She returned to New York for greater educational opportunities and describes herself as having grown up “between Nepal and New York”.
For Sherpa, crises in both countries have produced a peculiar sense of having two homes but, at moments, feeling secure in neither.
“As a Nepali American … it’s not just Nepal, but it’s America too,” she said. “I think it is a very chaotic time for us to feel like there is no safe space … and we feel very easily overwhelmed.”
Still, both teenagers described action as an antidote to helplessness. Friends in Nepal were preparing aid kits and collecting donations for food and clothing, Sherpa said, while young Nepalis in New York were sharing information and checking on relatives.
“There’s only so much that we can do, especially being so far away,” Sherpa said.
![A younger woman smiles in front of a wall with certificates and pictures hung on it.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/33bad176ebc4c70c7184cbc5082dfa56798ed9fb/110_0_1332_1066/master/1332.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Tsomo Dasel, 40, is the owner of Himalayan Yak. Tucked on Roosevelt Avenue in Jackson Heights, Queens, it was New York’s first Nepali restaurant and is now a staple in the community. On Friday afternoon, she expressed her growing frustration with the US government’s response to the climate crisis. “The world needs to pay attention,” she said.
Back home in Nepal, her husband’s family is safe – but it’s not just her loved ones that she’s worried about. Dasel said the priority in the aftermath should be to exhaust all available resources to find the missing. Each passing moment is crucial to the search, which she fears won’t match the enormity of the disaster.
She voiced her distaste with the Trump administration’s humanitarian response, after the state department pledged an initial $500,000 in emergency aid for Nepal – an amount she called an “insult” to address a catastrophe with a death toll that’s in the hundreds, and still rising. “It’s a joke – if you don’t want to do anything, then don’t do it.”
Dasel is particularly concerned about a media landscape that often overlooks Tibet. “[Tibet] is a climate issue – what kind of world will we leave behind if our president doesn’t believe in climate change?” she asked.
While local non-profits addressing the disaster have advised direct donation, Dasel is ready to help in any way that’s needed. Since she arrived in the US in 2002, she’s been a champion of her community. However, it’s been difficult for her to help delegate support, with power outages slashing lines of communication in Nepal and Tibet.
“We don’t know how we can help them … so we’re sitting down together, like, OK, what are the resources? … Maybe their emergency needs … anything that, you know, they may not have, and we can provide them.”
When the time comes, she’ll be ready: “Whatever the team needs.”
summary: Following a catastrophic Himalayan glacier collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border that left hundreds dead and thousands missing, Nepali and Tibetan communities in New York City are experiencing intense grief, fear, and frustration. Diaspora members are scrambling to contact relatives, share updates, and coordinate aid despite disrupted communications. The disaster has heightened local concerns about climate change injustices and the adequacy of international and US humanitarian responses.
key_points: A Himalayan glacier collapse in Rasuwa swept away villages, resulting in over 600 confirmed deaths and nearly 3,000 missing people.
Nepali and Tibetan residents in Jackson Heights, Queens, faced intense anxiety as they tried to reach relatives and share news of the disaster.
Community members expressed deep frustration over the warming planet's impacts on regions that contributed little to global emissions, alongside criticism of limited US humanitarian aid.
Younger Nepali Americans in New York have responded to the crisis by following updates, organizing support, and collecting donations for victims.
Disaster response efforts have been complicated by power outages and cut off communication lines in Nepal and Tibet.

title: Norway mourns King Harald as new era begins under Haakon VIII
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![TOPSHOT - Flowers and candles have been placed in tribute to late King Harald V of Norway at the Palace Square in Oslo on August 28, 2026.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/afp_6a92946e2522-1787991150.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Norwegians are saying goodbye to King Harald at the Royal Palace in Oslo where he lies in state, with many well-wishers remembering a unifying leader who was on the throne for 35 years.
A national period of mourning was declared in the Nordic kingdom following the death of Europe’s oldest monarch on Friday, aged 89. Thousands have gathered in the capital since then to pay their respects and lay flowers. He was known in Norway as a reformer and the embodiment of a tolerant and open nation who embraced inclusivity.
