“He has meant a great deal and has been a unifying king,” Line Stousland, 49, told AFP news agency. “He has been a king of the people, like a grandfather to the whole nation”.
King Harald died in Oslo University Hospital where he had been since August 17. He was suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells that leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
A date for the funeral has not yet been set.
Flags are flying at half-mast throughout Norway with portraits of him in gala uniform spotted everywhere, from bus stops to offices, shops and public buildings.
As Norwegians mourned, the transition to a new reign began immediately. Harald’s 53-year-old son, who will be known as King Haakon VIII, became Norway’s new monarch the moment his father passed away. He is due to take the oath in front of parliament on Tuesday, when he will swear to defend Norway’s constitution and laws.
Haakon takes over a monarchy hailed for its modernity and modesty, but which has been beset by a series of recent scandals. Earlier this year, two high-profile Norwegian politicians and the crown princess were linked to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
A police investigation was opened into former Prime Minister Thorbjorn Jagland on suspicion of corruption, while the princess’ 29-year-old son, Marius Borg Hoiby, the new king’s stepson, was sentenced in June to four years in prison on two counts of rape and 32 other charges, including domestic violence.
“An era has ended. A new one begins. The king is dead. Long live the king,” Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said in a speech shortly after meeting the new monarch. “We will remember King Harald for his love for his people, for his humour and warmth and for his unwavering faith in us.”
summary: Norwegians are mourning the death of King Harald V, who has lain in state at the Royal Palace in Oslo after passing away at age 89. Thousands have gathered to honor the reformer and unifying monarch, who ruled for 35 years and was known for promoting inclusivity. His 53-year-old son immediately succeeded him as King Haakon VIII and is scheduled to take his constitutional oath before parliament.
key_points: King Harald V died at age 89 following treatment for haemolytic anaemia at Oslo University Hospital.
A national period of mourning was declared, with citizens leaving flowers and tributes at the Royal Palace.
King Haakon VIII succeeded his father immediately upon his death and will take his oath on Tuesday.
The new king assumes the throne amidst recent scandals involving family members and political figures.

title: China censors footage of Tibet floods
author: Jörg Luyken; Samaan Lateef
content:
![Army personnel rescue survivors from a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa, Nepal](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499903159_17880051735300_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqQDfO_Li8BnuRdRCVfSGXucZep65cP_bgWtqbEQ5fF5Q.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Army personnel rescue survivors from a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa, Nepal](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499903159_17880051735300_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqQDfO_Li8BnuRdRCVfSGXucZep65cP_bgWtqbEQ5fF5Q.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
China has censored footage of the floods in Nepal and Tibet.
Beijing authorities removed footage of the moment people fled before a wall of mud swept through the Gyirong border crossing.
Only a still from the footage appeared in Chinese state media coverage.
The Chinese public has been largely reliant on state media for information, with official reports focusing on rescue efforts while providing little detail about the extent of the destruction.
On Saturday, state media said 554 people were missing on the Chinese side of the border and seven had been confirmed dead.
![China's state news agency said dangerous conditions were hampering relief efforts](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499898301_17880049199300_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
In Nepal, more than 620 people have been confirmed dead and thousands more remain missing.
Nepalese authorities have published lists of the missing, including foreign nationals.
Foreign journalists face severe restrictions on travelling to Tibet or interviewing people in the region by telephone, making it difficult to assess independently the devastation on the Chinese side.
Rajendra Bajgain, a former member of the Nepalese parliament, accused Beijing of a lack of transparency and questioned “what they are trying to hide” within its region.
“China should open the border to allow Nepalese rescuers to search for our missing people and to investigate what happened and monitor the glaciers,” Mr Bajgain told The Telegraph.
![A Nepalese army soldier carries a newborn baby rescued from an area cut off by the flooding](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499910357_17880052682352_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Mr Bajgain added: “Instead, China is preventing our people from crossing into its territory, even as families are still waiting for their loved ones to be found.
“Now we are being told that China is deleting footage of flooding. It raises very serious questions about what they are trying to hide. Removing evidence does not help establish the truth; it prevents people from asking legitimate questions.
“First we were told the disaster was caused by an earthquake. That explanation has now been discarded. By deleting footage, China is making it harder to establish what really happened.”
![Workers use excavators to clear mud in Nepal's Nuwakot district](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/29/TELEMMGLPICT000499906674_17880044923000_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Chinese state media footage released on Saturday showed more than 50 rescue workers combing through rubble in the disaster zone looking for signs of life.
The first rescue team to reach the Gyirong border crossing complex on Friday afternoon found little more than ruins, according to state media.
Xinhua, China’s state news agency, said dangerous conditions at the main disaster zone, compounded by severed roads and communications, continued to hamper relief efforts.
In Nepal, army rescue teams attempted to reach about 100 people trapped inside a hydropower tunnel, using drilling equipment to clear the entrance.
“The government has been continuing efforts... to rescue people trapped inside the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project in Rasuwa,” the office of Nepal’s prime minister said in a statement.
“Work to clear the tunnel entrance has been intensified since early Saturday morning,” it added.
Neighbouring India has sent a specialist tunnel rescue team, including so-called “rat-hole” miners, to assist with the operation.
The miners are trained to crawl through narrow spaces and have experience carrying out rescues in difficult Himalayan tunnel systems.
Wednesday’s catastrophic flooding has affected as many as 93,000 people in Nepal, the Red Cross said.
Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless or sheltering in temporary facilities.
“Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach,” the Red Cross said.
summary: Chinese authorities have censored video footage of recent catastrophic floods at the Tibet-Nepal border, replacing moving images with stills and limiting public information to official rescue reports. The disaster has left hundreds dead and thousands missing across both regions, with severe infrastructure damage hampering rescue efforts. Former Nepalese lawmaker Rajendra Bajgain criticized Beijing's lack of transparency and accused officials of hiding information by deleting evidence.
key_points: Beijing removed video footage of people fleeing mud at the Gyirong border crossing, using only stills in state media coverage.
On the Chinese side of the border, state media reported 554 missing and seven confirmed dead, while Nepal confirmed over 620 deaths.
Foreign journalists face severe travel and interview restrictions in Tibet, preventing independent damage assessments.
Former Nepalese parliament member Rajendra Bajgain criticized China for blocking Nepalese rescuers and deleting footage.
India sent a specialist tunnel rescue team to Nepal to help rescue people trapped inside a hydropower tunnel.

title: Nepal-Tibet floods: rescuers work through night at hydropower tunnel as number of missing climbs to almost 3,000 – latest updates
author: Wendy Frew; Taz Ali
content:
Nepal-Tibet floods: rescuers work through night at hydropower tunnel as number of missing climbs to almost 3,000 – latest updates
Nepali army digs through thick mud that has filled tunnel at plant in Rasuwa, as death toll from flash floods rises to 626 with seven confirmed dead in Tibet
Search and rescue efforts intensify to locate people trapped inside mud-filled tunnel
The Nepalese government said the army is digging through the thick mud that has filled a hydropower tunnel where people are believed to be trapped inside.
“The work to open the tunnel’s entrance has been intensified since early on Saturday morning,” the Nepalese prime minister’s office said in a post on Facebook.
A team of 82 personnel from the Nepalese army and police “has been continuously working since last night to excavate the tunnel entrance and accelerate the search operation”, it added.
“The rescue efforts, however, have been made extremely challenging by the persistently adverse weather in the area.”
A handout photo made available by the Nepal army shows personnel rescuing survivors from a hydropower tunnel following flash floods in Rasuwa district, Nepal. Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPA
A rescuer pulls a survivor through the thick mud to safety. Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPA
It was not immediately clear how many people remain trapped inside the tunnel. The Nepalese government said two people were pulled from the mud yesterday, with footage of the dramatic rescue operation shared on social media. You can watch that here:
Survivors pulled from mud in Nepal after deadly flash floods – video
This is an interesting piece in the Conversation by Dibyesh Anand, professor of international relations and deputy vice-chancellor at the University of Westminster, about how China’s control over Tibet can make it harder for Nepal and other countries downstream to prepare for sudden Himalayan disasters, such as glacial lake outburst floods.
This screengrab from footage released by the Tibet military command shows an aerial view of the mudslide-affected area near Gyirong border port in Tibet. Photograph: Tibet Military Command/AFP/Getty Images
Tibet is governed by China, which took control of the previously self-governing region by force in the early 1950s. Nepal shares a long, mountainous border with Tibet, and the two regions are closely connected by their geography, rivers and trade, making events on the Tibetan plateau particularly significant for communities downstream in Nepal.
Anand writes:
Despite warm relations with Beijing, and the Nepalese government’s assurances that it follows the “One China” principle and permits no support for Tibetans, China’s tight control over Tibet creates complications.
The region is administered as a militarised frontier. Access runs on permits and clearances, the area is closely watched by armed police and the military and outsiders – foreign journalists, independent researchers, at times even diplomats – are routinely kept out. Tibet is an information black hole.
Beijing’s anxiety extends across the border as Nepal is home to more than 10,000 Tibetan refugees and has long been the main escape route out of Tibet. China pressurises Nepal to police Tibetan activism, seal crossings and fold border management into a security partnership meant to insulate the plateau from the outside world.
The glacial and hydrological data from the Tibetan plateau, the information often needed to anticipate flooding, is also treated as strategically sensitive by China and is closely held. Nepal has no mechanism to receive real-time glacial lake and river data from the Chinese side and its officials have sometimes gone further, accusing Beijing of withholding it.
When a disaster in the Nepal-Tibet border region demands that rescuers cross quickly or that a warning travel downstream from an upstream lake, it runs into a system built for control rather than speed.
The Guardian’s senior China correspondent Amy Hawkinsalso writes about how China’s tight control over information and restrictions on journalists in Tibet have made it difficult to independently assess the full extent of the flooding and damage on the Chinese side of the border. You can read her report here:
Search and rescue efforts intensify to locate people trapped inside mud-filled tunnel
The Nepalese government said the army is digging through the thick mud that has filled a hydropower tunnel where people are believed to be trapped inside.
“The work to open the tunnel’s entrance has been intensified since early on Saturday morning,” the Nepalese prime minister’s office said in a post on Facebook.
A team of 82 personnel from the Nepalese army and police “has been continuously working since last night to excavate the tunnel entrance and accelerate the search operation”, it added.
“The rescue efforts, however, have been made extremely challenging by the persistently adverse weather in the area.”
A handout photo made available by the Nepal army shows personnel rescuing survivors from a hydropower tunnel following flash floods in Rasuwa district, Nepal. Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPA
A rescuer pulls a survivor through the thick mud to safety. Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPA
It was not immediately clear how many people remain trapped inside the tunnel. The Nepalese government said two people were pulled from the mud yesterday, with footage of the dramatic rescue operation shared on social media. You can watch that here:
Survivors pulled from mud in Nepal after deadly flash floods – video
India said it is increasing surveillance of glaciers and glacial lakes in its Himalayan regions bordering Nepal and China.
The deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border were believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse that was detected as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event by geologists. You can read this explainer to find out more about how a collapsing glacier can generate a powerful flood, and whether the climate crisis is contributing to the risk.
Distant view of the snow capped Indian Himalayas in the Binsar region of Uttarakhand. Photograph: Steve Taylor ARPS/Alamy
Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India’s Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, said: “Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbour, and also have a similar geographic situation … we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region.”
Uttarakhand is one of the most ecologically sensitive regions of India, with 1,266 glacial lakes. As glaciers melt, water can accumulate in lakes held back by natural barriers. If those barriers fail, vast volumes of water can be released suddenly, triggering devastating floods.
“We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state,” Kaushik told AFP.
‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal
The Guardian’s south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen and journalist Gaurav Pokharel report from the Nepalese town of Bidur, where rescue efforts are being coordinated. They spoke to survivors mourning loved ones and confronting the loss of their homes and livelihoods after devastating floods swept through their communities.
Sangke Dolma Tamang (in red), 61, watched flood waters tear away her husband, her home and almost everything she held dear. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian
Among those caught in the floods was Sangke Dolma Tamang, who described the moment she watched her husband being swept away and returned to find her home and village destroyed:
Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.
“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.
“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”
Nepal’s government has appealed for financial help as it faces the daunting task of recovering from the devastating flash floods and braces for the possibility of more flooding.
Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless or sheltering in temporary facilities.
“Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach,” the Red Cross says.
At least 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged, leaving about 10,000 school-age children affected, according to the UN Children’s Fund.
The disaster comes just ahead of the anniversary of last year’s 8-9 September mass anti-corruption protests that toppled the government.
Nepal is now led by prime minister Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper turned politician widely known as “Balen”. The former Kathmandu mayor swept March elections on a wave of euphoria calling for political change.
Machines clear a road at the mudslide-hit area in Gyirong County, in southwest China’s Xizang Autonomous Region. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock
Members of the Nepali Army load relief material into a helicopter to be transported to areas affected by flash floods. Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters
Residents watch as an excavator helps people to collect some of their belongings from their house in the aftermath of flash floods at Trishuli, in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images
The risk of a lake formed after the glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border where the devastating flood occurred earlier this week has decreased, Chinese authorities said today, as its size appears to have shrunk.
Satellite images from Thursday this morning suggest water in the lake – straddling the China-Nepal border at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the water resources ministry.
The ministry said satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake at Purepu Tsangpo river showed it was 99,000 sq metres in size this morning – around the size of 14 football fields combined – having shrunk by 21,000 sq metres compared with images from Thursday.
An aerial drone photo shows a view around a barrier lake formed after a mudslide upstream of the Gyirong Port in Tibet. Photograph: Jigme Dorje/Xinhua/AP
Experts and authorities have warned of the extremely high risk of secondary disasters in the valley, especially from the lake that was formed by glacier debris, potentially endangering rescue operations downstream.
State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng, which has been monitoring the lake since Thursday, dispatched a 15-member team on Friday with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to gather more data about the lake.
An overflow from the lake on Friday temporarily halted rescue work before further assessment deemed the risks manageable.
Thank you for joining us for our continuing coverage of the aftermath of Wednesday’s catastrophic flash floods in the Himalayan mountains near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Poor weather has hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal as the search for thousands of people missing enters its fourth day.
Nepal’s finance minister says his country will need up to $5bn to rebuild after the floods, believed to have been caused by a melting glacier high up in the mountains that set off a deadly cascade of water into the valleys below.
Finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters today those figures are “just an estimate” and that “loss and damage is being assessed”.
Here’s a summary of what we know so far:
Nearly 3,000 people are missing. Nepal’s disaster agency on Saturday said 2,426 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554.
The death toll in Nepal has now risen to 626, while China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.
At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.
summary: Rescue teams in Nepal are working through adverse weather to dig through thick mud filling a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa, where people are believed trapped following catastrophic flash floods. The death toll has risen as the number of missing climbs toward 3,000, leaving communities destroyed and infrastructure severely damaged. China's strict control over information and hydrological data in Tibet has complicated downstream disaster response and rescue coordination. Meanwhile, Indian authorities are increasing surveillance of glacial lakes in neighboring Himalayan regions, and Nepal estimates it will need up to $5 billion to rebuild.
key_points: Nepalese army and police personnel are excavating a mud-filled hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa to search for trapped survivors.
The deadly flash floods were believed to be triggered by a glacier collapse detected as a seismic event.
China's tight control over the Tibet region and restriction of real-time hydrological data complicates disaster preparedness and response for downstream Nepal.
Nepal's finance minister estimates the country will need up to $5 billion to recover and rebuild from the disaster.
India is increasing surveillance of glaciers and glacial lakes in its Himalayan regions bordering Nepal and China following the floods.

title: Tibet-Nepal floods: Shocking footage isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
author: Laura Bicker
content:
Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border
- Published
The dramatic footage was almost impossible to miss. A torrent of water tearing through Gyirong Port, one of the main border crossings between Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away all in its path as hundreds of people fled for their lives.
The scenes, captured by CCTV cameras, quickly spread on social media and onto screens around the world.
Except here, in China.
Only a single still-frame shot has been broadcast so far by the country's state-run flagship news bulletin.
It has also been difficult to find the video on China's heavily censored internet. It is just as hard to even find posts describing the flash flooding that has claimed hundreds of lives, with just as many still unaccounted for since Wednesday.
Beijing has launched a massive rescue operation involving hundreds of emergency workers, which is continuing, and President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting with officials to co-ordinate efforts.
But when you compare the country's internet content to what much of the world has been seeing online these past few days, China's firewall becomes more visible than ever.
Tibet, which Beijing annexed in the 1950s, had long resisted rule by the Chinese Communist Party.
China has quashed protests over the years, sometimes violently, and has been accused of grave rights violations in the Buddhist region. It has labelled the exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, a separatist.
That history means the very name Tibet draws China's censors. Beijing's sensitivities are especially apparent at times likes this.
There have been daily updates on the missing and the dead, and Beijing has also been posting updates on the rescue operations, as well as the dangers posed by a barrier lake that has been at risk of overflowing.
But there is little detail beyond that. There are no accounts from survivors in Tibet, and almost no user-generated footage showing the deadly moments or their aftermath.
We are yet to hear from anxious families of those missing. Trying to contact people there is near-impossible during regular times.
As a journalist who has covered North Korea, it has often been easier for me to contact interviewees in Pyongyang than it is in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa.
![CCTV shows people running as mud and water destroys buildings in Gyirong, Tibet](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/8d37/live/67a7cd10-a2fa-11f1-8d5b-155abe464768.jpg)
On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".
Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled.
Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.
Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.
This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.
China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.
The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.
The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it.
It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.
Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.
![Rescue workers operating in Shigatse in Tibet after devastating flooding and landslides](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/0ef3/live/ef865270-a2f9-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.
A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents.
The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".
It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.
That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.
The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".
To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.
There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.
They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long.
Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.
Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.
  - Published2 July 2025
 ![A monk walks across a courtyard at Langcuo Ma Monastery](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/0d8b/live/0ba12f20-57e7-11f0-960d-e9f1088a89fe.jpg)
- ![A composite image showing map and a screengrab from a verified video that has emerged from Nepal following floods. The picture on the left shows a map of the Trishuli river, the picture on the right shows people fleeing from the flood water](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/dbe8/live/ecb52260-a23b-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png)
  - Published16 hours ago
 ![Subhrasree Chakraborty](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/01ad/live/9696afa0-a2c9-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
summary: Flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border have claimed hundreds of lives and left many unaccounted for, triggering a massive rescue operation by Beijing. However, dramatic user-generated footage of the disaster has been heavily censored and largely kept off the internet within China. The strict information control is driven by Beijing's desire to maintain social stability and prevent potential discontent in the politically sensitive Tibetan region.
key_points: A severe flash flood at Gyirong Port on the Nepal-Tibet border has caused hundreds of deaths and left many missing.
Chinese state media and internet platforms have heavily suppressed user-generated footage and survivor accounts of the disaster.
President Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang coordinated emergency responses and rescue operations, prioritizing social stability and control.
Contacting people in Tibet remains nearly impossible due to intense censorship, strict surveillance, and restricted access for foreign journalists.

title: King Harald V of Norway obituary
author: Stephen Bates
content:
King Harald V of Norway, who has died aged 89, Europe’s oldest serving monarch, was the country’s third king since it regained independence in 1905 following the dissolution of its union with Sweden. Although he ceased to be head of the Lutheran state church in 2012 and subsequently lost his constitutional status as “holy” six years later, he did exhibit the Scandinavian moderation, stoicism and genial approachability that led a newspaper to name him Norway’s person of the year in 2017.
The first Norwegian king to be born in the country since 1370, Harald was also related to both the Swedish and the British royal families. His parents were Crown Prince Olav, who was king as Olav V between 1957 and 1991, and his wife, Princess Märtha, a member of the Swedish royal dynasty. His grandparents were King Haakon VII, the first king of the independent country, who reigned for 52 years from 1905, and his wife, Queen Maud, daughter of Britain’s Edward VII. The family roots are Danish – from the Glücksburg dynasty – as were those of the Duke of Edinburgh and the former Greek royal family. The mixed heritage made him sympathetic to refugees: “It is not easy to say where we come from. Home is where the heart is,” he said.
![King Harald V greets Queen Elizabeth II at the Royal Palace, Oslo, during a state visit, May 2001.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/7443e81d510321a6d36fa730f05d1c379774a79e/0_0_1388_1129/master/1388.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
He was Queen Elizabeth II’s second cousin and a knight of the garter. At the time of his birth, Harald was 16th in line to the British throne, though he had fallen in the rankings to around 80th in more recent years. Confusingly, he was not the fifth Harald to rule his country, but the sixth – the 10th-century Harald Bluetooth generally not being assigned a number in the list of Norwegian kings. The king never attracted a picturesque title as did some of his Viking predecessors – such as Bluetooth, Harald Fairhair and Harald Hardrada, who tried to seize the English throne a few weeks before the Norman invasion in 1066 and was killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge.
Harald himself was only three at the time of the Nazi invasion of Norway in 1940, and he and his mother and two older sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, initially fled to Sweden, which, trying to maintain its neutrality while accommodating the Germans’ attack on their neighbour, was reluctant to let them in. It is alleged that the royal party was initially turned back at the border, and allowed to proceed only when the driver of their car threatened to ram it through the border post. Within three months, Harald, his sisters and mother had escaped to the US. They spent the war years in Washington DC and Harald thereafter spoke English with a slight American accent.
Meanwhile, Harald’s grandfather and father escaped to England, where they led a government in exile. Famously Haakon, turning up at the BBC to make a broadcast to his people, was asked by a receptionist: “Where did you say you were king of, dear?”
Following the liberation of Norway at the end of the war, the family was reunited and Harald was enrolled first at a state primary and then at Oslo cathedral school. From there he studied at Oslo University and the Norwegian military academy, before following in his father’s footsteps to read history, economics and politics at Balliol College, Oxford, where he also rowed for the college. A keen competitive yachtsman, he and his crews represented Norway at successive Olympics in Tokyo in 1964, Mexico City in 1968 and Munich in 1972, and won world championship medals through the 1980s and a European championship gold medal in 2005.
If this was a conventional career, much less so was his determination to marry a commoner, Sonja Haraldsen, a shop assistant who was the daughter of an Oslo textile manufacturer, whom he had met at a sailing party in 1959. The friendship was kept secret for several years, partly because of Olav’s reluctance to have the heir to the throne marry someone who was not royal. In the end, Harald forced the issue by declaring to his father that if he was not allowed to marry her he would not marry anyone, thus bringing an end to the dynasty. The couple married in 1968.
![King Harald V aboard the Fram XI vessel, as part of the One Ton Cup international sailing contest, Copenhagen, July 1992.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/12fc1b8deee2de1838e06ed38dbc7b614ca2aaae/0_0_4747_3313/master/4747.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Harald was sworn in as king automatically following Olav’s death in January 1991. Although lacking his father’s easy bonhomie, the king attempted successfully – and popularly – to open up the institution and its palace and estates more freely to the public. The Norwegian monarch’s duties are similar to those in Britain, with non-exercised executive power, and all official acts having to be endorsed by the governing council of state, equivalent to a British cabinet. The Norwegian parliament constitutionally debates whether to continue the monarchy every four years, and earlier this year, despite controversies concerning the royal family, voted in favour of its continuation by 141 to 26.
The greatest crisis in the country’s modern history occurred on 22 July 2011 when the domestic terrorist Anders Behring Breivik murdered 77 people, mainly at a young socialists’ holiday camp on Utøya island. The king attracted public praise in the wake of the tragedy, when he met bereaved relatives and called for national solidarity and mutual support. He was seen to weep at the memorial service for the victims.
Harald was treated for bladder cancer in 2003, contracted Covid, had a pacemaker fitted in 2024 and was being treated for the blood disorder haemolytic anaemia.
He is survived by Sonja and their children, Princess Märtha Louise and Prince Haakon, whose wife, Mette-Marit (nee Tjessem-Høiby), was obliged to apologise in February this year for email exchanges with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in which her name was mentioned nearly 1,000 times. The king said that she had not broken any law. Mette-Marit’s son by a previous relationship, Marius, was jailed for four years in June following convictions for two rapes and drug offences.
Haakon succeeds Harald as King Haakon VIII and will adopt the monarchy’s traditional motto: “All for Norway”.
summary: King Harald V of Norway, Europe's oldest serving monarch, has died at the age of 89. Known for his Scandinavian moderation and approachability, he succeeded his father in 1991 and successfully modernized the monarchy. He famously married a commoner, Sonja Haraldsen, after nine years of secret dating, and navigated the nation through major challenges including the 2011 terrorist attacks. He is succeeded by his son, Prince Haakon.
key_points: King Harald V died at age 89 as Europe's oldest serving monarch.
He was the first Norwegian king to be born in the country since 1370 and had extensive royal relations across Europe.
He married commoner Sonja Haraldsen in 1968 after declaring he would not marry anyone else.
He was an accomplished competitive yachtsman, representing Norway at multiple Olympic Games.
He is succeeded by his son, who takes the throne as King Haakon VIII.

title: Nepal-Tibet flash flood: helicopter rescue operations suspended as lake overflows; death toll rises to 469
author: Mabel Banfield-Nwachi; Adam Fulton
content:
A flood-affected area in Nuwakot, Nepal, after outburst of a glacial lake in Tibet. Follow live for latest updates. Photograph: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/Shutterstock
A flood-affected area in Nuwakot, Nepal, after outburst of a glacial lake in Tibet. Follow live for latest updates. Photograph: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/Shutterstock
Helicopter rescue operations halted in Nepal as lake dam breaks in Rasuwa district
Authorities in Nepal have stopped rescue operations for the next 90 minutes, an army officer said on Friday, after reports that a dammed lake in the flood-hit region began to overflow.
Helicopter rescue operations in the flood hit Rasuwa district were stopped and locals were seen rushing up the hill, according to a Reuters witness.
Nepal does not need foreign assistance for search-and-rescue operations following the devastating flash flood, its foreign ministry said on Friday, despite offers of help from several countries with nationals missing in the disaster.
Nepal’s foreign ministry said that it was managing the rescue efforts. “The offer for help is natural. Our security agencies are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, spokesperson for the foreign ministry, said without providing further details.
South Korea’s foreign ministry said Nepal had indicated it was not yet planning to accept foreign rescue teams.
A South Korean rapid response team is already in Kathmandu but has not been deployed, it added.
It said:
South Korea will keep negotiating with Nepal over the matter.
Seoul has pledged $1 million in humanitarian assistance through international organisations, its foreign minister said on X. Nine South Koreans working in a hydropower plant were missing and 10 were stranded, South Korea’s foreign ministry said on Wednesday.
Helicopter rescue operations halted in Nepal as lake dam breaks in Rasuwa district
Authorities in Nepal have stopped rescue operations for the next 90 minutes, an army officer said on Friday, after reports that a dammed lake in the flood-hit region began to overflow.
Helicopter rescue operations in the flood hit Rasuwa district were stopped and locals were seen rushing up the hill, according to a Reuters witness.
In case you’re just joining us, here’s a snapshot of the latest in the Nepal-Tibet calamity.
Chinese authorities warned that an artificial lake formed after a catastrophic flash flood hit the China-Nepal border on Wednesday faces a “high risk of breaching and sending flood waters downstream”, state media reported.
Nepal also warned of new flooding risks, with the country’s disaster authority saying water levels were rising in a lake formed by debris clogging a flooded site and that it was at risk of bursting its banks.
Rescue teams and military helicopters continue their search for hundreds of missing people along the mountainous border. Wednesday’s flash flooding after a glacial collapse killed at least 469 people and has left more than 1,500 missing.
Efforts to locate those unaccounted for have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 40km (25 miles) of roads. The missing include hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada.
The Red Cross said about 93,000 people might have been affected and launched an emergency appeal for $31m for disaster relief.
People rescued from an area cut off by flash flooding line up to register at an army camp in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Friday. Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP
China paused a rescue operation at the epicentre of the Tibet disaster due to the high risk of renewed flooding in Tibet. State broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by immense piles of debris had begun overflowing towards the area that rescue teams were headed.
Nepali army helicopter rescue teams are working to rescue about 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project swamped by Wednesday’s flash flood, an army spokesperson said.
UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said he ordered the release of $2m from the UN’s central emergency response fund to help with medical care, shelter and water.
Rescuers found bodies in Nepal’s Chitwan district, hundreds of kilometres downstream from the hardest-hit areas.
The overall death toll in Nepal has risen to 469 people, with more than 1,500 missing, and China has paused rescue work at the epicentre of the Tibet flooding amid fears that an artificial lake formed at the site was at risk of bursting.
The scale of the destruction from the flooding in Nepal’s northern border region was becoming clearer on Friday, with roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure destroyed and survivors describing scenes of extraordinary devastation.
Amid the rescue attempt unfolding at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
“There were at least 400 workers at the site,” Dev Shrestha, who was airlifted from the site where he was working, said after his rescue.
More people died than were rescued.
Worker Buddha Tamang said he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck – but he had managed to get out and reach help, Agence France-Presse reports.
“I survived as I was in the tunnel,” said Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours.
The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away.
Another worker, Arjun Kumar Tamang, spoke of “massive damage” at the hydropower site where he had been.
I don’t know how many people died but the force of the water swept everything away.
More now on the Nepali army’s rescue operation to save about 100 people trapped in a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by Wednesday’s flooding.
“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.
Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.
The prime minister’s office said the army had been working in tough conditions.
“A Nepali army team has successfully rescued 350 workers and locals who were trapped in the tunnel a while ago facing extremely risky and challenging conditions amid adverse weather and rapid floodwaters,” the statement read.
The army is still working to safely evacuate more than 100 people trapped in the same tunnel.
Here are some of the latest images coming in amid the Nepal-Tibet border devastation as rescuers continue to search for more than 1,300 people missing, including hundreds of tourists and pilgrims.
A resident awaits news of missing relatives at a military camp in Trishuli, Nepal. Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images
Nepali army members prepare to leave on rescue missions in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Friday. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images
People move through a mud-covered road in Trishuli in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters
Flash flood survivors receive medical treatment at an army base in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA
A man looks at pictures of missing people at the Trauma Centre in Kathmandu, Nepal. Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters
Firefighters assemble near a drone during rescue operations after the mudslide in Gyirong county in Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region, China. Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters
People (left) speak with the police as they search for their missing relatives at Bir hospital in Kathmandu. Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images
School children board a helicopter on a transit flight back to their family at Trishuli camp after being stranded by the flash flooding in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images
China halts rescue at Tibet epicentre over flood risk – state media
China has paused a rescue operation due to the high risk of renewed flooding in Tibet, where hundreds remain missing after the deadly mudslide in the border region.
State broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by immense piles of debris had begun overflowing towards the area that rescue teams were headed.
“So all rescue teams have been ordered to stand by in place and wait for further instructions,” it said on Friday, cited by AFP.
CCTV added that emergency teams which had earlier accessed the area “have been ordered to withdraw one kilometre”.
Rescue workers carrying relief supplies in Gyirong county in Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region, China, on Thursday. Photograph: China Daily/Reuters
Nepal army trying to rescue 100 trapped in hydropower tunnel
Nepali army helicopter rescue teams are working to rescue about 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by Wednesday’s flash flood.
“Our focus is in search and rescue of people ... some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Agence France-Presse.
The prime minister’s office said in a statement on Friday that 350 people had been rescued from the area but 100 more were trapped.
Nino Bucci and Henry Belot report that the mother’s sister Vaishnavi said she had lost contact with the family shortly after breakfast on the morning of the flood.
They planned to head towards an immigration checkpoint on the Tibet-Nepal border soon after, as part of the group of 15 Australians trekking as part of a tour.
Vaishnavi told the Guardian:
Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful. Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued.
It’s a very difficult time for our whole family … I just want to make people aware that they’re there, and we’re waiting, and we just want them to return.
The 39 Australians missing in Nepal include Sydney family (from left) Shylaja, Aarush, Ashwin and Chandrasekaran Muralitharan; and couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan (bottom right) and Chitra Venkatraman (top right). Composite: Provided by the families
Nepal police have said that the death toll from Wednesday’s flash flood now stands at 469.
It’s a jump of 80 since the last reported update, and comes as search teams continue recovery efforts across the disaster-struck area. More than 1,300 remain missing, including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada.
Efforts to locate those unaccounted for have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 40km (25 miles) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.
Summary: river at risk of flooding again amid race to find survivors
Chinese authorities have warned that an artificial lake formed after a catastrophic flash flood hit the China-Nepal border on Wednesday faces a “high risk of breaching and sending flood waters downstream”, according to state media.
“According to forecasts, inflows into the lake could reach about 3 million cubic meters over the next three days amid continued rainfall, increasing the risk of a breach that could send flood waters downstream and potentially cause further damage in areas including Gyirong Port and elsewhere downstream”, state news agency Xinhua reported late on Thursday.
Nepal has also warned of new flooding risks, with the country’s disaster authority saying water levels were rising in a lake formed by debris clogging a flooded site and that it was at risk of bursting its banks. It did not name the specific site.
It comes as rescue teams and military helicopters continue their search for hundreds of missing people along the mountainous border, with the Red Cross saying about 93,000 people might have been affected. The aid agency launched an emergency appeal for $31m to respond to the disaster.
People walking in a flood-hit area in Nuwakot, Nepal, on Thursday. Photograph: Sulav Shrestha/Xinhua/AP
Also today:
Rescue teams and military helicopters are searching for hundreds of missing people along the mountainous Nepal-Tibet border after the huge torrent of water and mud swept through communities following a glacier collapse on Wednesday.
More than 390 people were killed, authorities in Nepal and China said, and more than 1,400 were missing, including hundreds of foreign citizens and pilgrims.
More than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 39 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.
Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.
UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said he ordered the release of $2m from the UN’s central emergency response fund to help with medical care, shelter and water.
US president Donald Trump said the flooding was terrible to see, describing how “strong, well-built buildings were wiped out like they were toothpicks”.
Nepaleseofficials said dozens of bridges were destroyed and nearly 40km of roads damaged, complicating search efforts.
The Nepalese army had rescued more than 100 people by helicopter, an army spokesperson said. Army teams also evacuated people trapped inside facilities linked to the Trishuli hydropower project, he said. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for medical care.
Rescuers found bodies in Nepal’s Chitwan district, hundreds of kilometres downstream from the hardest-hit areas.
The Nepal Red Cross Society said the agency has shifted its focus from rescue to large-scale relief operations in the flood-hit districts.
China’s premier, Li Qiang, arrived in Gyirong on Thursday to direct rescue efforts, alongside 500 military and paramilitary personnel.
This aerial image released on the Chinese social media platform Weibo shows a barrier lake which formed after a landslide near where Nepal's Chhochen Khola River flows into the Purepu Tsangpo River, in Gyirong county, in China's Tibet region.
Photograph: Lhasa Mobile Fire and Rescue Detachment/AFP/Getty Images
summary: The death toll from a catastrophic flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border has risen to 469, with more than 1,300 to 1,500 people still missing. Helicopter rescue operations were temporarily halted as authorities in both Nepal and China warned that debris-clogged artificial lakes were overflowing and at high risk of bursting. Meanwhile, the Nepali army successfully rescued hundreds of trapped individuals, including workers at a hydropower project tunnel, while international aid and emergency funds poured in.
key_points: The death toll has reached at least 469 people, with over 1,300 to 1,500 people remaining missing, including numerous international tourists.
Helicopter rescue operations were temporarily suspended after reports that dammed lakes formed by debris in the flood-hit regions began overflowing.
China paused its rescue operations at the Tibet epicentre due to the high risk of renewed flooding from an overflowing artificial lake.
The Nepali army successfully rescued hundreds of people, including workers trapped inside a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project.

Nepal's foreign ministry stated that the country does not currently require foreign assistance for search-and-rescue operations, though international aid organizations and nations have pledged humanitarian funds.

title: France to relax cheese production rules after drought takes toll on grazing land
author: Angelique Chrisafis
content:
Strict production rules will be loosened for some of France’s most famous cheeses after drought and repeated heatwaves dried out grazing pastures, threatening the livelihoods of traditional dairy workers.
Comté, a hard cheese made from raw cows’ milk in the Jura mountains, is France’s top-selling traditional cheese, with more than 62,000 tonnes produced last year. The government announced on Wednesday that its producers would be granted a temporary change to strict rules on grazing after farmers said extreme heat had scorched their pastures, putting production at risk.
Makers of beaufort and abondance, two cheeses made from cows grazed in the Alps, were also granted temporary changes to production rules because of the impact of the drought on grazing land.
All three cheeses carry the coveted label “appellation d’origine protégée” (AOP, protected designation of origin) to ensure their authenticity and protect traditional farming methods. This means producers must follow rigid rules on where their animals graze and what they eat.
![Brown cows graze in a lush, green mountain field with peaks in the background.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6f7a52fe8780d9c221ccf08ae969e2be8e274641/0_0_4500_3000/master/4500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
But the drought, which affected 95% of mainland France in July, has left normally rich green pastures dry, yellow and bare. French authorities said makers of comté, beaufort and abondance could temporarily supplement the animals’ diet with more fodder and grain brought in from elsewhere.
The National Institute of Origin and Quality (INAO), the government agency that administers and enforces rules on traditional food production, told Agence France-Presse it was also planning to grant temporary relief for the producers of several other cheeses including reblochon, cantal, bleu d’Auvergne, and fourme d’Ambert. It said the drought was “historic”.
Droughts are becoming more common and more severe in some parts of the world, including Europe, the fastest-warming continent, due to human-caused climate breakdown.
![A woman holds out a half-moon of artisan cheese with a thick, slightly mouldy rind and soft, creamy-looking pale yellow centre.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/629cb2e7e737ef1a31fe0cd4a64198e270efc009/0_0_7353_4912/master/7353.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
France’s numerous cheeses are a source of national pride and a key part of identity and local economy in rural areas.
Hubert Genty, a dairy farmer who produces neufchâtel cheese in Richemont in Normandy, said: “There really is no grass left to eat, this grass is totally scorched and has no value.” He told the TF1 TV channel his cows were producing less milk, which in turn would affect cheese production.
His wife, Angélique, who makes the heart-shaped cheeses by hand in the farm’s dairy, said she usually made 600 to 700 cheeses a day at this time of year and was now down to making 400-450 because of the low milk yield. She said she would struggle to meet customers’ demands.
![Large circular slabs of cantal cheese sit on a surface in a darkened cellar.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e447284455961c7b01b69e3606556f8434d39c9e/0_0_7360_4912/master/7360.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Farmers in many traditional French cheesemaking areas have warned about the damage of the drought and heatwaves. About 70% of producers of salers cheese, which has a protected AOP label, had to pause production over the summer because of the drought, the local newspaper La Montagne reported. Makers of roquefort have also called for a temporary easing on their traditional rules on grazing sheep, after many pastures were left scorched.
The French agriculture ministry’s statistical service said growth on permanent grasslands measured on 10 August was one-third less than the 1989-2018 average. The fodder situation was “highly degraded” in almost all regions, the ministry said earlier this month.
The agriculture minister, Annie Genevard, is expected to hold crisis talks with local authorities next week before announcing emergency measures for farmers.
![A half-moon of roquefort, showing its blue veins in a creamy centre. Its packaging bears a red stamp with the AOP designation.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/90ae68ebddf622e138fb381488af92feccb9f09d/0_0_5568_3712/master/5568.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Photograph: Bertrand Guay/AFP/Getty Images
The vegetable sector has been particularly affected. The French union of potato farmers, the UNPT, warned this week of a slump, saying it expected a “23% drop in this year’s crop “after five successive heatwaves and an exceptional lack of water”.
In the northern Hauts-de-France, a key potato-producing region, farmers said potatoes were much smaller than usual, raising concerns among local factories that produce chips, crisps and processed mashed potato.
Cider makers have voiced concerns about this year’s apple yield, and for many wine producers the grape harvest has begun early, amid uncertainty over the quantity of wine that will be produced.
summary: Severe droughts and heatwaves in France have scorched grazing pastures, prompting the government to temporarily relax strict production rules for famous AOP cheeses like comté, beaufort, and abondance. The historic lack of water has reduced milk yields and forced some farmers to pause production or supplement animal feed with grain brought in from elsewhere. Authorities are planning further relief for other traditional cheeses as the agricultural sector faces widespread impacts on dairy, potatoes, cider, and wine.
key_points: Producers of comté, beaufort, and abondance have been granted temporary rule changes to supplement dairy cows' diets with imported fodder and grain.
Strict AOP regulations normally require animals to graze on specific local pastures and follow rigid feeding guidelines.
The INAO plans to offer temporary relief for other cheeses, including reblochon, cantal, bleu d’Auvergne, and fourme d’Ambert.
About 70% of salers cheese producers had to pause production over the summer due to the drought.
Other agricultural sectors, including potatoes, cider apples, and wine grapes, are also experiencing reduced yields and early harvests.

title: Nepal flash flood: more than 350 killed amid warning of fresh danger from rising lake water – latest updates
author: Adam Fulton; Mabel Banfield-Nwachi; Martin Belam; Yu-chen Li; Nino Bucci
content:
A drone view shows mud covering buildings and property following devastating floods at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, on Thursday Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters
A drone view shows mud covering buildings and property following devastating floods at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, on Thursday Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters
New risk as lake in flood area threatens to burst as 353 confirmed dead
A lake formed at the site where the flood in Nepal occurred is rising and is at risk of bursting, the country’s disaster authority said, as it appealed to residents and rescuers to stay away from the river banks.
The blockage of a river on Wednesday led to the lake’s formation, Reuters reports the authority said.
Meanwhile Abi Narayan Kafle, the central spokesperson for the Nepal Police, has told AP 353 people were now confirmed dead in the floods as of Thursday.
My wife and I are heartbroken to hear of the devastating flooding that has struck the Nepal-China border.
Many in the United Kingdom have strong, deep and personal ties to this part of the world.
We send our most profound sympathy to all those who have so tragically lost their loved ones and we feel deeply for the many families awaiting anxiously the news of friends and relations.
Our hearts go out also to the families of all the police and Armed Forces personnel who lost their lives while carrying out their courageous duty in the service of others and we give our deepest thanks to those who have responded so selflessly in undertaking rescue efforts.
Our special thoughts and prayers remain with all those affected and, as always, the United Kingdom stands ready to help support those in need.
Kabita Dhungana, deputy mayor of Nuwakot in Nepal, the district affected by the floods, said “please help us”, as she spoke to BBC Radio 4’s The World at One about the flash floods her region is experiencing.
She said:
Family members, children, parents are missing, and this is a very critical bad situation…
Everything, basic needs are destroyed, so please help us. We are really in need of help.
Srijana Gurung, Plan International Nepal acting country director, said the climate crisis means floods and landslides are “far more frequent and intense”, as she highlighted the need of urgent medical care and risk of waterborne diseases in the aftermath of the floods in Nepal.
The statement said:
Across Nepal, communities are facing climate shock after shock with barely any time to recover. Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense.
The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones, and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.
Children and their families who have lost their homes and livelihoods will be in urgent need of medical attention, shelter, water, food and hygiene kits. There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged.
Particular attention must be given to those most at risk, including girls, women, older people and people with disabilities, while ensuring their rights, safety, dignity and voices remain at the centre of the response.
New risk as lake in flood area threatens to burst as 353 confirmed dead
A lake formed at the site where the flood in Nepal occurred is rising and is at risk of bursting, the country’s disaster authority said, as it appealed to residents and rescuers to stay away from the river banks.
The blockage of a river on Wednesday led to the lake’s formation, Reuters reports the authority said.
Meanwhile Abi Narayan Kafle, the central spokesperson for the Nepal Police, has told AP 353 people were now confirmed dead in the floods as of Thursday.
Reuters has a quick snap that local media has reported that 332 bodies have now been recovered by authorities after the deadly flood in Nepal.
More than 900 people remain unaccounted for. In addition China’s state broadcaster has issued a figure of three confirmed deaths and more than 500 people missing in Tibet.
Rescue teams have found bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Indian border.
Vivian Balakrishnan, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Singapore, said Singapore stands in solidarity with Nepal and China and pledged emergency assistance.
Singapore stands in solidarity with Nepal and China during this difficult time. We are putting together a humanitarian assistance package to support relief efforts in Nepal. A Consular Response Team will be deployed to assist affected Singaporeans on the ground.
Here are some of the latest images from the news wires.
More than 160 people have died and hundreds remain missing across northern Nepal after a suspected avalanche triggered massive flash floods and mudslides along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river near the Nepal-Tibet border. Houses in the Devighat Village, Nuwakot district, were among those affected. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA
Community stands together for thoughts and prayers for those affected by the disaster in Nepal. Diggers rest, Melbourne. Photograph: Jesse Thompson/AAP
An aerial view shows houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality, along the confluence of the Trishuli and Tadi rivers in Nepal's Nuwakot district. Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty Images
The IFRC (International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies), the world’s largest humanitarian network, posted a clip on X showing the destruction caused by the flooding.
It said Red Cross teams are on the ground with food, safe drinking water, emergency shelter materials, first aid and other essential supplies, though roads are damaged and access is “extremely limited”.
It wrote:
Severe flash floods have devastated northern Nepal, destroying homes, washing away bridges and cutting off communities.
Nepal Red Cross teams are responding with food, safe drinking water, emergency shelter materials, first aid and other essential supplies, despite damaged roads and extremely limited access.
The IFRC has released CHF 997,000 from its Disaster Response Emergency Fund, including an immediate CHF 100,000 advance to support urgent response efforts.
As the full scale of the disaster becomes clearer, we stand ready to provide further support and international assistance if needed.
Britain has pledged £5m and offered to send emergency responders to Nepal following the “devastating” flash floods there, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said.
Speaking to journalists during a visit to South Wales, the prime minister said:
It’s a devastating picture that is emerging from what has happened in Nepal.
Scenes that we’ve never seen the like before, I don’t think, certainly the scale of the devastation.
So there is immediate action being taken. We are deploying consular support staff to the region so that British nationals will be able to access support 24/7. An offer has been made of emergency responders to head to the region but that’s obviously a matter for the Nepalese government.
But also we’ve offered £5m to help with that response effort.
Obviously, there are a number of British nationals who currently are thought to be missing and we’ll be providing all the support we can to their families in what is a very distressing and devastating situation.
Nepal police say 270 bodies found after Himalayan flood
A total of 270 bodies have been found by authorities in Nepal after a torrential flood swept through the Himalayan border areas of the country and China’s Tibet, Reuters reports, citing what Nepal’s police said in a post on X.
Climate change is leading to conditions that can destabilise high-mountain rock and ice, strengthening prospects for disasters such as this week’s Himalayan flood along the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet, scientists say.
While the exact cause of Wednesday’s disaster is still being analysed, scientists say it probably began with a massive ice-rock avalanche on the northern slopes of Nepal’s Langtang Lirung peak into the Lhende Khola river on the Tibetan side.
Experts caution against describing climate change as the sole, immediate trigger for Wednesday’s collapse, though they say that rising temperatures and melting glaciers probably played a role in the disaster.
Simon Cox, chief scientist at the Mountains to Sea programme at Earth Sciences New Zealand, said:
Climate change is generating conditions that can destabilise high-mountain rock and ice.
That in turn makes collapses and cascading hazards of the kind seen this week more frequent, he added.
summary: Devastating flash floods and mudslides triggered near the Nepal-China border have resulted in hundreds of confirmed deaths and left many people missing.
